means: Active-passive keeps a standby idle and fails over. Active-active serves from both and must resolve conflicting writes.
example: Active-passive is far simpler and wastes the standby's capacity. Active-active doubles usable capacity and forces you to answer 'what if both regions write the same row?'
diagram:
Active-passive: standby idle, promote on failure
  simple, RTO = failover time, capacity wasted

Active-active: both serve
  no failover delay, full capacity,
  conflict resolution is now YOUR problem

means: A translation layer between your model and an external or legacy one, so their concepts don't leak into your domain.
example: A payment provider's 20-field webhook payload is translated into your four-field PaymentResult at the boundary. Switching providers touches one adapter, not forty files.
diagram:
external model → [ ACL adapter ] → your model
                        ↑
        all provider quirks stop here

Without it, the vendor's schema becomes yours forever

means: A strategy for changing an API without breaking existing clients. Mobile apps you cannot force-update make this permanent, not optional.
example: An old app version stays in use for 18 months. Removing a field is a crash for those users, so v1 must keep working while v2 exists alongside it.
diagram:
URL:    /v1/orders, /v2/orders   (explicit, clear)
Header: Accept-Version               (clean URLs)
Field-level: additive only, never remove

Also decide: deprecation window, sunset headers,
             how you'll know who's still on v1

means: For work too slow for a request cycle: accept it, return a job ID immediately, and let the client poll or receive a callback.
example: A 4-minute document analysis behind a synchronous endpoint hits every gateway timeout. Returning 202 with a status URL makes the slowness a first-class part of the API.

means: An append-only record of who did what, when, and to which resource. Regulators and incident reviews both need it, and neither accepts 'we have application logs'.
example: 'Who changed this customer's credit limit in March?' is unanswerable from application logs. A dedicated immutable audit table with actor, action, target, before and after answers it.
diagram:
actor + action + target + timestamp
  + before/after + request id + ip

Append-only, separate store, own retention
Never mixed into debug logs (different lifecycle)

means: Availability multiplies across dependencies in series. Adding components lowers your ceiling unless they're redundant.
example: Three services each at 99.9% in a request path give 99.7% combined — 26 hours of downtime a year, not 8.7. Redundancy is what pushes it back up.
diagram:
99.9%   → 8.7 hrs/year
99.99%  → 52 min/year
99.999% → 5 min/year

In series:  0.999³ = 99.7%  (worse)
In parallel: 1-(0.001)² = 99.9999% (better)

means: Rough arithmetic done early to rule architectures in or out before you build anything. Being within an order of magnitude is the whole point.
example: 10M daily users × 20 requests = 200M/day ≈ 2,300 req/sec average. Peak at 3x is ~7,000/sec. That number alone tells you whether one database will do.
diagram:
DAU × actions/day = daily requests
÷ 86,400            = average req/sec
× peak factor (2-5x) = peak req/sec

2,300/s avg → 7,000/s peak
One Postgres? Maybe. One Postgres for writes? No.

means: Populating new columns or systems with historical data without taking production down. Volume makes the naive approach impossible.
example: One UPDATE across 80M rows locks the table and blows up replication lag. Batches of 5,000 with a pause, throttled on replica lag, takes hours and hurts nobody.
diagram:
UPDATE 80M rows → lock, WAL flood, replica lag ✗

loop: 5,000 rows → commit → sleep
      pause if replica lag > 5s
resumable (track last id), idempotent, observable

means: Backward compatible means new code reads old data. Forward compatible means old code tolerates new data — which is what makes rolling deploys safe.
example: During a rolling deploy both versions run at once. If the old version crashes on an unknown enum value, every deploy is a partial outage.
diagram:
Backward: new code reads old data ✓
Forward:  old code ignores unknown fields ✓
   ↓
Safe: add optional fields, add enum values
      that old code can ignore
Unsafe: rename, remove, retype, change semantics

means: A boundary within which a term has one unambiguous meaning. Two contexts can both have a 'Customer' and correctly mean different things.
example: In billing, a Customer has a tax ID and payment terms. In support, a Customer has a ticket history and a sentiment score. Forcing one shared model makes both worse.
diagram:
Billing:  Customer = tax id, terms, invoices
Support:  Customer = tickets, SLA tier, contacts
Shipping: Customer = addresses, delivery prefs

One shared "Customer" table serves none of them well

means: The gap between normal load and your breaking point. Running at 80% of capacity looks efficient and leaves no room to absorb a spike or a failed node.
example: A cluster at 85% CPU cannot survive one node loss — the survivors need 100%. Target 50-60% steady state so failure and traffic spikes are both absorbable.
diagram:
target steady state: 50-60%
  ↓ absorbs: 1 node loss, 2x spike,
             deploy overhead, GC pauses

85% steady state = one bad Tuesday from cascading

means: Choreography means services react to events with no central brain. Orchestration means one coordinator drives the steps. Choreography scales; orchestration is debuggable.
example: A 7-step order flow in pure choreography is impossible to trace when step 5 silently never fires. An orchestrator makes the state machine explicit and queryable.
diagram:
Choreography: A→event→B→event→C
  decoupled, no single owner,
  emergent behaviour nobody can draw

Orchestration: coordinator → A, B, C
  explicit state, easy to trace,
  coordinator becomes a dependency

means: Splitting a large upload into parts so a dropped connection resumes rather than restarts, and no single request holds 2GB.
example: A 2GB upload on mobile fails at 90% and restarts from zero. With 8MB chunks and a resume token, it continues from chunk 231.
diagram:
file → 8MB chunks
  upload each with an index + upload id
  server tracks received chunks
  drop → client asks "what's missing?" → resume ✓
  all received → assemble + verify checksum

means: Testing that a provider still satisfies what its consumers actually depend on, without spinning up both systems.
example: The provider's own tests pass while a field a consumer relies on gets renamed. A consumer-driven contract test fails in the provider's CI, before the deploy.
diagram:
consumer records its expectations → contract
provider's CI verifies the contract

Breaks in the PROVIDER's pipeline ✓
not in the consumer's production ✗

means: Coupling is how much modules depend on each other; cohesion is how related the things inside a module are. Good design maximises cohesion and minimises coupling.
example: A 'utils' module is low cohesion — nothing in it belongs together. Two services that must always deploy together are high coupling — they're really one service.
diagram:
High cohesion: everything in the module
               serves one purpose
Low coupling:  changing module A rarely
               forces a change in B

"These two always deploy together" = one service

means: OFFSET makes the database count and discard rows, so deep pages get slower and results shift as data changes. Cursors seek directly to a position.
example: `OFFSET 500000 LIMIT 20` scans half a million rows to throw them away. `WHERE (created_at, id) < (?, ?) LIMIT 20` uses the index and is constant time.
diagram:
OFFSET 500000 → scan + discard 500k rows ✗
  also: new rows shift pages, items duplicate/vanish

Cursor: WHERE (created_at, id) < (?, ?)
  constant time, stable ✓
  cost: no random page access

means: Modelling a pipeline as a directed acyclic graph of tasks with dependencies, so independent branches run in parallel and failures retry at task level.
example: A nightly pipeline of 40 sequential steps takes 6 hours. As a DAG, independent branches run in parallel and it finishes in 90 minutes — and a failed task retries alone.
diagram:
┌ extract_a ┐
start ┤             ├ join → transform → load
      └ extract_b ┘

Parallel where possible, retry per task,
backfill a single date range

means: Legal requirements that certain data physically stays in a jurisdiction. It constrains architecture before any technical consideration does.
example: If EU user data cannot leave the EU, a single global primary is illegal regardless of how well it performs. That shapes sharding, backups and even log routing.
diagram:
Constrains: primary location, replicas, backups,
            logs, analytics exports, support tooling

Usually forces regional sharding by user
Check before designing, not during audit

means: Deciding how long each class of data lives and how it's actually removed — including from backups, replicas, caches, logs and the warehouse.
example: Deleting a user row leaves them in nightly backups, the search index, the analytics warehouse and six months of logs. Crypto-shredding solves the backup problem.
diagram:
delete request → primary ✓ replicas ✓ cache ✓
              → search index ✓ warehouse ✓ logs ✓
              → backups ✗ (can't rewrite them)

Crypto-shredding: per-user key, destroy the key
                  → backup ciphertext is unreadable

term: Data Warehouse vs Data Lake vs Lakehouse
means: A warehouse stores structured, modelled data. A lake stores raw files of any shape. A lakehouse puts warehouse table semantics on top of lake storage.
example: Dumping everything into a lake with no catalog or schema produces a data swamp nobody can query. Table formats like Iceberg or Delta are what prevent that.
diagram:
Lake:      raw files, cheap, schema-on-read
Warehouse: modelled tables, fast, schema-on-write
Lakehouse: lake storage + ACID table format
           (Iceberg / Delta / Hudi)

Lake with no governance = swamp

means: Each service owns its schema and no other service reads it directly. It's the boundary that makes microservices real rather than a distributed monolith.
example: Two services sharing a table means neither can change its schema alone — you've paid the microservice cost and kept the monolith's coupling.
diagram:
Shared DB: service B reads A's tables
  → A cannot change its schema ✗
  → distributed monolith

Own DB: access only via A's API/events ✓
  cost: no joins across services, eventual consistency

means: Collecting individual per-item lookups within one tick and issuing them as a single batched query. The standard fix for GraphQL's N+1 problem.
example: A query resolving 50 posts each fetching an author issues 51 queries. A DataLoader collapses the 50 author lookups into one `WHERE id IN (...)`.
diagram:
resolver calls load(1), load(2), ... load(50)
  ↓ batched within the same tick
one query: WHERE id IN (1..50)
  ↓ results distributed back

51 queries → 2. Also dedupes repeated ids.

means: Deliberately duplicating data to avoid joins on a hot read path. You trade write complexity and consistency risk for read speed.
example: A feed query joining five tables takes 400ms. Storing a precomputed feed row takes 8ms — and now every author name change must fan out to those rows.
diagram:
5-way join → 400ms
precomputed row → 8ms ✓

Cost: writes fan out, data can drift
Rule: denormalise for a MEASURED read problem,
      never pre-emptively

means: Generating unique IDs across many nodes without coordination. Random UUIDv4 destroys index locality; time-ordered IDs preserve it.
example: Switching a high-insert table from UUIDv4 to UUIDv7 cut index bloat sharply — inserts append to the right edge of the B-tree instead of scattering across it.
diagram:
UUIDv4:  random → every insert a random B-tree page ✗
UUIDv7 / ULID / Snowflake:
  [ timestamp | node | sequence ]
  → sortable, append-friendly, still unique ✓

Auto-increment: ordered, but needs coordination

means: Encrypting data with a per-object data key, then encrypting that key with a master key held in a KMS. Rotating the master key doesn't require re-encrypting the data.
example: 10TB encrypted with 4M data keys. Rotating the master key re-wraps 4M small keys instead of rewriting 10TB of ciphertext.
diagram:
data → encrypted with data key (DEK)
DEK  → encrypted with master key (KEK, in KMS)
stored: ciphertext + wrapped DEK

Rotate KEK → re-wrap DEKs only, data untouched

means: ETL transforms before loading; ELT loads raw and transforms inside the warehouse. ELT won because storage got cheap and warehouses got fast.
example: With ELT the raw data is retained, so when the transform logic turns out to be wrong you re-run it. With ETL, the pre-transform data is gone.
diagram:
ETL: extract → transform → load (raw discarded)
ELT: extract → load raw → transform in-warehouse ✓
                  ↑
      bad transform? re-run it. Raw is still there.

means: Moving data to cheaper, slower storage as it ages, because access frequency drops far faster than data volume.
example: Last 30 days on SSD, 30-365 days on object storage, older in archive. Storage cost drops by an order of magnitude and 95% of queries never notice.
diagram:
0-30d    SSD / hot         ← 95% of queries
30-365d  object storage     ← occasional
1y+      archive (glacier)  ← audit only

Define the retrieval SLA per tier BEFORE moving data

means: A map from term to the list of documents containing it. It's what makes full-text search fast, and why search engines are not databases.
example: Finding 'payment failed' across 40M documents by scanning is impossible. An inverted index intersects two posting lists and returns in milliseconds.
diagram:
"payment" → [doc 3, 91, 402, ...]
"failed"  → [doc 91, 402, 8871, ...]
             ↓ intersect
          [91, 402]

Then score by relevance (BM25) and rank

means: Scheduled work needs the same rigour as request handling: what happens on overlap, on missed runs, on partial failure, and when two instances both fire.
example: A cron running on every replica fires six times. One that takes 70 minutes on a 60-minute schedule overlaps itself. Both are silent until they corrupt something.
diagram:
Decide explicitly:
  overlap?   → lock, or skip if still running
  missed?    → catch up, or skip
  duplicate? → leader election / distributed lock
  partial?   → idempotent + resumable
  visible?   → alert on "didn't run", not just "failed"

means: B-trees update in place — good for reads, random writes. LSM trees append to memory then flush sorted files — excellent write throughput, reads may check several files.
example: Postgres uses B-trees; Cassandra, RocksDB and LevelDB use LSM. A write-heavy time-series workload on a B-tree thrashes; on an LSM it's sequential.
diagram:
B-tree: in-place update, random I/O,
        fast reads, slower writes
LSM:    memtable → flush → sorted files
        sequential writes ✓, reads check many files,
        needs compaction

means: Turning an uploaded original into the derivatives you serve — thumbnails, transcodes, previews — asynchronously, because it's slow and CPU-heavy.
example: Generating five thumbnail sizes inline makes upload take 12 seconds. Uploading raw, returning immediately, and processing off a queue makes it feel instant.
diagram:
upload original → S3 → event → queue
  ↓ workers
thumbnails, transcodes, OCR, virus scan
  ↓ write derivative locations
UI shows a placeholder until ready

Keep the original. Derivatives are re-derivable.

means: One deployable with hard internal module boundaries. You get most of the design discipline of microservices without the distributed-systems tax.
example: Modules communicate only through published interfaces, each owns its tables, and no module imports another's internals. Extracting one into a service later is then mechanical.
diagram:
single deploy
 ├ module: billing   (owns billing_* tables)
 ├ module: catalog   (owns catalog_* tables)
 └ module: identity

Cross-module access only via public interface
→ extract to a service when a team needs it

means: Microservices buy independent deployment and scaling, and cost you network failure, distributed transactions and operational overhead. Most teams pay before they need the benefit.
example: Six engineers running eleven services spend more time on service plumbing than on product. The same team on a modular monolith ships faster and can split later.
diagram:
Monolith:      1 deploy, in-process calls, easy txns
Microservices: independent deploys + scaling
               distributed txns, network failure,
               tracing, service discovery, versioning

The split is justified by TEAM boundaries,
not by code size.

means: Running in more than one region for latency or survivability. The hard part is never the compute — it's the data.
example: Stateless services in three regions is a weekend. Deciding what happens to writes when regions can't reach each other is the actual multi-region project.
diagram:
Easy:  stateless compute in N regions
Hard:  where do writes go?
       what's the conflict resolution?
       what's the failover data loss (RPO)?
       what does data residency law require?

means: Whether tenants share infrastructure. Pooled is cheap and risks cross-tenant leakage; siloed is isolated and expensive; bridge splits the difference.
example: Pooled with a tenant_id column costs one missing WHERE clause to leak data. Schema-per-tenant makes leakage structurally harder and complicates migrations across 4,000 schemas.
diagram:
Pool:   shared tables + tenant_id
        cheapest, one bug = leak, noisy neighbours
Bridge: shared cluster, schema/db per tenant
Silo:   separate stack per tenant
        strongest isolation, highest cost

Enterprise tier often BUYS the silo

means: One tenant's load degrading everyone else's experience on shared infrastructure.
example: One customer's bulk import consumes the entire connection pool and every other tenant sees timeouts. Per-tenant quotas and separate queues contain it.
diagram:
tenant A: bulk import ████████████████
tenant B: ▏ starved
tenant C: ▏ starved

Fix: per-tenant rate limits, separate queues,
     fair scheduling, dedicated pools for big accounts

means: Fan-out to email, push, SMS and in-app with per-user preferences, deduplication, batching and quiet hours. Deceptively large.
example: 'Send an email on comment' becomes: don't notify the author of their own comment, batch 30 comments into one digest, respect quiet hours, and never send twice on retry.
diagram:
event → preference check → channel routing
      → dedupe window → batching/digest
      → quiet hours → rate cap per user
      → provider (with fallback) → delivery tracking

The fan-out is easy. The suppression rules are the system.

means: Money needs an append-only, double-entry ledger — never a mutable balance column. The balance is derived, and every change has a traceable cause.
example: `UPDATE balance SET amount = amount - 500` loses all history and races. Two ledger entries that must sum to zero are auditable and reconcilable.
diagram:
Never: UPDATE balance SET amount = amount - 500

Ledger (append-only, immutable):
  entry 1: account A  -500
  entry 2: account B  +500
  ↓ must sum to zero
balance = SUM(entries), or a cached snapshot

means: Counting usage per tenant for both enforcement and billing. It must be accurate enough to invoice and cheap enough to run on every request.
example: Counting in-process gives wrong totals across replicas. Counting synchronously in Postgres adds a write to every request. Redis counters flushed periodically is the usual compromise.
diagram:
per request: INCR in Redis (fast, approximate)
periodically: flush to durable store (billable truth)

Decide: hard limit or soft?
        overage billed or blocked?
        what happens if the counter store is down?

means: Role-based grants permissions to named roles. Attribute-based evaluates a policy over attributes of the user, resource and context. RBAC is simple until roles explode.
example: 'Managers can approve expenses under ₹50,000 in their own department during business hours' is one ABAC policy, or a combinatorial explosion of RBAC roles.
diagram:
RBAC: user → role → permissions
  simple, auditable, roles multiply

ABAC: policy over (user, resource, action, context)
  expressive, harder to audit and debug
  "who can access X?" becomes a search problem

means: Sending reads to replicas to scale read capacity, while accepting that replicas lag. Which reads may be stale is a product decision.
example: Analytics and list views go to replicas. Anything read immediately after a write by the same user must go to the primary, or their own change appears to vanish.
diagram:
writes → primary
reads:
  ├ dashboards, lists, search → replica ✓
  └ read-after-write, balances → primary ✓

Route by query intent, not by load

means: REST is simple and cacheable. GraphQL lets clients ask for exactly what they need and moves complexity server-side. gRPC is fast and typed and awkward from browsers.
example: A mobile client over-fetching 40 fields to render 6 is a GraphQL case. High-volume internal service-to-service calls are a gRPC case. A public API is usually REST.
diagram:
REST:    cacheable, simple, over/under-fetching
GraphQL: precise fetching, one endpoint,
         caching + rate limiting get hard, N+1 risk
gRPC:    binary, typed, streaming, fast
         needs a proxy for browsers

Public API → REST. Internal high-volume → gRPC.

means: RPO is how much data you can afford to lose; RTO is how long you can afford to be down. They drive completely different investments.
example: RPO of 5 minutes means continuous WAL shipping, not nightly backups. RTO of 5 minutes means a warm standby, not a restore-from-S3 procedure.
diagram:
RPO 24h / RTO 8h  → nightly backup, manual restore
RPO 5m  / RTO 8h  → WAL shipping + manual promote
RPO 5m  / RTO 5m  → hot standby, automated failover
RPO 0   / RTO 0   → active-active, expensive

means: A central store of message schemas with enforced compatibility rules, so a producer literally cannot publish a breaking change.
example: A producer tries to remove a required field. The registry rejects the schema at publish time, instead of 40 consumers discovering it at 2am.
diagram:
producer → register schema
  registry checks compatibility (BACKWARD/FULL)
  incompatible → REJECTED at publish time ✓

Without it, the contract is tribal knowledge

means: Search is a separate system fed from your primary store, not a query against it. That means an indexing pipeline, a lag window and a reconciliation job.
example: Writing to Postgres and OpenSearch in the same request is a dual write that will drift. Feeding the index from CDC gives you a single source of truth and a measurable lag.
diagram:
Postgres (truth) → CDC → indexer → OpenSearch
                                       ↓
                                  query path

Always: measure index lag,
        run a periodic full reconcile

means: Sending a copy of real production traffic to a new system without using its responses. Real load, real data shapes, zero user risk.
example: The new search service handles a mirrored 100% of queries for two weeks. Results are diffed against the old one; nothing is served until the diff rate is near zero.
diagram:
request → old system → response to user ✓
        └→ new system → response DISCARDED
                        ↓ compare + record diffs

Watch for: duplicated side effects.
Shadow reads are safe; shadow writes are not.

means: Soft delete flags a row as deleted; hard delete removes it. Soft delete is recoverable and quietly leaks deleted data into every query that forgets the filter.
example: A `deleted_at IS NULL` filter missing from one report exposes deleted records. And soft delete is not compliant with a legal deletion request — the data is still there.
diagram:
Soft: recoverable, keeps FKs valid,
      every query must filter, table grows
Hard: gone, clean, unrecoverable

Legal erasure request → hard delete or crypto-shred.
"deleted_at" does not satisfy a deletion right.

means: Replacing a sensitive value with a meaningless reference, keeping the real value in a separate vault. It shrinks the systems in scope for compliance.
example: Storing a token instead of a card number takes your application out of PCI scope. Only the vault holds real card data, and only it needs the strictest controls.
diagram:
card 4111... → vault → token tok_9f2c

App stores the token. Vault holds the value.
Compliance scope shrinks to the vault.
Unlike encryption, the token has no math link to the value.

means: Delivering events to someone else's HTTP endpoint. You now own retries, ordering, signing and the fact that their server will be down.
example: A receiver returning 500 for six hours needs exponential retries, a dead-letter path, and signed payloads so they can verify the call really came from you.
diagram:
POST + HMAC signature + timestamp (replay window)
  → 2xx? done
  → else retry: 1m, 5m, 30m, 2h, 6h → disable + alert

Give receivers: an event id (dedupe),
                a replay endpoint, a delivery log

means: Changing a schema in phases so old and new code both work throughout, because during a rolling deploy both are running.
example: Renaming a column in one step breaks whichever version is mid-deploy. Expand-contract takes four releases and never breaks anything.
diagram:
1. add new column (nullable)
2. dual-write both, backfill old rows
3. switch reads to new, verify
4. stop writing old, then drop it

Four boring releases beat one exciting outage

means: Traffic arriving faster than you can process it, and the system deliberately pushing back instead of silently piling up.
example: Flash sale: 500,000 checkout hits in 10 seconds, capacity is 10,000/sec. The system queues, sheds, or slows accepts. Without backpressure the queue grows until memory dies.
diagram:
Arrival: ████████████████████
Capacity: ████████
              ↓
    Queue → Delay → Shed load
    (signal the producer to slow down)

means: Writing up an incident to fix the system, not to identify who to punish. Blame makes people hide information, which makes the next outage worse.
example: 'Engineer ran the wrong migration' becomes 'Migrations run against prod with no confirmation prompt and no dry-run.' The second version generates fixes.
diagram:
Blame:     who did it → hiding → repeat
Blameless: what allowed it → guardrail

Output = action items with owners,
not a name

means: How much of the system (or how many users) a single failure can take down. Every architecture decision either grows or shrinks it.
example: One shared DB for all tenants: blast radius = everyone. Sharded per region: blast radius = one region. Canary at 5%: blast radius = 5%.
diagram:
Shared everything → 100% of users
Per-region shard   → 1 region
Cell architecture  → 1 cell
Canary 5%          → 5%

means: Two identical production environments. Deploy to the idle one, verify, then flip all traffic at the load balancer. Rollback is another flip.
example: Blue serves live traffic. v2 goes to green, smoke tests pass, the LB switches. A bad release is undone in seconds instead of a redeploy.
diagram:
LB
       │ (flip)
  ┌────┴────┐
BLUE v1   GREEN v2
 live      idle → tested → live

Rollback = flip back

means: Isolate resources per dependency so one slow thing can't drink the whole pool. Named after ship compartments.
example: One shared 50-connection pool. The reporting DB hangs, 50 threads block on it, and login breaks too. With bulkheads: reporting gets 10 connections, auth gets 20 — reporting dies alone.
diagram:
Shared pool:    [50] → reporting hangs → all dead
Bulkheaded:
  auth      [20]  ✓ still serving
  reporting [10]  ✗ contained
  search    [20]  ✓ still serving

means: How fast you are consuming the error budget relative to normal. The alert that actually pages people.
example: Burn rate 1x means you'd exactly use the budget by month end. Burn rate 14.4x means the whole monthly budget is gone in two hours — page immediately.
diagram:
1x    → on track, no alert
6x     → budget gone in 5 days → ticket
14.4x  → budget gone in 2 hrs  → page now

Alert on burn rate, not raw error count

means: The thundering herd applied to caches, plus the fix: only one caller recomputes while everyone else waits or serves stale.
example: Instead of 8,000 recomputes, the first miss takes a lock and refreshes; the other 7,999 get the slightly stale value. One DB query instead of 8,000.
diagram:
Miss → acquire lock?
  YES → recompute → store → serve
  NO  → serve stale / wait for holder

1 recompute, not 8000

means: Release new code to a small slice of traffic first, watch the metrics, then expand.
example: New recommendation model goes to 5% of users. Error rate and latency hold for 20 minutes, so it rolls to 100%. If it had spiked, only 5% were affected.
diagram:
v2 → 5% traffic → observe 20 min
       ↓ healthy        ↓ regression
    25% → 100%        rollback
                     (5% blast radius)

means: Deliberately injecting failure in production-like conditions to verify your resilience actually works before reality tests it.
example: You kill a random pod during business hours to confirm the failover you designed a year ago still fires. Half the time, it doesn't.
diagram:
Hypothesis: killing 1 replica = no user impact
   ↓ inject failure
   ↓ measure SLI
Matched?  → confidence earned
Diverged? → you just found a bug for free

means: Stops your system from repeatedly calling a service that is already failing. Like a fuse — it trips before everything burns.
example: Payment API starts failing. Without a breaker the app retries endlessly and takes the whole process down. With one, failures are counted, the breaker opens, and a fallback is served.
diagram:
CLOSED  → calls pass, failures counted
   ↓ threshold hit
OPEN    → fail fast, no calls made
   ↓ cool-down elapsed
HALF-OPEN → let 1 probe through
   ↓ success        ↓ failure
 CLOSED           OPEN

means: Extra delay when a server, container or function starts from scratch after being idle.
example: A Lambda sits idle 30 minutes. Next request loads the runtime, imports dependencies, loads the model. User waits 6s instead of 0.3s.
diagram:
Request arrives
  ↓ load runtime
  ↓ load dependencies
  ↓ load model
  ↓ init connections
Response (finally) — 6s

means: How much failure you're allowed before breaching the SLO. It converts reliability into a currency the team can spend on shipping speed.
example: 99.9% monthly SLO = 43 minutes of downtime allowed. A week-1 incident burns 20. With 23 left, the team freezes risky deploys until the window resets.
diagram:
Budget: 43 min/month
  incident −20 min
  remaining 23 min
     ↓
healthy budget → ship fast
burnt budget   → freeze, fix reliability

means: The thing message brokers cannot actually give you over a network. What you get is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing, which behaves like exactly-once.
example: RabbitMQ redelivers a message after a consumer crashes post-work, pre-ack. The work runs twice. Only your dedupe table makes the outcome once.
diagram:
At-most-once  → may lose
At-least-once → may duplicate  ← reality
Exactly-once  → at-least-once
                + idempotent consumer

means: Wait longer after each failed retry, with randomness added so clients don't all retry on the same tick.
example: 1000 clients fail at the same instant. Fixed backoff means 1000 retries hit at exactly t+1s — a synchronized wave. Jitter spreads them randomly across the window.
diagram:
No jitter:  ▮        ▮        ▮   (thundering)
Jitter:     ▪ ▪  ▪ ▪▪   ▪  ▪ ▪   (spread)

sleep = random(0, base * 2^attempt)

means: Turn behaviour on or off without redeploying. Separates deploy (shipping code) from release (exposing it).
example: New summarisation feature ships behind a flag that is off. On for internal team, bugs fixed, on for 10%, then 100%. No deployment at any step.
diagram:
Deploy code (flag OFF) — nobody sees it
  ↓ internal ON  → dogfood
  ↓ 10% ON       → watch metrics
  ↓ 100% ON      → released
Kill switch = flip OFF, zero deploys

means: The reality that database changes usually can't be rolled back with the code. Schema changes must be backward compatible so old and new code can both run.
example: Dropping a column in the same release that stops using it breaks rollback instantly. Instead: stop writing it (release 1), drop it (release 2, a week later).
diagram:
✗ one release: stop using + DROP COLUMN
✓ release 1: stop writing, keep column
✓ release 2: verify unused
✓ release 3: DROP COLUMN

Expand → migrate → contract

means: Losing a feature instead of losing the product when a dependency fails.
example: The recommendation service dies. Instead of a 500 on the homepage, the page renders with a static bestsellers list. Users notice worse suggestions, not an outage.
diagram:
Recommender ✗
   ↓
Homepage still renders
Personalised rail → static bestsellers
   ↓
Feature lost, product alive

means: One slow item at the front of a queue stalls everything behind it, even work that would have been instant.
example: A single 400-page PDF sits at the head of the OCR queue for 9 minutes. Two thousand one-page invoices behind it wait, though each takes 200ms.
diagram:
[400-page PDF ▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓ 9 min][1pg][1pg][1pg]
  ↑ everything behind waits

Fix: separate queues by size class

means: Send a duplicate request to a second replica once the first is slower than P95, then take whichever answers first.
example: Read P99 drops from 1.8s to 240ms by sending a second copy after 100ms. Costs ~5% extra traffic because you only hedge the slow tail.
diagram:
t=0    → replica A
t=95ms → still waiting
t=95ms → also ask replica B
t=140  → B answers → use it, cancel A

+5% load, -85% tail

means: Doing the same operation N times leaves the system in the same state as doing it once. The single most important property for anything involving money or messages.
example: User clicks "Pay ₹500", network hiccups, client retries. Without idempotency: ₹1000 charged. With an idempotency key: the server recognises the key, returns the original result, charges ₹500 once.
diagram:
POST /pay  Idempotency-Key: abc123
   ↓
Key seen before?
  NO  → charge ₹500 → store result
  YES → return stored result (no charge)

means: A client-generated unique ID attached to a mutating request so the server can dedupe retries. Stored with the result, usually for 24h.
example: Stripe requires one on every charge. Your mobile app generates a UUID per checkout attempt and reuses it across all retries of that same attempt — new attempt, new key.
diagram:
Client generates UUID per intent
   ↓
Server: INSERT key ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
   ↓
Inserted? → do the work, save response
Conflict? → replay saved response

means: Rate limiting that smooths instead of bursting. Requests drain at a fixed rate no matter how they arrive.
example: 200 requests arrive in one second against a 10/sec leak. They queue and drain evenly over 20 seconds. Downstream sees a perfectly flat line.
diagram:
in (bursty)  ▮▮▮▮▮▮▮▮▮▮▮▮
                  │
               ┌──▼──┐
               │     │ ← queue absorbs the burst
               │     │   full? → drop
               └──┬──┘
                  ▼ fixed 10/s
out               ▪  ▪  ▪  ▪  ▪  ▪

means: Deliberately dropping low-value requests to keep high-value ones alive under overload.
example: During a spike, the API rejects analytics writes and prefetch calls with 503, but keeps checkout and login at full speed. Revenue traffic survives.
diagram:
Overload detected
   ↓
Drop: prefetch, analytics, recommendations
Keep: login, checkout, payments
   ↓
Degraded, but alive

sub: Mean time to recovery / between failures
means: MTTR is how fast you recover; MTBF is how rarely you break. Mature teams optimise MTTR harder, because you cannot prevent all failure.
example: Team A: fails once a quarter, takes 6 hours to fix. Team B: fails weekly, recovers in 4 minutes. Team B has far better availability.
diagram:
A: MTBF 90d, MTTR 6h  → 99.72%
B: MTBF  7d, MTTR 4m  → 99.96%

Fast recovery beats rare failure

means: Different percentiles answer different questions. P50 is the typical user, P95 is your unhappy tail, P99.9 is the one whale customer whose CEO emails yours.
example: A dashboard alerting on P50 stayed green for six weeks while P99 tripled. The retry storm was only visible above P95.
diagram:
P50   → typical user      → product feel
P95   → unhappy tail      → SLO target
P99   → worst 1%          → churn signal
P99.9 → your biggest acct → escalation

means: Capping how many requests a caller can make in a time window, so one client can't starve everyone else.
example: API allows 100 req/min per key. Request 101 gets 429 with a Retry-After header. Your DB never sees the flood.
diagram:
Limit 100/min
Req 1–100 → 200 OK
Req 101+  → 429 + Retry-After: 23
Window rolls → counter resets

means: Retries meant to help end up destroying the system. Every layer multiplies the load on a service that was only slightly sick.
example: DB slows down 20%. Service A retries 5x, B retries 5x, C retries 5x. Traffic multiplies 15x. The DB, which would have recovered on its own, collapses.
diagram:
DB: slightly slow
  A → ×5   B → ×5   C → ×5
             ↓
       traffic × 15
             ↓
        DB dies

means: Replace instances a few at a time so capacity never drops to zero. The default in Kubernetes.
example: 12 pods, maxSurge 2, maxUnavailable 1. New pods come up and pass readiness before old ones are killed. During the roll, both versions serve traffic — your API must tolerate that.
diagram:
[v1][v1][v1][v1]
[v2][v1][v1][v1]
[v2][v2][v1][v1]
[v2][v2][v2][v2]

Both versions live mid-roll

means: The actual measurement your SLO is defined on. Vague SLOs fail because nobody agreed on the SLI.
example: 'The API is fast' is not an SLI. 'Proportion of GET /search requests returning 200 in under 400ms, measured at the load balancer' is.
diagram:
SLI = good events / valid events

good  = status 2xx AND latency < 400ms
valid = all GET /search (excl. health checks)
measured at = load balancer, 1-min buckets

means: Rate limiting that avoids the boundary bug in fixed windows, where a client sneaks 2x the limit across the reset line.
example: Fixed window of 100/min: 100 requests at 11:59:59 and 100 at 12:00:01 = 200 in two seconds, both 'legal'. A sliding window weights the previous window and blocks it.
diagram:
Fixed:   [100]|[100]  → 200 in 2s ✗
Sliding: weighted overlap
         count = prev*0.9 + curr
         → correctly rejects

means: Your internal target, always stricter than the SLA. The SLA is the floor; the SLO is where you aim so you never touch the floor.
example: SLA to customers is 99.9%. Team SLO is 99.95%. The gap is your safety buffer. Aim exactly at the SLA and you will breach it regularly.
diagram:
SLO 99.95%  ← team targets here
SLA 99.90%  ← customers hold you here
       ↑
   safety buffer

means: Fanning out to many services makes slow responses near-certain. If each call has a 1% chance of being slow, 100 parallel calls are almost guaranteed to contain one.
example: A page fans out to 100 microservices, each with P99 = 1s. The chance all 100 are fast is 0.99^100 ≈ 37%. So 63% of page loads hit at least one 1s call.
diagram:
1 call:   99% fast
100 calls: 0.99^100 = 37% all fast
   ↓
63% of pages hit the tail
Fix: hedged requests, fewer fan-outs

means: Many clients wake up and hit the same resource at exactly the same moment.
example: A popular cache key expires at 12:00:00. In that instant 8,000 in-flight requests all miss and all query the database for the identical row.
diagram:
Key expires at 12:00:00
   ↓
8000 concurrent misses
   ↓
8000 identical DB queries
   ↓
DB CPU 100%

means: Each layer in a call chain gets a slice of the caller's remaining time, so nothing waits longer than the user already has.
example: Gateway timeout is 3s. It passes 2.8s to the service, which passes 2.5s to the DB. Without budgets, a 30s DB timeout keeps working on a request the user abandoned 27 seconds ago.
diagram:
User 3.0s
 └ Gateway  2.8s
    └ Service 2.5s
       └ DB    2.0s

Deadline propagates down the chain

means: The rate-limit algorithm that allows bursts. Tokens refill at a steady rate; each request spends one; an empty bucket means rejection.
example: Bucket holds 100 tokens, refills 10/sec. An idle client can burst 100 requests instantly, then is throttled to 10/sec. Feels generous and still protects you.
diagram:
Bucket [██████████] cap 100
refill +10/sec
request → take 1 token
empty?  → 429

Allows burst, enforces average

means: The single entry point in front of your services: auth, rate limiting, routing, request shaping.
example: Mobile clients hit one gateway. It validates the JWT once, applies per-key rate limits, and routes to six internal services that no longer need their own auth code.
diagram:
Client → Gateway
          ├ authn/authz
          ├ rate limit
          ├ route
          └ aggregate
       → internal services

means: A dedicated gateway per client type, so a mobile app isn't forced to consume an API shaped for a web dashboard.
example: Web needs 40 fields; mobile needs 6 and is on a slow connection. One shared endpoint over-fetches for mobile. Two BFFs let each shape its own payload.
diagram:
Web app    → Web BFF    → services
Mobile app → Mobile BFF → services

Each BFF owns its own aggregation shape

means: During a network partition, you choose consistency or availability. You never get to skip the partition — networks fail.
example: Two data centres lose their link. A CP system rejects writes on the minority side to stay correct. An AP system accepts them and reconciles later, risking conflicts.
diagram:
Partition happens (not optional)
   ↓
CP → reject writes, stay correct
AP → accept writes, reconcile later

'CA' is not a real production choice

means: Streaming a database's write-ahead log as events, so downstream systems learn about changes without polling or dual writes.
example: Debezium tails the Postgres WAL and publishes every row change to Kafka. Search index, cache and analytics warehouse all update from one source of truth.
diagram:
Postgres WAL
   ↓ Debezium
Kafka topic (row changes)
   ├→ search index
   ├→ cache invalidation
   └→ analytics warehouse

means: Different machines disagree about the current time. Any logic that compares timestamps across servers is quietly wrong.
example: Two nodes' clocks differ by 400ms. 'Last write wins' by timestamp silently discards the newer write. Use logical clocks or a single sequencer instead.
diagram:
Node A clock: 12:00:00.000
Node B clock: 11:59:59.600
   ↓
last-write-wins picks the wrong one
Fix: logical clocks, version vectors, DB sequence

means: Mapping keys to nodes on a ring so adding or removing a node only remaps 1/N of keys, not all of them.
example: With `hash % N`, going from 8 to 9 cache nodes invalidates ~89% of keys at once. With consistent hashing, only ~11% move.
diagram:
0°
       node A ●
            ╱   ╲
   key k → ●     ● node B
           │     │
   node D  ●     ● node C
            ╲   ╱
              ●
each key walks clockwise to the next node

add node E → only keys between D and E move
hash % N   → 8→9 nodes remaps 89% ✗
the ring   → 8→9 nodes remaps 11% ✓

means: Separating the write model from the read model so each can be shaped for its own job.
example: Writes go to a normalised Postgres schema. Reads come from a denormalised Elasticsearch projection built from the write stream. Read latency drops; you now own the sync lag.
diagram:
Command → write model (normalised)
              ↓ events
Query   ← read model (denormalised)

Faster reads, eventual consistency between them

means: A lock held in shared storage so only one process across the fleet does something. Correct only with a TTL and a fencing token.
example: A Redis lock with SET NX PX 30000 prevents two workers from processing the same file. Without a TTL, a crashed holder blocks the job forever.
diagram:
SET lock:job1 <uuid> NX PX 30000
  acquired? → do work → DEL if uuid matches
  no?       → skip

No TTL = deadlock on crash
No token = zombie writes

means: Storing the sequence of changes as the source of truth, and deriving current state by replaying them. Powerful, and heavier than teams expect.
example: Instead of an `balance = 400` row, you store Deposited 500, Withdrew 100. You get a perfect audit log and time travel — and every schema change becomes a replay problem.
diagram:
Events (immutable, append-only)
  Deposited 500
  Withdrew  100
     ↓ fold
  State: balance 400

Rebuild any past state by replaying

means: Replicas converge to the same value if writes stop. Between write and convergence, different readers can see different truths.
example: User updates their avatar. Replica in Mumbai shows the new one instantly; the read replica in Frankfurt shows the old one for 300ms. Fine for avatars, not for account balances.
diagram:
t=0    write to primary
t=0ms  replica A: new ✓
t=300  replica B: old  ← stale read window
t=310  replica B: new ✓ converged

means: Precompute results for every consumer at write time, or compute per request at read time. The classic timeline problem.
example: A celebrity with 50M followers posts. Fan-out on write means 50M inserts for one action. Fan-out on read means 50M timeline queries. Real systems do both, split by follower count.
diagram:
Write fan-out: 1 post → 50M feed rows
  fast reads, brutal celebrity writes
Read fan-out: query followed authors at load
  cheap writes, slow reads
Hybrid: normal users write, celebs read

means: A monotonically increasing number handed out with a lock, so a resumed zombie process can be rejected as stale.
example: Node A holds a lock, GC-pauses for 20s, loses the lease. Node B takes it with token 34. Node A wakes and writes with token 33 — storage rejects it.
diagram:
A acquires lock → token 33
A pauses (GC)
B acquires lock → token 34 → writes ✓
A wakes, writes token 33 → REJECTED ✓

means: One shard receiving disproportionate traffic because the partition key isn't uniformly distributed.
example: Sharding events by `tenant_id` looks fine until one enterprise customer produces 60% of all events. That shard saturates while the other 15 idle.
diagram:
shard 0  ████████████████ 60% (BigCorp)
shard 1  ██
shard 2  █
   ↓
Fix: composite key tenant_id + bucket

means: Picking exactly one node to coordinate, and detecting fast when it dies. Every 'only one worker should do this' problem is this problem.
example: Three schedulers run; without election all three fire the same cron. With a lease in Redis or etcd, only the lease holder runs and the others stand by.
diagram:
3 schedulers, 1 lease key
  A holds lease → runs cron
  B, C          → standby
A dies → lease expires (10s) → B takes over

means: Writing your domain change and the event to publish in the same DB transaction, then relaying the event separately. Removes the dual-write bug.
example: Naively: save the order, then publish to RabbitMQ. The broker call fails and the order exists with no event. With an outbox both writes commit atomically and a relay drains the table.
diagram:
BEGIN
  INSERT order
  INSERT outbox(event)
COMMIT              ← atomic
   ↓
relay polls outbox → publish → mark sent

means: Requiring a majority for reads and writes so the two sets always overlap by at least one node holding the latest value.
example: N=3 replicas, W=2, R=2. Any read touches at least one node that saw the last write. Setting W=1, R=1 is fast and returns stale data.
diagram:
N=5   [1][2][3][4][5]
W=3   [1][2][3]
R=3         [3][4][5]
             ↑ overlap guaranteed

R + W >  N  → 3+3 > 5 ✓ read sees the last write
R + W <= N  → 2+2 < 5 ✗ read can miss it

W up → durability.  R up → freshness.

means: The weakest guarantee users actually notice: after I write something, I must see it. Someone else seeing it late is fine.
example: User edits a comment, is routed to a read replica, and their own edit vanishes. Fix: pin that user's session to the primary for a few seconds after writing.
diagram:
Write → primary
Read  → replica (lagging) → old value ✗

Fix: sticky read-from-primary window
     or pass a write timestamp/LSN

means: How far behind a replica is from the primary, measured in time or bytes. It's zero in the design doc and never zero in production.
example: A batch job writes 2M rows. Replica lag climbs to 45 seconds. Every read-replica query for the next minute returns stale data, and dashboards show 'missing' orders.
diagram:
Primary  LSN 9,000,412
Replica  LSN 8,997,001
   ↓
lag = 45 sec

Alert on lag, not just on replica 'up'

means: Replacing a distributed transaction with a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action to undo it.
example: Book flight → charge card → reserve hotel. Hotel fails, so you run 'refund card' then 'cancel flight'. There's no rollback, only compensation.
diagram:
T1 flight ✓ → T2 charge ✓ → T3 hotel ✗
              ↓ compensate backwards
C2 refund ✓ ← C1 cancel flight ✓

Eventually consistent, never atomic

means: How a service finds the current network address of another, when instances come and go constantly.
example: Hardcoded IPs break the moment autoscaling replaces a pod. Kubernetes DNS resolves `payments.prod.svc` to whatever healthy pods exist right now.
diagram:
Instance starts → registers (or gets Endpoint)
Caller asks registry/DNS → healthy addresses
Instance dies → deregistered

Hardcoded IPs = guaranteed 3am page

means: The control plane that configures all those sidecars centrally: traffic policy, mTLS, retries and observability across every service.
example: Istio lets you shift 10% of traffic to v2 and enforce mTLS everywhere from one config, instead of changing 40 codebases.
diagram:
Control plane (policy, certs, routing)
   ↓ configures
[sidecar][sidecar][sidecar]
   ↓
Uniform retries, mTLS, traffic splits
Cost: real operational complexity

means: Splitting data horizontally across independent databases by a key, so no single node holds everything.
example: Users are sharded by `hash(user_id) % 16`. Each shard holds ~6% of the data. Cross-shard queries — 'all orders last month' — become genuinely hard.
diagram:
hash(user_id) % 16 → shard
  shard 0  users A, D, K...
  shard 15 users B, F, Z...

Easy: single-user reads
Hard: joins, global aggregates, resharding

means: Running a helper container alongside your app in the same pod to handle cross-cutting concerns like mTLS, retries and telemetry.
example: Envoy sits next to every service. Your Node app makes a plain HTTP call; the sidecar adds mutual TLS, retries and tracing headers without a line of app code.
diagram:
┌──────── Pod ────────┐
│  app  ↔  sidecar    │ → network
│           (Envoy)   │
└─────────────────────┘
mTLS, retries, tracing — outside your code

means: A partition leaves two nodes each believing they are the primary. Both accept writes; the data diverges irreconcilably.
example: Network blips between two DB nodes. Both promote themselves. For 40 seconds each takes writes. Merging afterwards means picking which customer's orders to discard.
diagram:
✂ partition
Node A "I'm primary" ← writes
Node B "I'm primary" ← writes
   ↓
divergent history, manual repair
Fix: quorum-based election / fencing

means: Replacing a legacy system incrementally by routing individual endpoints to new code until nothing is left of the old one.
example: The proxy sends /orders to the new service and everything else to the monolith. Over eight months routes migrate one by one. There is never a big-bang cutover.
diagram:
Proxy
   ┌────┴────┐
new service  legacy monolith
 /orders     /everything-else
   ↓ month by month
new service  (monolith shrinks to nothing)

means: Every read returns the most recent committed write, always. You pay for it in latency and availability.
example: A ledger balance must be strongly consistent — reading a stale balance lets a user double-spend. That means reads go to the primary or through a quorum.
diagram:
write → commit → visible everywhere
   ↓
reads must coordinate (quorum / primary)
   ↓
higher latency, lower availability
Worth it for money, not for like counts

means: Debounce waits until activity stops, then fires once. Throttle fires at most once per interval during activity. Search boxes want debounce; scroll handlers want throttle.
example: Typing 'production' in a search box: debounce 300ms sends 1 request. Throttle 300ms sends about 4. Without either, 10 requests and a race condition.
diagram:
typing: p r o d u c t i o n
debounce(300) →              ▮ (1 call, at end)
throttle(300) → ▮   ▮   ▮   ▮ (regular)

means: A union where every member carries a literal tag field, so the compiler can prove which branch you're in and force you to handle all of them.
example: Modelling API results as `{status:'loading'} | {status:'error',error} | {status:'ok',data}` makes 'render data while loading' a compile error rather than a runtime crash.

means: The scheduler that lets single-threaded JavaScript do concurrent I/O: it runs your code, then drains queues of completed async work.
example: A 400ms synchronous JSON.parse of a 60MB payload blocks the loop. Every other request on that Node process waits 400ms, including health checks.
diagram:
[ call stack ] ← runs your sync code
      ↓ empty?
[ microtasks ]  promises, queueMicrotask
      ↓ drained fully
[ macrotasks ]  timers, I/O, setImmediate
      ↺ repeat

means: Using `never` in the default branch so adding a new union member becomes a compile error everywhere it isn't handled.
example: You add a 'cancelled' order status. Twelve switch statements fail to compile immediately, instead of silently falling through in production.

means: Limiting what a type parameter can be, so you can safely use its properties inside the generic.
example: `function pick<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]` gives you a correctly typed return and rejects `pick(user, 'nope')` at compile time.
diagram:
function pick<T, K extends keyof T>(o: T, k: K): T[K]

pick(user, "email")  ✓ returns string
pick(user, "nope")   ✗ compile error

means: Objects that are no longer needed but still reachable, so GC can't collect them. In long-lived Node processes this ends as an OOM kill.
example: An in-memory Map cache keyed by userId never evicts. After a week it's 3GB and the container gets OOM-killed nightly at peak traffic.
diagram:
Common causes:
  ├ unbounded Map/array cache
  ├ event listeners never removed
  ├ closures over big objects
  └ timers never cleared

Fix: TTL, LRU bound, off(), clearInterval()

means: Promise callbacks (microtasks) run before timers and I/O (macrotasks), and the entire microtask queue drains before the loop moves on.
example: A recursive promise chain starves setTimeout forever — the timer never fires because microtasks keep the queue non-empty.
diagram:
console.log(1)
setTimeout(→4)      macrotask
Promise.then(→3)    microtask
console.log(2)

Output: 1, 2, 3, 4

means: Checks a value against a type without widening it, so you keep the literal inference and still get validation.
example: `const routes = {...} satisfies Record<string, Handler>` validates the shape but keeps the exact keys, so `routes.` autocompletes real route names instead of `string`.
diagram:
const c: Record<string, string> = {a:"1"}
  → c.a is string, keys widened to string

const c = {a:"1"} satisfies Record<string,string>
  → validated AND keys stay literal ✓

means: TypeScript compares shapes, not names. If it has the right properties, it's assignable — no explicit `implements` needed.
example: A plain object literal with `id` and `name` satisfies `interface User` without declaring anything. Convenient, and it means two unrelated types can be accidentally interchangeable.

means: The bundler removing exports nothing imports. Only works reliably with ES modules and no side effects.
example: `import { debounce } from 'lodash'` still ships all of lodash under CommonJS. `lodash-es` or `import debounce from 'lodash/debounce'` ships 2KB.
diagram:
CJS require()  → dynamic → can't shake ✗
ESM import      → static  → shakeable ✓

Beware: "sideEffects": false in package.json
is what actually unlocks it

means: TypeScript shrinking a union to a specific member based on a runtime check it can follow.
example: `if (typeof v === 'string')` makes `v` a string in that branch. A custom type guard `function isUser(x): x is User` does the same for your own shapes.
diagram:
type R = { ok: true; data: X } | { ok: false; err: E }

if (r.ok) { r.data }   ← narrowed
else      { r.err  }   ← narrowed

Discriminated union = the safest pattern

means: Built-in transformations that derive types from other types, so a DTO stays in sync with its source instead of drifting.
example: `type CreateUser = Omit<User, 'id' | 'createdAt'>`. Add a field to User and the create payload updates automatically — no forgotten second edit.
diagram:
Partial<T>   all optional
Required<T>  all required
Pick<T,K>    subset
Omit<T,K>    everything but
Record<K,V>  map type
ReturnType<F> infer from a function

means: References that don't stop garbage collection. Perfect for attaching metadata to objects you don't own the lifetime of.
example: Caching per-request metadata in a Map keyed by the request object leaks every request forever. A WeakMap lets the entry vanish when the request is collected.
diagram:
Map:     key object stays alive forever ✗
WeakMap: entry disappears with the key ✓

Use for: object metadata, private fields,
         caches keyed by live objects

means: Parsing untrusted input against a schema that also produces the TypeScript type, so validation and typing can't drift apart.
example: `const User = z.object({email: z.string().email()})` gives both a validator and `z.infer<typeof User>`. One source of truth instead of two that quietly disagree.
diagram:
schema → validate at boundary
       → infer TS type
   ↓
Invalid payload rejected with a clear error
instead of an undefined 4 layers deep

means: Any synchronous CPU work stalls every concurrent request on that process. The most common Node performance bug in production.
example: bcrypt with cost 12 takes ~250ms of pure CPU. Under 40 logins/sec, one Node process serves nothing else. Move it to a worker thread or a pool.
diagram:
Culprits: JSON.parse of huge payloads,
  sync crypto, regex backtracking,
  fs.readFileSync, big array sorts
  ↓
Fix: worker_threads, streams, offload to a queue

means: Running one Node process per CPU core behind a shared socket, because a single process uses a single core.
example: An 8-core box running one Node process wastes 7 cores. `pm2 start -i max` runs 8 workers and throughput scales roughly 7x for I/O-bound work.
diagram:
Primary process
  ├ worker (core 1)
  ├ worker (core 2)
  ...
  └ worker (core 8)
Shared listening socket, OS load balances

means: Every DB connection is checked out and requests queue for one that never returns. Almost always a leak, not a sizing problem.
example: A handler forgets to release a client on the error path. After 20 errors the pool is empty and every request times out, though the DB is idle.
diagram:
pool size 20, all checked out
  ↓ new query waits
  ↓ acquire timeout → 500s everywhere

DB CPU: 3%    ← the tell
Fix: always release in finally

means: The four-argument Express handler `(err, req, res, next)`. It must be registered last, and it does not catch async throws automatically in Express 4.
example: An async route that throws just hangs the request in Express 4 — you need `next(err)` or an async wrapper. Express 5 fixes this by forwarding rejections.
diagram:
Express 4: async throw → request hangs ✗
  fix: wrap handlers, call next(err)
Express 5: rejections auto-forwarded ✓

app.use((err, req, res, next) => {...}) LAST

means: On SIGTERM: stop accepting new connections, finish in-flight requests, close DB pools and consumers, then exit. Kubernetes gives you ~30 seconds.
example: Without it, a rolling deploy kills pods mid-request and users see connection resets. With it, the pod drains cleanly and nobody notices the deploy.
diagram:
SIGTERM
  ↓ server.close()      stop new conns
  ↓ finish in-flight     (with timeout)
  ↓ close DB / broker / consumers
  ↓ process.exit(0)
Hard-kill timer as a backstop

means: Express handlers run in registration order, each deciding whether to pass control on. Order is behaviour, not style.
example: Registering the rate limiter after the body parser means you parse a 10MB body before rejecting the request. Order matters for both security and cost.
diagram:
req → helmet → rateLimit → bodyParser
    → auth → route handler → errorHandler → res

Wrong order = parsing bodies you'll reject

means: Reading a huge payload into memory kills the process. Streams process it in chunks, and `pipeline()` propagates the consumer's backpressure to the producer.
example: Uploading a 2GB file with `readFileSync` needs 2GB of RAM. `pipeline(read, transform, write)` holds ~64KB and handles the slow consumer automatically.
diagram:
readFileSync → 2GB in heap → OOM ✗

pipeline(src, gzip, dest)
  ↓ 64KB chunks, backpressure honoured
  ↓ errors + cleanup handled ✓

means: A rejected promise nobody caught. Since Node 15 it crashes the process by default — which is correct, and surprises teams upgrading.
example: A missing `await` on a background write means the rejection escapes the handler. In Node 14 it logged a warning; in Node 18+ the container restarts.
diagram:
async work without await
   ↓ rejects
no .catch(), no try/catch
   ↓
Node ≥15: process exits (code 1)
Fix: await it, or attach .catch explicitly

means: Real OS threads inside one Node process, for CPU-bound work. They share memory via SharedArrayBuffer, unlike child processes.
example: PDF page rasterisation moved to a pool of 4 workers. The main thread's P99 dropped from 2.4s to 60ms because it stopped doing the rasterising.
diagram:
main thread  → handles I/O, stays responsive
   ↓ postMessage
worker pool (4) → CPU work
   ↑ result

For CPU only. I/O is already async.

means: WSGI (Flask, Django classic) is one request per worker thread. ASGI (FastAPI, Starlette) is async and supports WebSockets and streaming.
example: A WSGI app holding 200 open SSE streams needs 200 workers. An ASGI app handles them on one event loop with a few processes.
diagram:
WSGI: sync, req/resp only, 1 thread per req
ASGI: async, WebSocket + SSE + lifespan

uvicorn/hypercorn = ASGI servers
gunicorn -k uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker

term: async def vs def in FastAPI
means: `async def` runs on the event loop; plain `def` is pushed to a threadpool. Putting blocking code in `async def` freezes the entire server.
example: A `requests.get()` inside an `async def` endpoint blocks the loop for 800ms. Every concurrent request stalls. Either use httpx async, or make the endpoint plain `def`.
diagram:
async def + await httpx  ✓ concurrent
async def + requests.get ✗ blocks everything
def       + requests.get ✓ threadpool, safe

Blocking code? Use def, or run_in_executor

means: BackgroundTasks runs after the response in the same process — lost on restart. Celery/RQ persists to a broker and survives crashes and deploys.
example: Sending a welcome email via BackgroundTasks is fine. Charging a card or running a 4-minute OCR job is not — a deploy mid-task loses it silently.
diagram:
BackgroundTasks: same process, no retry,
  lost on restart → fire-and-forget emails
Celery/RQ/Arq: durable, retries, visible
  → anything you'd be sad to lose

means: Only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time in CPython. Threads help I/O-bound work and do nothing for CPU-bound work.
example: Running 8 threads to parse documents gives no speedup — they take turns holding the GIL. `multiprocessing` or a native extension does.
diagram:
I/O-bound  → threads help ✓ (GIL released on I/O)
CPU-bound  → threads useless ✗
   ↓
Use multiprocessing, or C/Rust extensions
(numpy, polars release the GIL)

means: Python does not check annotations at runtime. `mypy` checks them at build time; Pydantic checks them at boundaries. Neither happens by accident.
example: A function annotated `-> int` returning a string runs perfectly and breaks three calls later. Only mypy in CI catches it.
diagram:
def f(x: int) -> int: return "oops"
f("also fine")   ← runs happily

mypy / pyright  → catch at CI
Pydantic        → catch at the boundary

means: Multiple OS processes each running an event loop, because one Python process still uses one core.
example: `gunicorn -w 4 -k uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker` on a 4-core box. In-memory caches are now per-worker — a common source of 'it works sometimes' bugs.
diagram:
4 workers × 1 event loop each
   ↓
In-process state is NOT shared:
  rate-limit counters, caches, locks
   ↓ move to Redis

means: Column order in a multi-column index decides which queries it can serve. The leftmost prefix rule.
example: An index on `(tenant_id, created_at)` serves 'this tenant, recent first' perfectly and is useless for 'all tenants by created_at'.
diagram:
INDEX (tenant_id, created_at)

WHERE tenant_id = ?                    ✓
WHERE tenant_id = ? ORDER BY created_at ✓
WHERE created_at > ?                    ✗ no prefix

means: Postgres forks a process per connection, so thousands of client connections will kill it. A pooler multiplexes many clients onto few server connections.
example: 200 serverless functions each open 5 connections = 1000, past `max_connections`. PgBouncer in transaction mode fronts them with 20 real connections.
diagram:
clients (1000) → PgBouncer → PG (20)

session mode     → 1:1 for the session
transaction mode → reused per txn (best density)
                   breaks prepared stmts/advisory locks

means: An index that carries every column the query needs, so Postgres answers from the index alone without touching the heap.
example: `CREATE INDEX ... ON orders(user_id) INCLUDE (total, status)` turns an Index Scan + heap fetch into an Index Only Scan. Often a 3-5x win on hot reads.
diagram:
Index Scan → heap fetch (random I/O)
Index Only Scan → answered from index ✓

Requires: visibility map current (vacuum!)

means: Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs. Postgres detects the cycle and kills one.
example: Transaction A locks row 1 then row 2; B locks row 2 then row 1. Fix: always acquire locks in a consistent order, e.g. sorted by primary key.
diagram:
A: lock(1) ─── waits for(2)
                    ↑        ↓
B: lock(2) ─── waits for(1)
   ↓
PG detects cycle → aborts one txn
Fix: consistent lock ordering

means: Runs the query and shows the real plan with actual row counts and timings. The only honest way to know why something is slow.
example: The plan estimated 12 rows and got 480,000. That gap means stale statistics, and it's why the planner picked a nested loop that takes 40 seconds.
diagram:
Seq Scan on orders
  (cost=0..91k rows=12 width=64)
  (actual time=0.1..38942 rows=480123)
                       ↑ estimate vs reality
Big gap = bad stats = bad plan

means: How much concurrent transactions can see of each other. Postgres defaults to Read Committed, which permits non-repeatable reads.
example: Two requests read a seat count of 1 and both book it. Read Committed allows this. `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` or Serializable prevents it.
diagram:
Read Uncommitted → dirty reads (not in PG)
Read Committed   → PG default, non-repeatable reads
Repeatable Read  → snapshot, phantom-safe in PG
Serializable     → as if run one at a time

means: Binary JSON storage with GIN indexing and operators. Great for genuinely variable data, bad as an excuse to avoid schema design.
example: Storing OCR metadata in JSONB with a GIN index lets you query `metadata @> '{"lang":"hi"}'` fast. Storing your core user fields there costs you constraints and type safety.
diagram:
json  → text, reparsed each time
jsonb → binary, indexable ✓

CREATE INDEX ON docs USING GIN (metadata);
WHERE metadata @> '{"lang":"hi"}'

means: A stored, precomputed query result. Fast to read, stale until refreshed — and REFRESH locks unless you use CONCURRENTLY.
example: A dashboard aggregate takes 14s live. Materialised and refreshed every 5 minutes, it reads in 20ms and is at most 5 minutes behind.
diagram:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_stats AS ...
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY daily_stats;

live query: 14s
matview:    20ms + staleness window
CONCURRENTLY needs a unique index

means: Postgres keeps old row versions so readers never block writers and writers never block readers. The cost is dead tuples that must be vacuumed.
example: A long analytics query holds a snapshot for 40 minutes. Every row updated during that window keeps its old version, and the table physically grows.
diagram:
UPDATE creates a NEW row version
old version kept for older snapshots
   ↓
readers never block ✓
dead tuples accumulate → VACUUM needed

means: Fetching a list, then issuing one query per item. The single most common ORM performance bug.
example: Loading 50 posts then each post's author = 51 queries and 380ms. One join or an `include` = 1 query and 12ms.
diagram:
SELECT * FROM posts          (1)
  → SELECT author WHERE id=1   (2)
  → SELECT author WHERE id=2   (3)
  ... ×50
Fix: JOIN, IN (...), or DataLoader batching

means: No locks. Read a version number, and on write require it to be unchanged. Cheap when conflicts are rare.
example: `UPDATE doc SET body=?, version=version+1 WHERE id=? AND version=7`. Zero rows updated means someone else won — retry or surface a conflict.
diagram:
read version 7
  ↓ user edits for 3 minutes
UPDATE ... WHERE version = 7
  rows=1 → success ✓
  rows=0 → someone else wrote → retry

means: An index with a WHERE clause, so it only stores rows you actually query. Smaller, faster, cheaper to maintain.
example: Only 0.3% of jobs are 'pending', but the queue query hits them constantly. A partial index on pending rows is 300x smaller than the full one.
diagram:
CREATE INDEX ON jobs(created_at)
  WHERE status = 'pending';

full index:    4,000,000 rows
partial index:    12,000 rows

means: Restoring a base backup and replaying WAL up to an exact moment — the only real answer to 'someone ran DELETE without a WHERE at 14:32'.
example: Bad migration at 14:32:10. Restore last night's base backup, replay WAL to 14:32:09. Nine minutes of data lost instead of a day.
diagram:
base backup (02:00)
  + WAL replay → 14:32:09
  ↓
state one second before the mistake

Untested backups are not backups

means: Two forms: an array of operations run atomically, or an interactive callback where you can branch. Interactive holds a connection for its whole duration.
example: Wrapping an external HTTP call inside `$transaction` holds a DB connection for 3 seconds. Twenty concurrent requests exhaust the pool.

means: `include` adds relations to the full model; `select` returns exactly the fields you list. Over-fetching is the default if you never use select.
example: `include: { posts: true }` on a user with 5,000 posts pulls all of them into memory. `select` plus `take` fetches the 10 you render.

means: Schema-first migrations generated from schema.prisma. `migrate dev` for local, `migrate deploy` for production — never `db push` against prod.
example: `db push` silently drops a column to match the schema. On production that's data loss with no migration record and no rollback path.
diagram:
schema.prisma (source of truth)
  ↓ migrate dev   → SQL file + apply (local)
  ↓ commit the SQL
  ↓ migrate deploy → apply in CI/prod

db push = prototype only

means: Row-level pessimistic locking. Other transactions touching those rows wait until you commit.
example: Decrementing inventory: read with FOR UPDATE so two concurrent checkouts can't both see 1 item left. `SKIP LOCKED` turns the same table into a work queue.

means: Splitting one logical table into physical child tables by range or list, so the planner skips irrelevant partitions and old data drops instantly.
example: Events partitioned by month: 'last 7 days' scans one partition instead of 400M rows, and archiving is `DROP TABLE events_2024_01` rather than a giant DELETE.
diagram:
events (parent)
 ├ events_2026_06
 ├ events_2026_07
 └ events_2026_08  ← query hits only this

Retention = DROP partition (instant)
vs DELETE (bloat + hours)

means: The background process reclaiming dead row versions and updating planner statistics. Ignore it and tables bloat while query plans go wrong.
example: A high-churn table gets 4x larger on disk than its live data and sequential scans slow to a crawl — autovacuum couldn't keep up with the update rate.
diagram:
dead tuples pile up
  ↓ autovacuum
space reusable + stats refreshed

Not running? → bloat, bad plans,
               eventually txid wraparound

means: Changes are written to a durable log before touching data files. It's what makes crash recovery, replication and PITR possible.
example: Power loss mid-write: on restart Postgres replays the WAL and the database is consistent. The same stream feeds replicas and CDC tools like Debezium.
diagram:
change → WAL (fsync) → ack client
             ↓
       data files (later, async)
             ↓
     replicas + PITR + CDC read the same WAL

means: Stages that transform documents in sequence. Order determines performance — filter and project early, before the expensive stages.
example: Putting `$match` after `$lookup` joins the entire collection then throws it away. Moving `$match` first cut a report from 40s to 300ms.
diagram:
$match  → shrink the set FIRST (uses index)
$project → drop unused fields
$lookup  → join (expensive)
$group   → aggregate
$sort    → needs index or 100MB memory cap

means: Subscribing to a collection's oplog to react to inserts, updates and deletes in real time, with resume tokens after a disconnect.
example: A search index stays in sync by tailing a change stream instead of polling every 30 seconds. Store the resume token or you replay or miss events after a restart.
diagram:
collection change
   ↓ oplog
change stream → your consumer
   ↓ persist resumeToken
reconnect → resume exactly where you stopped

means: Order compound index keys as Equality, then Sort, then Range. Getting it wrong forces an in-memory sort.
example: Query filters `status = 'active'`, sorts by `createdAt`, ranges on `score > 80`. Index `{status:1, createdAt:-1, score:1}` serves it fully.
diagram:
ESR:
  E  equality fields first
  S  sort fields next
  R  range fields last

Wrong order → SORT stage in explain() → slow

means: Embed when data is read together, bounded and owned by the parent. Reference when it's shared, unbounded or updated independently.
example: Embedding comments in a post works until a post gets 50,000 comments and the document nears the 16MB limit and rewrites on every insert.
diagram:
Embed if:  read together, bounded, 1:few
Reference if: shared, unbounded, 1:many,
              independently updated

16MB document cap is a hard wall

means: What you're allowed to see. `local` may show writes that could still be rolled back; `majority` only shows durably committed data.
example: Reading with `local` after a failover can show data that no longer exists. `majority` costs a little latency and never lies.
diagram:
local     → may include rollback-able writes
majority  → only majority-committed ✓
linearizable → strongest, slowest

means: Horizontal scaling via a shard key. Choosing that key badly is close to unfixable, so it's the decision to get right first.
example: Sharding by a monotonic ObjectId sends every insert to the highest chunk — one shard takes all writes. Hashed or compound keys distribute properly.
diagram:
mongos router → config servers
   ↓
shard A   shard B   shard C

Monotonic key → hot shard ✗
Hashed/compound key → even ✓

means: The data and indexes you actually touch regularly. If it doesn't fit in RAM, Mongo hits disk and latency collapses.
example: A 200GB collection with an 8GB working set is fine on a 16GB box. Add a report that scans everything and the cache thrashes for every user query.
diagram:
total data 200GB
┌──────────────┬───────────────────────┐
│ working  8GB │      cold  192GB      │
└──────┬───────┴───────────────────────┘
       ▼ fits in 16GB RAM ✓ sub-ms reads

one full scan → cold evicts hot → thrash
                → 100x slower, for everyone

Watch: cache eviction rate, page faults

means: How many nodes must confirm a write before it's acknowledged. `w:1` is fast and can lose data on failover; `w:majority` is durable.
example: With `w:1`, a write acked by the primary that then crashes before replicating is rolled back — the user saw success and the data is gone.
diagram:
w:1            → primary only, fast, lossy
w:"majority"   → survives failover ✓
j:true         → fsynced to journal

Money → majority + journal

means: A tiny probabilistic set: 'definitely not present' or 'probably present'. Kills pointless lookups for a fraction of the memory.
example: Checking whether a URL was already crawled: a Bloom filter for 100M URLs fits in ~180MB with 1% false positives, versus tens of gigabytes for a real set.
diagram:
query → filter
  "not present" → 100% certain, skip DB ✓
  "present"     → maybe → check DB

False positives yes, false negatives never

means: Removing or updating stale entries. Hard because correctness depends on knowing every key derived from a piece of data.
example: A user updates their name. You invalidate `user:42` but forget `feed:99` which embedded the old name. Versioned or tag-based keys avoid the guesswork.
diagram:
Strategies:
  TTL only         → simple, bounded staleness
  explicit DEL     → precise, easy to miss keys
  version in key   → user:42:v7 (old keys age out)
  tag-based purge  → needs a tag index

means: The default pattern: read cache, on miss read the DB and populate. Simple, and every miss pays full latency.
example: First request for a product takes 120ms and warms the cache; the next 10,000 take 2ms. Combine with a lock to avoid a stampede on hot keys.
diagram:
GET key
 ├ hit  → return ✓
 └ miss → query DB → SET key ttl → return

App owns the cache logic

means: One key receiving a disproportionate share of traffic, saturating a single Redis shard or single-threaded core.
example: A homepage config key served 80,000 req/sec from one shard while others idled. Fixed with a short-TTL in-process cache in front of Redis.
diagram:
shard 1 ████████████████ 80k/s (hot key)
shard 2 █
shard 3 █

Fix: local L1 cache, or key sharding
     key:{n} with n in 0..9

means: A tiny in-process cache in front of Redis. L1 removes the network hop entirely for the hottest keys; the price is per-instance staleness.
example: Feature flags cached 5 seconds in-process and 60 seconds in Redis. Redis traffic drops 95%, and a flag flip takes up to 5 seconds to reach every pod.
diagram:
request → L1 (in-process, 5s TTL)
        → L2 (Redis, 60s TTL)
        → DB

L1 hit = 0ms, no network
Cost: up to 5s of inconsistency between pods

means: Caching the fact that something doesn't exist, so repeated lookups for missing keys don't hammer the database.
example: A scraper requests 40,000 non-existent product IDs. Without negative caching every one is a DB miss. With a 60s null marker, 39,900 never reach Postgres.
diagram:
miss in DB → SET key "__null__" EX 60
   ↓
repeat lookups served from cache ✓

Keep the TTL short so real creations appear

means: RDB is periodic snapshots — compact, loses the window since the last one. AOF logs every write — larger, near-zero loss. Default configs can lose minutes.
example: Treating Redis as a durable store with default RDB means a crash loses up to 5 minutes of writes. If that matters, it belongs in Postgres.
diagram:
