RDB: snapshot every N sec → fast restart,
     loses up to N sec
AOF: append every write (fsync everysec)
     → ~1s loss, slower restart
Both can be enabled together

means: Sending many commands without waiting for each reply, collapsing N round trips into one.
example: 1000 GETs at 0.6ms RTT = 600ms. Pipelined, it's one round trip plus processing — around 8ms.
diagram:
Sequential: cmd→reply ×1000 = 600ms
Pipelined:  1000 cmds → 1 flush → 8ms

MGET/MSET are the built-in version

means: MULTI/EXEC queues commands with no rollback and no reads mid-transaction. A Lua script runs atomically and can branch on values it reads.
example: Check-then-decrement in two commands races. The same logic in one Lua script is atomic because Redis is single-threaded for execution.
diagram:
MULTI/EXEC: queued, atomic, no logic
Lua EVAL:   read → branch → write, atomic ✓

Keep scripts short — they block the server

means: TTL expires keys by time; the eviction policy decides what to drop when memory is full. `noeviction` means writes start failing.
example: A cache with `noeviction` fills up and every SET returns OOM errors — an outage caused by a cache. `allkeys-lru` would have quietly dropped cold keys.
diagram:
maxmemory-policy:
  noeviction     → writes ERROR at limit ✗
  allkeys-lru    → drop least recently used ✓
  volatile-ttl   → drop soonest-to-expire
  allkeys-lfu    → drop least frequently used

means: Write-through updates cache and DB together — consistent, slower writes. Write-behind updates cache first and flushes later — fast, and lossy on crash.
example: Write-behind for a view counter is fine (losing 5 seconds of counts is acceptable). Write-behind for an order is not.
diagram:
Write-through: app → cache + DB → ack
  consistent, slower

Write-behind: app → cache → ack
              (flush to DB later)
  fast, data loss window on crash

means: Multiple workers on one queue, each message going to exactly one of them. The standard way to scale throughput horizontally.
example: One consumer clears 200 docs/min; four clear 800. Scale by queue depth, not CPU — depth is the metric that reflects user-visible lag.
diagram:
queue → ┌ worker 1
        ├ worker 2
        └ worker 3
Each message to exactly one worker

Autoscale on queue depth / message age

means: Telling the broker you've finished with a message. Ack too early and a crash loses work; ack too late and you risk redelivery.
example: Acking on receipt then crashing mid-processing loses the job. Acking after the work completes means a crash causes a redelivery — which is why the consumer must be idempotent.
diagram:
deliver → process → ack   ✓ at-least-once
deliver → ack → process   ✗ at-most-once

nack(requeue=false) → DLQ
Auto-ack = you accepted data loss

means: How far behind the consumer is: queue depth, or the age of the oldest unprocessed message. Age is the better alert.
example: Depth of 50,000 is fine for a fast consumer and catastrophic for a slow one. 'Oldest message is 14 minutes old' tells you the actual user impact.
diagram:
depth  = messages waiting
age    = oldest message timestamp ← alert here

depth 50k, age 20s  → fine
depth 200,  age 40m → something is stuck

means: A separate queue for messages that failed repeatedly, rejected, or expired. Instead of silent loss, they're held for investigation.
example: A payment notification fails three times and moves to the DLQ with the failure reason in the headers. An engineer replays it next morning instead of discovering it in a support ticket.
diagram:
message → process ✗
  → retry ✗ → retry ✗
        ↓ after N attempts
   Dead Letter Queue
        ↓
  alert on DLQ depth > 0

means: Publishers send to an exchange, never to a queue. Bindings and routing keys decide which queues get a copy.
example: A `direct` exchange with routing key `invoice.created` delivers to one queue. A `topic` exchange with `invoice.*` delivers to every queue bound to that pattern.
diagram:
publisher → exchange
              ├ binding "invoice.*"  → queue A
              ├ binding "invoice.paid" → queue B
              └ (no match) → dropped silently

direct | topic | fanout | headers

means: A consumer that can process the same message twice with no additional effect. Non-negotiable, because at-least-once delivery is what you actually get.
example: Store processed message IDs with a unique constraint. On redelivery the insert conflicts, you ack and move on — no double charge, no duplicate email.
diagram:
receive msg id
  INSERT INTO processed(id) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
  rows = 0 → already done → ack, skip ✓
  rows = 1 → do the work → ack

means: Order holds within a single queue and single consumer. Add concurrency and ordering is gone.
example: Two consumers on one queue process 'user created' and 'user updated' in parallel; the update lands first and fails. Fix by partitioning per entity key.
diagram:
1 queue, 1 consumer  → ordered ✓
1 queue, N consumers → unordered ✗

Fix: consistent-hash exchange by entity id,
     or design events to be order-independent

means: Producers and consumers deploy independently, so a message format change must be backward compatible or you break live consumers.
example: Renaming a field breaks every consumer that hasn't deployed yet. Add the new field, dual-write both, migrate consumers, then remove the old one.
diagram:
✓ add optional fields
✓ widen types
✗ rename fields
✗ remove fields still read
✗ change semantics of an existing field

means: A message that always fails, gets requeued, and blocks the queue forever in an infinite loop.
example: A malformed payload nacked with requeue=true reprocesses thousands of times per second, burning CPU and drowning the logs. A retry counter plus a DLQ stops it.
diagram:
bad message → fail → requeue → fail → ...
   ↓ infinite loop, 100% CPU

Fix: count attempts in a header,
     after N → DLQ, never requeue blindly

means: How many unacked messages one consumer may hold. Unlimited prefetch means one consumer grabs the whole queue and the others idle.
example: Default unlimited prefetch: consumer A takes 10,000 messages, B and C sit empty. `prefetch=20` spreads work and keeps memory bounded.
diagram:
prefetch = unlimited
  A ████████████████ 10000
  B (idle)   C (idle)

prefetch = 20
  A ██  B ██  C ██   ✓ balanced

means: The broker acknowledging it has taken responsibility for a message. Without confirms, a publish that vanished still looks successful to your code.
example: The broker restarts mid-publish. Without confirms your service already returned 200 to the user and the message never existed.
diagram:
publish → broker
  confirm mode ON → basic.ack from broker ✓
  confirm mode OFF → fire and hope ✗

Pair with the outbox pattern for real safety

means: RabbitMQ's Raft-based replicated queue. Survives node failure without the data-loss and split-brain problems of classic mirrored queues.
example: A classic mirrored queue can lose messages on a partition. A quorum queue with 3 replicas needs a majority to accept a write and stays correct.
diagram:
3 replicas, majority commit
  node dies → leader re-elected
  messages survive ✓

Trade-off: higher latency, more disk
Default choice for durable queues today

means: Immediate requeue retries a transient failure while the dependency is still down. A delay queue with TTL spaces attempts out.
example: A message TTLs on a wait queue for 30s, then dead-letters back to the main queue. Retries at 30s, 2m, 10m instead of 400 attempts per second.
diagram:
main queue → fail
  → retry.30s (TTL 30s, DLX = main)
  → retry.2m
  → retry.10m
  → parking lot (manual)

means: The directive marking where the client bundle starts. Everything imported below it becomes client code, so boundary placement decides bundle size.
example: Putting "use client" at the top of your layout drags the entire tree into the client bundle. Push it down to the leaf that actually needs interactivity.
diagram:
layout (server)
  └ page (server)
      └ InteractiveButton "use client" ← boundary here ✓

Boundary too high = whole tree client-side ✗

means: A component that catches render-time errors in its subtree and shows a fallback instead of unmounting the whole app.
example: One widget throws on undefined data. Without a boundary the entire dashboard goes blank. With one, that panel shows an error and the rest works.
diagram:
<ErrorBoundary fallback={<Panel/>}>
  <BuggyWidget />
</ErrorBoundary>

Does NOT catch: event handlers, async,
                SSR, errors in the boundary itself

means: Attaching React event handlers to server-rendered HTML. The page looks ready before it's interactive.
example: A 400KB bundle means the page paints at 800ms and stays unresponsive until 3.2s. Clicks in that window do nothing — users click twice.
diagram:
HTML from server → paints fast ✓
   ↓ JS downloads + parses
   ↓ React attaches handlers
interactive (TTI) ← the real gap

means: The server HTML differs from what the client renders, so React discards it and re-renders. Usually caused by time, randomness or browser-only APIs.
example: Rendering `new Date().toLocaleTimeString()` produces different output on server and client. React logs a mismatch and throws the SSR work away.
diagram:
server: "3:42:01 PM"
client: "3:42:02 PM"
   ↓ mismatch → full client re-render

Fix: render after mount, or suppressHydrationWarning
Culprits: Date, Math.random, window, locale

means: Serving a static page while regenerating it in the background after a revalidation window. CDN speed with fresh-enough content.
example: A product page with `revalidate: 60` serves instantly from cache. After 60 seconds the next visitor gets the stale copy and triggers a rebuild for everyone after them.
diagram:
request → cached page (instant) ✓
  age > 60s? → serve stale, rebuild in background
  next request → fresh page

Stale-while-revalidate for your whole page

means: Updating the UI before the server confirms, then reconciling. The app feels instant; you must handle rollback.
example: A like button fills immediately, then reverts with a toast if the request fails 400ms later. Without rollback handling, the UI lies.
diagram:
click → update UI now ✓
     → send request
       success → keep
       failure → revert + tell the user

Skipping the revert path = state that lies

means: React diffing the new element tree against the previous one to compute the minimum DOM mutations.
example: Re-rendering a 200-row table produces 200 new element objects, but React only touches the DOM for the 3 cells whose text changed.
diagram:
state change → render() → new element tree
   ↓ diff against previous
   ↓ minimal DOM ops (commit)

Render is cheap. DOM writes are not.

means: React compares props and dependencies with Object.is. A new object or function literal each render is always 'different', defeating memoisation.
example: Passing `style={{margin: 4}}` to a memoised child re-renders it every time, because the object literal is new on each render.
diagram:
<Child style={{m:4}} />   → new object every render
   ↓ memo comparison fails → re-renders ✗

Fix: hoist the constant, or useMemo

means: Route handlers are real HTTP endpoints for external callers and webhooks. Server actions are RPC for your own UI.
example: A Stripe webhook needs a route handler with a stable URL and signature verification. A form submit from your own page is better as a server action.
diagram:
Route handler → public URL, any client,
  webhooks, third-party integrations
Server action → called from your own components,
  generated endpoint, form-friendly

means: Functions marked "use server" that a client component can call directly; Next.js generates the HTTP endpoint for you.
example: A form submits straight to a server action with no API route and no fetch. The endpoint is still public — validate and authorise inside it like any other route.
diagram:
"use server"
async function save(formData) { ... }

client calls it → Next generates POST endpoint
   ↓
SECURITY: it IS a public endpoint.
authn + authz + validation still required

means: Components that run only on the server and ship serialised output instead of JavaScript. They can query the database directly and never hydrate.
example: A markdown renderer with a 90KB parser as a server component ships 0KB of that to the browser — the client receives rendered output only.
diagram:
Server Component: runs on server, 0 JS shipped
  ✓ direct DB/fs access
  ✗ no useState/useEffect/onClick

"use client" → back to normal React

means: An effect or callback capturing the value of state from the render it was created in, and never seeing updates.
example: A `setInterval` inside `useEffect(..., [])` logs the initial count forever, because the closure captured count = 0. Use a ref or a functional update.

means: Static pages are built once and served from cache. Dynamic pages render per request. Touching cookies, headers or searchParams silently makes a route dynamic.
example: A marketing page reads a cookie for an A/B test and quietly leaves static rendering. TTFB goes from 20ms (CDN) to 340ms (origin).
diagram:
Static:  build once → CDN → 20ms TTFB
Dynamic: render per request → 340ms

Dynamic triggers: cookies(), headers(),
  searchParams, no-store fetch

means: Sending HTML in chunks as it's ready instead of waiting for the slowest data source.
example: The header and nav flush at 80ms while a slow recommendations query resolves at 1.4s. Without streaming the user stares at a blank page for 1.4s.
diagram:
Blocking: [====wait 1.4s====] then all HTML
Streaming: [shell 80ms]...[section 400ms]...
                                [recs 1.4s]

First paint no longer gated by slowest query

means: useMemo caches a computed value; useCallback caches a function reference. Both cost memory and comparison work, so they only pay off with a real problem.
example: Memoising `a + b` is slower than recomputing it. Memoising a 30ms filter over 10,000 rows, or a callback passed to a memoised list, is worth it.
diagram:
useMemo(() => expensiveCalc(x), [x])
useCallback(fn, [deps])  ≡ useMemo(() => fn, [deps])

Worth it when: expensive compute,
or the value is a dependency/prop of a memo child

means: Rendering only the visible slice of a long list. The DOM stays small no matter how much data there is.
example: A 50,000-row table with real DOM nodes freezes the tab. Virtualised, only ~30 rows exist at once and scrolling is smooth.
diagram:
50,000 rows in DOM → 8s render, jank
virtualised → ~30 nodes + spacers → 16ms

react-virtual / react-window
Cost: Ctrl+F and native scroll anchoring break

means: Sequential dependent requests where each waits for the last. Common in components that fetch their own data.
example: user → org → billing runs 3 requests serially for 900ms. Fetching them in parallel where possible takes 320ms.
diagram:
Sequential: [user 300][org 300][billing 300] = 900ms
Parallel:   [user 300]
            [org 300]      = 320ms
            [billing 300]

Promise.all, or hoist the fetch upward

means: The parallel structure screen readers consume. Divs with click handlers don't appear in it as controls, so they're invisible to assistive tech.
example: `<div onClick>` isn't focusable, has no role and can't be triggered by keyboard. `<button>` gives you all three for free.
diagram:
<div onClick>  → no role, no focus, no keyboard ✗
<button>       → role=button, tabbable,
                 Enter/Space activate ✓

Use semantic elements before reaching for ARIA

means: A header listing which script, style and connect sources are allowed. The strongest defence against XSS actually executing.
example: With `script-src 'self'`, an injected `<script src=evil.com>` is blocked by the browser even if your sanitisation failed.

means: The flags that decide whether JavaScript can read a cookie, whether it's sent cross-site, and whether it travels over plain HTTP.
example: A session cookie without HttpOnly can be read by any XSS payload. Without SameSite it's attached to cross-site requests, enabling CSRF.
diagram:
HttpOnly → JS cannot read it (blocks XSS theft)
Secure   → HTTPS only
SameSite=Lax → not sent on cross-site POST
Path/Domain → scope

Sessions: HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite=Lax

means: Google's user-experience metrics: how fast the main content paints, how fast the page responds to input, and how much it visually jumps.
example: LCP under 2.5s, INP under 200ms, CLS under 0.1. These affect search ranking and correlate directly with bounce rate.
diagram:
LCP  largest contentful paint  < 2.5s
INP  interaction to next paint  < 200ms
CLS  cumulative layout shift    < 0.1

Measured on real users (field), not lab

means: The sequence from HTML to pixels: parse HTML, build CSSOM, layout, paint. Render-blocking resources stall the whole thing.
example: A 90KB stylesheet in the head blocks first paint until it downloads and parses, even though only 6KB of it applies above the fold.
diagram:
HTML → DOM
CSS  → CSSOM  (render-blocking)
   ↓ Render tree → Layout → Paint → Composite

Blocking CSS/JS in <head> delays first pixel

means: A malicious page making the browser send an authenticated request to your site using cookies it automatically attaches.
example: A hidden form on evil.com POSTs to your /transfer endpoint. The browser attaches the session cookie and the transfer succeeds — unless you check a token or SameSite.
diagram:
evil.com → auto-submit form → your-api.com
browser attaches cookie automatically ✗

Defence: SameSite=Lax/Strict,
         CSRF token, check Origin header
Bearer tokens in headers aren't auto-sent ✓

means: Content jumping as late resources load. The reason you click the wrong button on a news site.
example: An image without width and height reserves no space. When it loads, everything below jumps 300px — often just as the user taps.
diagram: with no dimensions → text renders → image loads → shift ✗ Fix: width/height attrs, aspect-ratio, reserve space for ads/banners

means: Even without a network call, updating state per keystroke re-renders the tree. On a heavy page this shows up as input lag.
example: Typing in a filter over a 3,000-row table drops to 8fps. Debouncing the state update to 150ms restores smooth typing.
diagram:
every keystroke → setState → full re-render
  heavy tree → 120ms per key → visible lag

Fix: debounce state, useDeferredValue,
     or make the input uncontrolled

means: Named design decisions (colour, spacing, radius) defined once and referenced everywhere, so a rebrand is one file rather than a search-and-replace.
example: Sixty components using `#2563EB` directly means a brand change touches sixty files. `--brand` or a Tailwind theme key means one.
diagram:
--brand: #2563EB
--space-4: 16px
--radius-md: 10px
   ↓ referenced everywhere

Rebrand = edit the token, not the components

means: Alternating DOM reads and writes in a loop, forcing a synchronous layout recalculation on every iteration.
example: Reading `offsetHeight` then setting `style.height` inside a 500-item loop causes 500 forced reflows and a 900ms freeze. Batch reads, then writes.

means: Resource hints. Preload fetches something needed now with high priority; prefetch grabs something likely needed next; preconnect warms the TLS handshake.
example: Preconnecting to your font CDN removes 180ms of DNS + TLS from the critical path before the font request is even made.
diagram:
preconnect → DNS + TCP + TLS warmed early
preload    → needed this navigation, high priority
prefetch   → probably needed next, idle priority

Over-preloading competes with what matters

means: Reflow recalculates geometry and is expensive; repaint only redraws pixels. Animating layout properties forces reflow every frame.
example: Animating `left` reflows on all 60 frames. Animating `transform: translateX()` is composited on the GPU and skips layout entirely.
diagram:
left / width / top   → Layout → Paint → Composite ✗
color / background   → Paint → Composite
transform / opacity  → Composite only ✓ 60fps

means: The browser rule that scripts from one origin can't read responses from another. Origin means scheme + host + port, all three.
example: https://app.com cannot read from https://api.app.com by default — different host. CORS headers are the opt-in that relaxes this.
diagram:
https://app.com:443  vs
https://api.app.com:443  → different origin
http://app.com:443       → different scheme
https://app.com:8080     → different port

means: A self-contained z-index layer. A child can never escape its parent's stacking context, no matter how large its z-index is.
example: Your modal has z-index 9999 and still renders behind the header, because an ancestor has `transform` or `opacity < 1` and created a context.
diagram:
parent { transform: translateZ(0) }  ← new context
  └ modal { z-index: 9999 }  ← trapped inside

Created by: transform, opacity<1, filter,
            position+z-index, will-change

means: Attacker-controlled input executing as script in another user's browser, giving it full access to their session.
example: A comment containing `` renders via dangerouslySetInnerHTML and steals every reader's session.
diagram:
Stored:    saved in DB, hits every viewer
Reflected: bounced back from a URL param
DOM-based: sink like innerHTML

Defence: escape on output, CSP, HttpOnly cookies

means: Emitting to a large room is N individual socket writes. At scale this becomes the bottleneck, not your business logic.
example: A 50,000-user room receiving 10 messages/sec means 500,000 socket writes per second. Batching and rate-limiting the broadcast is the only way through.
diagram:
1 message × 50,000 sockets = 50,000 writes
× 10 msg/sec = 500,000 writes/sec

Fix: batch, throttle, or shard the room

means: Periodic frames confirming the connection is alive, because a dead TCP connection can look open for minutes.
example: A phone loses signal in a tunnel. The server holds the socket and keeps sending until a ping times out at 20 seconds and it's cleaned up.
diagram:
server → ping (every 25s)
client → pong
no pong within timeout → close + cleanup

Also keeps proxies from idle-timing you out

means: Deciding what happens to messages sent while a client was disconnected. Silence is a design choice, usually the wrong one.
example: A user's train enters a tunnel for 40 seconds. Without an offset or sequence number they miss 12 messages and the chat has a hole. With one, the server replays on reconnect.
diagram:
client stores lastSeq = 812
reconnect → send lastSeq
server replays 813..847 ✓

No sequence = silent gaps users notice

means: Tracking who is online. Deceptively hard: crashes don't send a disconnect, so presence must expire rather than be deleted.
example: A browser tab is force-quit. No disconnect event fires. Without a TTL heartbeat key in Redis, that user appears online forever.
diagram:
heartbeat every 10s → SET presence:u42 EX 30

crash → no disconnect event
       → key expires in 30s → offline ✓
Never rely on the disconnect handler alone

means: Clients must reconnect on drop — with exponential backoff and jitter, or a server restart becomes a self-inflicted DDoS.
example: 50,000 clients drop when a pod restarts. Fixed 1s retry means 50,000 simultaneous handshakes every second. Jittered backoff spreads them over a minute.
diagram:
disconnect → wait 1s ±jitter
  fail → 2s → 4s → 8s (cap 30s)

Fixed interval + 50k clients = you DDoS yourself

means: Rooms are server-side groupings for targeted broadcast. Namespaces split the connection into logical channels over one transport.
example: `socket.join('doc:42')` then `io.to('doc:42').emit(...)` sends only to that document's editors, instead of every connected user.
diagram:
socket.join("doc:42")
io.to("doc:42").emit("patch", data)

Namespace /admin vs /chat
  → same TCP connection, separate handlers

means: One-way server-to-client streaming over plain HTTP, with automatic reconnect and event IDs. Simpler than WebSocket when the client doesn't need to push.
example: Streaming LLM tokens to a browser is a perfect SSE case — the client sends one request and just reads. It also works through ordinary HTTP infrastructure.

means: Mesh means every participant sends to every other — fine for 3, impossible at 10. An SFU receives one stream per peer and forwards selectively.
example: A 10-person mesh call means each client uploads 9 streams. On home broadband that's unusable. An SFU means each uploads once.
diagram:
Mesh:  n×(n-1) streams → 10 people = 90
SFU:   each uploads 1, SFU forwards
MCU:   server mixes into 1 stream (CPU heavy)

>4 participants → SFU

means: The component that broadcasts events across server instances. Without it, `io.emit` only reaches clients connected to that one process.
example: Two pods, users split between them. A message emitted on pod 1 never reaches pod 2's users. The Redis adapter relays it through pub/sub.
diagram:
pod 1 emit → only pod 1's clients ✗

with Redis adapter:
pod 1 → Redis pub/sub → pod 2 → its clients ✓

means: Routing a client's requests to the same server instance. Required for Socket.io's polling handshake, and a scaling constraint everywhere else.
example: Without sticky sessions, the polling handshake lands on server A and the upgrade lands on server B, which has never heard of that session. Connection fails, mysteriously.
diagram:
LB round-robin
  handshake → server A
  upgrade   → server B → "unknown sid" ✗

Fix: ip_hash / cookie affinity,
     or a shared session store

means: A relay server used when a direct peer connection is impossible. It carries all the media, so it costs real bandwidth money.
example: Symmetric NAT on a corporate network blocks direct connection. TURN relays the stream — reliable, and now you're paying for every megabyte of that call.
diagram:
direct fails (symmetric NAT / firewall)
   ↓
Peer A → TURN relay → Peer B

~10-20% of calls need TURN
Budget bandwidth accordingly

means: A CPU limit is enforced per 100ms period. Exceeding your quota inside a period means the process is frozen until the next one — huge latency spikes, low average CPU.
example: A pod limited to 0.5 CPU that needs a 60ms burst gets throttled mid-request. P99 jumps to 300ms while the CPU graph shows a comfortable 40%.
diagram:
quota 50ms per 100ms period
  work needs 60ms
  → run 50ms → FROZEN 50ms → resume
   ↓
P99 spikes, average CPU looks fine
Watch: container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds

means: A runtime image with no shell or package manager. Fewer CVEs, and no shell for an attacker who gets code execution.
example: Switching from `node:20` to `gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20` dropped reported vulnerabilities from 180 to 3. Debugging now needs an ephemeral debug container.
diagram:
node:20           ~1.1GB, 180 CVEs, full shell
node:20-alpine    ~180MB, fewer
distroless        ~120MB, no shell at all ✓

Trade-off: no `docker exec sh` to poke around

means: Compose is a local development tool. It has no scheduling, self-healing, rolling updates or multi-node placement.
example: Compose on a single production VM works right up to the moment that VM reboots. Kubernetes or ECS reschedules; Compose does not.
diagram:
Compose: local dev, single host, no scheduler
K8s/ECS: scheduling, self-heal, rolling deploys,
         autoscale, service discovery

Compose in prod = a single point of failure

means: The container filesystem dies with the container. Anything written locally and not in a volume is gone on the next deploy.
example: Uploads saved to `/tmp/uploads` work perfectly in staging with one pod and vanish in production the moment a pod is rescheduled.
diagram:
write to container fs
  ↓ pod restarts / reschedules
gone ✗

Persist to: object storage (S3), a volume,
            or a database. Never local disk.

means: Liveness asks 'should I restart this?'. Readiness asks 'should I send traffic?'. Conflating them causes restart loops during a slow dependency.
example: A liveness probe that checks the database restarts every pod when the DB is briefly slow — turning a small blip into a full outage.
diagram:
Liveness  → process wedged? → restart
Readiness → deps ready? → route traffic
Startup   → slow boot? → don't kill it yet

Liveness must NOT check external deps

means: Each Dockerfile instruction creates a layer. Changing one invalidates every layer after it, which is why instruction order controls build time.
example: Copying the whole source before `npm ci` means every code change reinstalls all dependencies — a 3-minute build instead of 20 seconds.
diagram:
COPY . .            ← any code change
RUN npm ci          ← invalidated every time ✗

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci          ← cached until deps change ✓
COPY . .

means: `latest` is not a version. Two deploys of the same tag can run different code, which makes rollback and debugging guesswork.
example: A pod restarts and pulls a newer `latest` than its siblings. You now have two versions running and no way to tell from the manifest.
diagram:
image: app:latest
  → pod A has build 412
  → pod B has build 418  ← same tag ✗

image: app:sha-9f2c1b  ← immutable, reproducible ✓

means: Deleting a file in a later layer doesn't shrink the image — the earlier layer still contains it. And without .dockerignore you ship node_modules and .git.
example: `RUN wget big.tar && tar -xf && rm big.tar` as three instructions keeps the tarball in a layer. One chained RUN removes it from the final image.
diagram:
RUN wget big.tar     ← 400MB in this layer
RUN rm big.tar       ← still 400MB in the image ✗

RUN wget big.tar && tar -xf && rm big.tar ✓
.dockerignore: node_modules, .git, .env

means: Building in one image and copying only the artifacts into a slim runtime image. Smaller, faster to pull, and far less attack surface.
example: A Node build image with toolchain is 1.2GB. Copying just `dist` and production node_modules into an alpine runtime gives 180MB.
diagram:
FROM node AS build
  ... compile ...
FROM node:alpine
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist

1.2GB → 180MB, no compilers in production

means: Requests are what the scheduler reserves; limits are the hard ceiling. Exceeding a memory limit means SIGKILL with no cleanup and exit code 137.
example: A Node process with a 512Mi limit but no `--max-old-space-size` lets V8 grow past it. The kernel kills it at 512Mi with no stack trace — just 137.
diagram:
requests: scheduler reservation
limits:   hard cap
  CPU over limit    → throttled (slow)
  Memory over limit → OOMKilled (137, instant)

Tell the runtime about the limit too

means: Maintaining a target number of instances based on a metric. Scaling on CPU is the default and often the wrong signal.
example: An I/O-bound API sits at 25% CPU while its queue backs up. Scaling on request count per target or queue depth reflects reality; CPU doesn't.
diagram:
target tracking:
  CPU 70%              ← often wrong for I/O work
  requests per target  ← better for APIs
  queue depth / age    ← best for workers

Scale-out fast, scale-in slow

means: Edge caches serving content close to users. Cache-Control and the cache key decide your hit ratio — and a bad key means you cache nothing.
example: Forwarding all cookies to the origin makes every request unique, so the CDN caches nothing and your origin serves 100% of traffic while you pay for both.
diagram:
user → nearest edge
  hit  → 15ms, origin untouched ✓
  miss → origin fetch → cached

Cache key includes forwarded headers/cookies/query
More variance = lower hit ratio

means: Data leaving the cloud (and crossing AZs and regions) is billed. Ingress is usually free, which shapes a lot of architecture decisions.
example: A service in AZ-a chatting constantly with a database in AZ-b pays cross-AZ transfer on every query. Zone-aware routing removed a five-figure annual line item.
diagram:
ingress        free
cross-AZ       $ per GB (both directions)
cross-region   $$ per GB
internet out   $$$ per GB

Chatty cross-AZ services quietly cost real money

means: Users have long-lived credentials; roles are assumed for temporary, auto-rotating ones. Long-lived keys in production are the number one cloud breach vector.
example: An access key committed to a repo grants access until someone notices. An instance role issues credentials that rotate automatically and can't leak the same way.
diagram:
User  → static access key (leaks forever) ✗
Role  → STS temp credentials, auto-rotate ✓

EC2/ECS/Lambda → attach a role
Human → SSO → assume role

means: Idle Lambdas are frozen; the next request pays init cost. Provisioned concurrency keeps N warm at a fixed hourly price.
example: A 6-second cold start on a user-facing endpoint is unacceptable. 10 provisioned instances remove it and cost money whether traffic arrives or not.
diagram:
no traffic → environment frozen
request → init runtime + deps + handler → 6s

Provisioned concurrency: N always warm
  → 40ms, billed hourly regardless of traffic

means: Granting exactly the permissions needed, no more. `s3:*` on `*` is the policy that turns one compromised service into a full account breach.
example: A thumbnail service needs `s3:GetObject` on one bucket prefix. It usually ships with `s3:*` on `*` because that made the error go away on a Friday.
diagram:
s3:*  on  *              → total blast radius ✗
s3:GetObject on
  arn:...:bucket/uploads/* → scoped ✓

Start deny-all, add what breaks

means: Private subnets reach the internet through a NAT gateway that charges per hour and per gigabyte processed. It's a classic surprise line item.
example: A service pulling 8TB/month of container images through NAT costs more in data processing than the compute running it. A VPC endpoint for ECR removes that entirely.
diagram:
private subnet → NAT GW → internet
  hourly + per-GB processed

8TB/month through NAT = significant $$
Fix: VPC endpoints for S3/ECR/DynamoDB

means: A time-limited signed URL letting a client upload or download directly from S3 without your server proxying the bytes.
example: Proxying 500MB uploads through your API burns memory and bandwidth. A presigned PUT lets the browser upload straight to S3 while your server only issues the URL.
diagram:
client → your API: "I want to upload"
API    → presigned PUT URL (15 min, size-capped)
client → S3 directly ✓

Your server never touches the bytes

means: A region is a geographic area; an AZ is an isolated datacentre within it. Multi-AZ survives a datacentre failure; multi-region survives a region failure.
example: Running all three replicas in one AZ means a single AZ outage takes you down. Spreading across three AZs costs cross-AZ transfer and survives it.
diagram:
Region ap-south-1
  ├ AZ a  ← replica 1
  ├ AZ b  ← replica 2
  └ AZ c  ← replica 3

Multi-AZ: standard. Multi-region: expensive, rare.

means: S3 is now strongly read-after-write consistent. Versioning keeps every overwrite, which is what makes accidental deletion recoverable.
example: Without versioning, an overwrite is permanent. With it plus MFA delete, a compromised key can't silently destroy your data.
diagram:
PUT → immediately readable ✓ (since 2020)
Versioning ON:
  overwrite → new version, old retained
  delete    → delete marker, recoverable ✓
Lifecycle rules → expire old versions

means: Secrets in a managed store can be rotated, audited and scoped by IAM. Secrets in plain environment variables leak into logs, crash dumps and process listings.
example: A DB password in an env var shows up in an error report sent to a third-party logging service. In a secrets manager it's fetched at boot with an audit trail.
diagram:
env var: visible in `ps`, crash dumps,
  child processes, error trackers ✗
Secrets Manager / Parameter Store:
  IAM-scoped, rotatable, audited ✓

means: Spot is cheap capacity reclaimed with two minutes' notice. Reserved trades commitment for discount. On-demand is flexible and most expensive.
example: Batch OCR on spot instances cuts cost 70% and needs checkpointing so a reclaim resumes rather than restarts. Never put a stateful primary on spot.
diagram:
On-demand  baseline price, no commitment
Reserved    ~40-60% off, 1-3 yr commitment
Spot        ~70-90% off, 2-min eviction notice

Spot: stateless, checkpointed, retryable work

means: The private network. Public subnets route to an internet gateway; private ones don't. Security groups are stateful instance-level firewalls.
example: Databases belong in private subnets with a security group allowing 5432 only from the app's security group — not from a CIDR block, and never from 0.0.0.0/0.
diagram:
VPC
 ├ public subnet  → IGW → internet
 └ private subnet → NAT → outbound only

SG: stateful, allow-only, reference other SGs
NACL: stateless, subnet-level, allow+deny

means: Resolvers cache DNS answers for the TTL. A failover with a 24-hour TTL means a day of traffic going to a dead address.
example: Lower the TTL to 60 seconds a week before a migration. Do it during the migration and you're still waiting on the old cached value.
diagram:
TTL 86400 → resolvers cache 24h
  failover → old IP served for a day ✗

Lower TTL to 60s BEFORE the change ✓
Some resolvers ignore very low TTLs anyway

means: Nginx opens a new connection to the backend per request unless you configure an upstream keepalive pool.
example: Adding `keepalive 64` plus HTTP/1.1 and clearing the Connection header removed 12ms of connection setup from every single request.

means: When the LB's idle timeout exceeds the backend's, the backend closes a connection the LB still thinks is open — producing intermittent 502s nobody can reproduce.
example: ALB idle timeout 60s, Node `keepAliveTimeout` 5s. Roughly 0.1% of requests get a 502 at random, and no log on either side explains it.
diagram:
LB idle timeout   60s
Node keepAlive     5s   ← closes first
   ↓ LB reuses dead connection
502, intermittent, unreproducible

Rule: backend timeout > LB timeout

means: Whether the location prefix is stripped depends on a trailing slash in proxy_pass. It's the most common Nginx configuration bug.
example: `proxy_pass http://api;` forwards `/api/users` as `/api/users`. Adding a trailing slash forwards it as `/users`. One character, completely different routing.

means: A new HTTPS connection costs a TCP round trip plus a TLS negotiation before any data moves. On mobile networks this dominates small requests.
example: At 80ms RTT, TCP plus TLS 1.2 costs ~240ms before the first byte of the request. TLS 1.3 cuts it to ~160ms; session resumption to ~80ms.
diagram:
TCP: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK        (1 RTT)
TLS 1.2: 2 RTT   TLS 1.3: 1 RTT
   ↓
then your request finally sends
Keep-alive amortises all of this

means: The backend pool and how requests are distributed. Round-robin ignores how busy a server actually is.
example: Round-robin sends equal traffic to a server stuck on slow requests. `least_conn` routes to the least busy one and smooths the tail.
diagram:
round_robin  → even count, ignores load
least_conn   → fewest active connections ✓
ip_hash      → session affinity

max_fails + fail_timeout = passive health check

means: Nginx's concurrency ceiling is workers × connections. Leaving defaults on a busy box causes refused connections while CPU sits idle.
example: 1 worker × 512 connections caps you at ~512 concurrent. `worker_processes auto` on 8 cores with 4096 connections gives ~32,000.
diagram:
max concurrent ≈ workers × worker_connections
  1 × 512   = 512   ← default, low
  8 × 4096  = 32768 ✓

Also raise the OS file-descriptor limit

means: Behind a proxy, the app sees the proxy's IP. Rate limiting and audit logs record the wrong address unless forwarded headers are set and trusted.
example: Every request appears to come from 10.0.1.4, so per-IP rate limiting throttles everyone at once. Setting `trust proxy` and X-Forwarded-For fixes it.
diagram:
client 1.2.3.4 → Nginx → app sees 10.0.1.4 ✗

proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
app: trust proxy ✓

Only trust it from your own proxy, or it's spoofable

means: Too many non-actionable alerts train people to ignore them, including the real one. Every alert should be actionable, urgent and linked to a runbook.
example: A team gets 60 pages a week, 58 self-resolve. When the real outage pages at 3am, on-call silences it out of habit.
diagram:
Every page must be:
  actionable (a human can do something)
  urgent (can't wait for morning)
  documented (runbook linked)

Otherwise → ticket or dashboard, not a page

means: The number of unique label combinations on a metric. High cardinality is what makes a Prometheus instance fall over.
example: Adding `user_id` as a label to a request counter with 2M users creates 2M time series. Prometheus OOMs; the label belongs in a trace or log, not a metric.
diagram:
http_requests{route, method, status}
  20 × 4 × 6 = 480 series ✓

+ user_id (2M users) = 960,000,000 series ✗

High-cardinality identifiers → logs/traces

means: A single ID threaded through every log line, span and message for one user action, so you can reconstruct it end to end.
example: A support ticket includes the request ID from the error page. One query returns every log line across seven services for that exact request.
diagram:
user action → generate/accept request_id
  ↓ every log line includes it
  ↓ propagated to queues, downstream calls
  ↓ shown to the user on error pages

means: A counter only goes up (use rate()). A gauge goes up and down. A histogram buckets observations so you can compute percentiles.
example: Using a gauge for request latency gives you the last value, which is meaningless. A histogram gives you P50/P95/P99 across the whole window.
diagram:
Counter   requests_total     → rate(...[5m])
Gauge     queue_depth        → current value
Histogram request_duration   → quantiles
Summary   client-side quantiles, can't aggregate

means: Following one request across every service it touches, so you can see exactly where the time went.
example: A 9-second search: auth 0.2s, retrieval 1s, reranking 6s, model 1.5s. Logs said 'slow'. The trace named the culprit in one screen.
diagram:
trace abc123 ───────────────────────── 9.0s
├ auth            ▌                     0.2s
├ retrieval       ███                   1.0s
│ └ vector search ██                    0.8s
├ rerank          ████████████████████  6.0s ←
└ model           ████                  1.5s

A tree of parent/child spans, not a flat list.
The indentation is where the time actually went.

means: Google's four: latency, traffic, errors, saturation. If you only get four graphs per service, these are the four.
example: Saturation is the one teams skip and the one that predicts the next outage — a queue growing steadily is a failure that hasn't happened yet.
diagram:
Latency     how slow
Traffic     how much
Errors      how broken
Saturation  how close to the limit ← leading indicator

means: A dashboard should answer a question, not display everything available. Forty panels means nobody reads any of them during an incident.
example: One overview per service with the four golden signals, and drill-downs behind links. Panels ordered so the top row answers 'is it broken?'.
diagram:
Row 1: is it broken? (SLI, error rate)
Row 2: where? (per-endpoint, per-dependency)
Row 3: why? (resources, saturation)

40 panels of everything = read by no one

means: You cannot average P99s across instances. Averaging percentiles is mathematically wrong and hides the worst instance.
example: Three pods report P99 of 100ms, 100ms and 3s. The average says 1.07s; the real fleet-wide P99 must be computed from the raw buckets.
diagram:
avg(P99 per pod)  ✗ meaningless
histogram_quantile(0.99,
  sum(rate(bucket[5m])) by (le))  ✓

Aggregate the buckets, then compute the quantile

means: `rate()` is per-second average over a window; `increase()` is the total over it. Applying either to a gauge produces nonsense.
example: `rate(http_requests_total[5m])` gives requests per second and handles counter resets on pod restart. Raw `http_requests_total` just climbs forever.
diagram:
counter: ▁▂▃▄▅ (monotonic, resets on restart)
rate(c[5m])     → per-second average ✓
increase(c[1h]) → total in that hour ✓

Never rate() a gauge

means: For every request-driven service, track Rate, Errors and Duration. Three metrics that cover most of what you need.
example: A new service ships with request rate, error rate and latency histogram on day one. That's enough to detect and triage nearly every incident.
diagram:
R  Rate      requests/sec
E  Errors    failed requests/sec
D  Duration  latency distribution

Same three for every service = comparable dashboards

means: Head sampling decides at the start (cheap, may miss the interesting request). Tail sampling decides after seeing the whole trace, so you can always keep errors and slow requests.
example: 1% head sampling misses 99% of the rare 8-second requests you actually want. Tail sampling keeps 100% of errors and slow traces plus 1% of normal ones.
diagram:
Head: decide at request start
  1% kept → rare failures usually missed ✗
Tail: buffer, decide at the end
  keep all errors + all slow + 1% normal ✓
  cost: buffering infrastructure

means: A trace is a tree of spans, each with an ID and a parent. Context must propagate through HTTP headers and message metadata or the trace breaks in half.
example: The trace stops at the queue boundary because traceparent wasn't copied into the message headers. The consumer's work appears as an unrelated trace.
diagram:
traceparent: 00-{trace_id}-{span_id}-01
  ↓ HTTP header ✓ usually automatic
  ↓ message header ✗ usually forgotten

Broken propagation = orphaned traces

means: Alert on what users experience, not on internal causes. Cause-based alerts fire constantly and miss the failures you didn't predict.
example: 'CPU > 80%' pages during a harmless batch job. 'Checkout success rate < 99%' pages only when users are actually hurting.
diagram:
Cause-based:   CPU high, pod restarted, disk 70%
  → noisy, misses novel failures

Symptom-based: error rate, latency SLI,
  checkout success → always matters ✓

means: For every resource, track Utilisation, Saturation and Errors. The counterpart to RED for CPU, memory, disk and pools.
example: CPU utilisation at 60% looks fine until you check saturation — the run queue is 12 deep, so processes are waiting despite 'spare' CPU.
diagram:
U  Utilisation  % busy
S  Saturation   queued work waiting ← the useful one
E  Errors       failed operations

Applies to: CPU, memory, disk, network, conn pools

means: A short-lived access token limits the damage from a leak; a long-lived refresh token, stored more carefully, mints new ones.
example: 15-minute access tokens mean a leaked one is nearly worthless. Refresh tokens live in an HttpOnly cookie and rotate on every use so reuse is detectable.
diagram:
access  15 min, sent on every request
refresh  30 days, HttpOnly cookie, rotates

Rotation: reuse of an old refresh token
  → the family is compromised → revoke all

means: Exposing a record ID and trusting the client not to change it. Consistently one of the most common real-world API vulnerabilities.
example: `GET /api/invoices/4471` returns any invoice to any authenticated user. Changing the number in the URL walks the whole table.
diagram:
GET /api/invoices/4471  ← authenticated ✓
   ↓ no ownership check
returns someone else's invoice ✗

Always: WHERE id = ? AND owner_id = :current_user

means: A signed, self-contained token. The server doesn't need to look it up — which is the feature, and also why you can't revoke it.
example: A 24-hour access token for a user you just banned stays valid for 24 hours. Short expiry plus a refresh token plus a denylist is the practical answer.
diagram:
header.payload.signature (base64url)
  signed, NOT encrypted → readable by anyone
  ↓
stateless ✓, revocation hard ✗
Short TTL (15m) + refresh token + denylist

means: Both sides present certificates, so the server verifies the client's identity too. The transport-level foundation of zero-trust networking.
example: Service A can only call service B if it presents a valid client certificate. A compromised pod without one can't talk to anything, even inside the VPC.
diagram:
normal TLS: client verifies server
mTLS: both verify each other ✓

Network position no longer implies trust
Usually handled by the service mesh sidecar

means: The standard browser and mobile flow. The code is exchanged server-side; PKCE stops an intercepted code from being redeemed by an attacker.
example: The implicit flow put tokens in the URL fragment where they leak via history and referrers. Auth code with PKCE is the current recommendation everywhere.
diagram:
app → /authorize?code_challenge=SHA256(v)
user logs in → redirect with ?code=xyz
app → /token  code=xyz + code_verifier=v
   ↓ verifier must hash to the challenge
tokens issued ✓

means: Changing credentials on a schedule and after any suspicion, with overlapping validity so nothing breaks mid-rotation.
example: A key from 2021 still in production is one leaked laptop from an incident. Rotation with two valid keys during the window means zero downtime.
diagram:
issue new key (both valid)
  ↓ deploy consumers to the new key
  ↓ verify no traffic on the old one
  ↓ revoke old key

Rotation that requires downtime never happens

means: Sessions are server-side state you can revoke instantly. Tokens are stateless and scale better. Most apps want sessions and think they want JWTs.
example: A single-domain web app gets simpler and safer with an HttpOnly session cookie. JWTs earn their complexity when multiple services must verify without a shared session store.
diagram:
Session: cookie → server store
  revoke instantly ✓, needs shared store
JWT: self-contained
  no lookup ✓, revocation is a workaround

Single web app? Session cookie is usually right.

means: Making your server fetch a URL an attacker controls, reaching internal services and cloud metadata endpoints your firewall trusts.
example: A 'fetch image from URL' feature pointed at the cloud metadata IP returns instance credentials. Allowlist destinations and block private ranges.
diagram:
user supplies URL → your server fetches it
  http://169.254.169.254/  → cloud credentials ✗
  http://localhost:6379/   → internal Redis ✗

Defence: allowlist domains, block private CIDRs,
         resolve DNS then validate the IP

means: Compromising a dependency instead of your code. A single malicious postinstall script runs with your build's full privileges.
example: A popular package publishes a version exfiltrating environment variables. Lockfiles, `npm ci`, and `--ignore-scripts` in CI reduce the exposure.
diagram:
attacker → popular package → your build
  postinstall script → reads env → exfiltrates

Defence: lockfile committed, npm ci,
  pin versions, audit in CI, SBOM,
  --ignore-scripts where possible

means: String comparison exits at the first mismatch, leaking how much of a secret was correct. Constant-time comparison always takes the same duration.
example: Verifying an API key with `===` leaks a few microseconds per correct character. Enough samples and an attacker reconstructs it byte by byte.
diagram:
"abcdef" === "axxxxx"  → exits at index 1 (fast)
"abcdef" === "abcdex"  → exits at index 5 (slower)
   ↓ measurable difference

crypto.timingSafeEqual(a, b) ✓

means: Defining when the system should decline to answer and hand off, instead of producing a confident guess.
example: If retrieval returns nothing above a similarity floor, the correct output is 'I don't have that' plus a route to a human — not a fluent, unsupported answer.
diagram:
no relevant context / low confidence / out of scope
  ↓
say so + offer a route (human, search, docs)

Measure abstention rate:
  too low  → hallucinating
  too high → useless
how:
Instruction-tuned models are shaped to be helpful, which means that when they don't know something they tend to produce an answer anyway. Not knowing is not a state they naturally express.

An abstention policy defines when the system should decline, and makes declining a real path rather than something you hope the model chooses.

The clearest trigger is retrieval: if nothing came back above a similarity threshold, the correct output is that you don't have the information — not an answer generated from training memory.

Other triggers: the request falls outside the supported scope, required fields failed validation, or a groundedness check found unsupported claims.

Crucially, declining should route somewhere. "I don't have that" is unhelpful on its own; "I don't have that — here's how to reach support" is a working product.
more: Track the abstention rate as a metric with bounds on both sides. Too low and the system is answering things it shouldn't, which is hallucination wearing a helpful face. Too high and it's useless, and users stop asking. Sample abstained requests weekly and read them — they show you where the corpus has genuine gaps.
diagram2:
Triggers:
  retrieval below the similarity floor
  out of supported scope
  validation failed · groundedness check failed
  ↓
say so, AND route somewhere

  "I don't have that."              incomplete
  "I don't have that — contact
   support, or try X."              a product ✓

Rate has bounds on BOTH sides:
  too low  → hallucinating helpfully
  too high → useless, users stop asking

Read abstained requests weekly.
They map your corpus gaps.

means: Hard ceilings on steps, tokens, wall time and spend per agent run. Without them a confused loop is unbounded.
example: An agent stuck retrying a failing tool ran 340 steps before anyone noticed. Caps of 25 steps and a token ceiling turn that into a clean, alertable failure.
diagram:
per run: max steps, max tokens, max wall time,
         max spend, loop detection
  ↓ exceeded → stop, surface partial result, alert

An agent without caps is an unbounded bill
with a plausible explanation
how:
An agent decides its own next step, which means it decides how long it runs. Left unbounded, a confused agent doesn't stop — it keeps taking locally reasonable actions that make no overall progress.

The typical shape: a tool returns an error the model reads as transient, so it retries. The retry fails identically. Each individual decision looks sensible in isolation, and the run continues indefinitely.

Caps make termination external rather than depending on the model recognising futility. Bound maximum steps, total tokens, wall-clock time and spend, per run, and stop on whichever trips first.

Add loop detection alongside them: the same tool called with the same arguments three times means no progress is being made, regardless of remaining budget.
more: When a cap trips, return the partial result with an explanation rather than failing silently. A user who receives "I got through three of five steps and then stopped" can act on that; a spinner that never resolves teaches them the feature is broken. Alert on cap trips too — a rising rate is usually a broken tool rather than a hard task.
diagram2:
Per run, bound:
  max steps · max tokens
  max wall time · max spend
  → stop on whichever trips first

Plus loop detection:
  same tool + same arguments, 3 times
  → no progress, stop regardless of budget

On trip:
  return the partial result + an explanation ✓
  never a spinner that never resolves

Alert on the trip RATE.
Rising usually means a broken tool, not a hard task.

means: Online inference answers a user now; batch processes large volumes on a schedule, often at a substantial discount and with far higher throughput.
example: Embedding a 40M-document backlog through the online API is slow and expensive. The batch endpoint runs overnight at roughly half the cost.
diagram:
Online: low latency, per-request price, interactive
Batch:  hours of latency, discounted, high throughput

Backfills, re-embeddings, bulk classification,
nightly enrichment → batch, always
how:
Online inference serves a user who is waiting. Latency is the constraint, and you pay standard rates for the privilege of an immediate answer.

Batch inference submits a large job and collects results later — typically within hours. Providers discount this substantially, often around half, because it lets them fill capacity when demand is low.

The distinction is about who is waiting, not about volume. Anything where nobody is watching should be batch: backfilling embeddings, classifying a historical archive, nightly enrichment, generating evaluation results, re-processing after a parser fix.

Running those through the online API is a common and expensive habit — it's the path already built, so it's the path used, and the discount is left on the table.
more: Batch changes the failure model, and that's the part to design for. A job submitted now returns hours later, so results arrive asynchronously and partial failures need reconciling against what was submitted. Track submitted, completed and failed counts per job, and make resubmission of just the failures straightforward.
diagram2:
Online: someone is waiting
  low latency · standard rate

Batch: nobody is waiting
  hours of latency · ~50% discount
  higher throughput

Batch candidates:
  backfills · historical classification
  nightly enrichment · eval runs
  reprocessing after a parser fix

Design for async failure:
  track submitted / completed / failed
  make resubmitting only the failures easy

means: Whether stated or derived confidence actually predicts correctness. Models are typically overconfident, so raw self-reported confidence is not a routing signal.
example: Answers the model rated 'high confidence' were wrong 22% of the time. Calibrating against labelled outcomes produced a threshold that was actually usable for auto-approval.
diagram:
plot stated confidence vs actual accuracy
  well calibrated: 0.9 stated → ~90% correct
  typical:         0.9 stated → ~70% correct ✗

Calibrate on real outcomes before you
route or auto-approve on confidence
how:
It's tempting to route on confidence — auto-approve above a threshold, review below it. That only works if the confidence number actually predicts correctness, and by default it usually doesn't.

Models are typically overconfident. Outputs rated highly confident are wrong more often than the number suggests, and self-reported confidence is the weakest signal of all — asking a model how sure it is produces a plausible number, not a measured one.

Calibration is checking empirically. Take a few hundred outputs with known correct answers, group them by stated confidence, and compare each group's claimed confidence against its actual accuracy. Well calibrated means 0.9 confidence corresponds to about 90% correct.

If it doesn't, you can still use the signal — but you need to derive your threshold from the measured curve rather than the stated number.
more: Derived signals often calibrate better than stated ones: agreement across several samples, retrieval similarity scores, whether output passed validation, or the model's token probabilities where the provider exposes them. Test a few against your ground truth and use whichever actually tracks correctness.
diagram2:
Stated 0.9 confidence → actual 70% correct
  → overconfident, threshold is meaningless

Measure it:
  group outputs by stated confidence
  compare each group's claimed vs actual accuracy

  0.9 → 90%  well calibrated ✓
  0.9 → 70%  derive your threshold from the curve

Better signals than "how sure are you?":
  agreement across samples · retrieval similarity
  validation pass/fail · token probabilities

means: Summarising or filtering retrieved content before it enters the prompt, so long context stays affordable and the model stays focused.
example: Feeding 40 pages of contract text costs a lot and buries the clause. Extracting only the passages relevant to the question keeps the answer sharp and the bill small.
diagram:
retrieved 40 pages
  ↓ extractive filter: keep query-relevant passages
  ↓ or abstractive: summarise per document
  ↓ 3 pages into the prompt

Risk: the compressor drops the one thing that mattered
how:
Prompt compression trims what you send. Context compression reduces retrieved content specifically, by summarising or filtering it before it enters the prompt.

Two approaches. Extractive filtering keeps only the sentences or passages relevant to the current query and discards the rest — cheap, and it preserves the original wording, which matters for grounding and citation. Abstractive summarisation has a model rewrite the content more compactly — higher compression, and now the model is reading a summary rather than the source.

That second point is the risk worth being explicit about. An abstractive summary is generated text, so it can drop the specific detail that mattered or introduce something that wasn't there.

Extractive filtering is the safer default in a grounded system, precisely because it can't invent anything.
more: Compression is usually the wrong first move. Better retrieval and reranking reduce context by selecting well rather than by discarding after the fact, and they improve quality instead of risking it. Reach for compression when you have genuinely long relevant documents — a full contract, a long transcript — that must be read rather than merely searched.
diagram2:
EXTRACTIVE — keep relevant passages, drop the rest
  cheap · original wording preserved
  citations and grounding still work ✓

ABSTRACTIVE — model rewrites more compactly
  higher compression
  generated text: can drop the key detail,
  can introduce something not in the source ✗

Try in this order:
  better retrieval → reranking → compression

Compression is for long documents that must
be READ, not for fixing weak retrieval.

means: Cost divided by tasks actually completed, not requests made. Retries, failures and abandoned sessions are real spend that per-request pricing hides.
example: Per-request cost looked fine until retries and abandonment were counted: the true cost per completed extraction was over twice the headline number.
diagram:
cost per request:        headline number
cost per SUCCESSFUL task: the real number

includes: retries, failed parses, abandoned
          sessions, human review time

Improving success rate cuts cost more than
switching models often does
how:
Cost per request is the number that's easy to measure and the wrong one to manage.

Real usage includes work that produced nothing: requests that failed validation and retried, outputs the user rejected and regenerated, sessions abandoned halfway, agent runs that hit a step cap without finishing.

All of that is billed. None of it delivered anything.

Cost per successful task divides total spend by tasks actually completed, and the two numbers can differ by a factor of two or more. That gap is where the real optimisation is.

The reframing changes what you work on. Improving success rate from 70% to 85% reduces cost per outcome by roughly 18% without touching prompts, models or infrastructure — and it improves the product at the same time, which switching to a cheaper model does not.
more: Include human cost where a review step exists. If 15% of documents need a minute of someone's attention, that labour usually dwarfs the inference spend, and reducing the review rate is worth far more than any token optimisation. Counting only API cost leads teams to optimise the smaller number.
diagram2:
cost per request:        the easy number
cost per SUCCESSFUL task: the real one

Includes:
  retries · failed validations · regenerations
  abandoned sessions · agent runs that hit caps

Often 2x+ the headline figure.

70% → 85% success rate
  = ~18% lower cost per outcome
  + a better product
  (switching to a cheaper model does the opposite)

Count human review time. It usually dominates.

means: The loop where production usage generates data that improves the system, which drives more usage. It only exists if you deliberately capture the signal.
example: Corrections in the review queue become labelled training data. Six months later the review rate has halved because the model learned from its own failures.
diagram:
usage → outputs → corrections/feedback
  ↓ captured, labelled
  ↓ evals + fine-tuning + retrieval improvements
  ↓ better product → more usage ↺

No capture mechanism = no flywheel, just usage
how:
The idea is that usage produces data, the data improves the system, and a better system drives more usage. It compounds, and it is the durable advantage in an AI product — anyone can call the same model, but nobody else has your corrections.

The part that doesn't happen automatically is capture. Usage alone produces logs, not training data. Turning one into the other requires deliberate mechanisms: a review queue where corrections are recorded, feedback controls whose results are stored in a usable shape, and outcome tracking that says whether a task actually completed.

Without those, you have traffic and a growing log bill.

The mechanisms are unglamorous and worth building early, because the compounding only starts once they exist — and a year of uncaptured usage is a year of the flywheel not turning.
more: Design the capture so a correction records what right looks like, not just that something was wrong. A thumbs-down is a signal; an edited output is a training example. The difference in value is enormous and the difference in interface effort is small, which makes it one of the better returns available in an AI product.
diagram2:
usage → outputs → corrections → better system → usage ↺

The loop only turns if you CAPTURE:
  ├ review queue records what was fixed
  ├ feedback stored in a usable shape
  └ outcomes tracked (did the task complete?)

Without capture: traffic and a log bill.

thumbs-down     → "wrong"          (weak)
edited output   → "here is right"  (strong) ✓
  small interface difference, huge data difference

means: Storing enough of a request — prompt, model version, retrieved context, parameters, seed — to reproduce it exactly during debugging.
example: 'The model gave a wrong answer' is unfixable without the retrieved context. With a full replay record you re-run it and see the retrieval returned nothing relevant.
diagram:
log per request:
  prompt (rendered), model + version, params, seed,
  retrieved chunk ids, tool calls, raw output

Replay → reproduce → find whether it was
retrieval, prompt or model
how:
"The model gave a wrong answer" is not a reproducible bug report. Re-running the same user question may produce something different, and the context that produced the original answer is gone.

Replay means capturing enough to reconstruct the request exactly: the fully rendered prompt, the model and version, all sampling parameters, the retrieved chunk IDs and their content, any tool calls and results, and the raw output.

The rendered prompt is the crucial piece. Your code assembles it from templates, retrieval results and conversation history, so the template alone doesn't show what the model actually received.

With a complete record, debugging becomes reading. Most surprising outputs turn out to be surprising inputs — retrieval returned nothing relevant, history was truncated oddly, a template variable was empty.
more: Capture this at a sampled rate on successful requests to control storage, and at full rate on anything that failed, was flagged, or received negative feedback. That gives you complete records exactly where you'll need them without paying to store every successful interaction in full detail.
diagram2:
Capture per request:
  ├ the RENDERED prompt  ← most skipped, most needed
  ├ model + version + all sampling parameters
  ├ retrieved chunk ids AND their content
  ├ tool calls and their results
  └ raw output

Most surprising OUTPUTS are surprising INPUTS:
  retrieval returned nothing relevant
  history truncated oddly
  a template variable was empty

Sample on success. Capture everything on failure.

means: Turning heterogeneous source formats into clean text with structure preserved. It's where most RAG quality is won or lost, before any model is involved.
example: PDFs parsed with a naive text extractor lost every table and heading. Switching to a layout-aware parser improved answer quality more than changing the model did.
diagram:
PDF / DOCX / HTML / scan
  ↓ format-specific parser
  ↓ preserve: headings, tables, lists, page numbers
  ↓ strip: nav, boilerplate, repeated headers/footers

Garbage in here cannot be fixed downstream
how:
Everything downstream inherits whatever the parser produced. A chunk can only be as good as the text it was cut from, and a model can only answer from what it was given.

The naive approach — extract all the text from a PDF — loses exactly what makes a document navigable. Headings vanish, so chunks lose their context. Tables become a stream of numbers with no column association. Repeated headers and footers appear in every chunk as noise.

Format-aware parsing preserves structure: which lines are headings, which regions are tables, what the reading order is, which page each piece came from.

The reason this matters more than it seems: a retrieval failure caused by bad parsing is indistinguishable, from the outside, from a model failure. Teams spend weeks on prompts and models when the actual problem was a parser that scrambled two-column pages.
more: Always keep the page number and source location with each chunk. It costs nothing at ingest and gives you citations, click-to-source verification, and the ability to debug a bad answer by looking at the original page. Retrofitting it means reprocessing the entire corpus, which is why it's worth doing on day one.
diagram2:
Bad parse, then:
  ├ chunks lose their heading context
  ├ tables become an unlabelled number stream
  ├ nav and footers repeat as noise in every chunk
  └ two-column pages are read across, scrambled

From the outside this looks like a MODEL problem.
Teams debug prompts for weeks.

Preserve: headings · tables · reading order
          page numbers · source location
                        ↑ do this on day one,
                          retrofitting = full reprocess

means: The embedding model or preprocessing changing so new vectors are no longer comparable with old ones. Retrieval quality degrades quietly.
example: A library upgrade changed default normalisation. New documents were embedded slightly differently and stopped matching queries the old ones matched fine.
diagram:
same text, different model/version/preprocessing
  → different vector → incomparable

Pin the embedding model version.
Record it alongside every vector.
Mixed-version indexes silently degrade recall.
how:
Every vector in your index was produced by a specific model, with specific preprocessing, at a specific version. Vectors are only comparable to others produced the same way.

Drift is when that quietly stops being true. A library upgrade changes default normalisation. The provider updates the embedding model behind an unversioned name. Someone changes the text-cleaning step for new documents but not for old ones.

Now part of your index lives in one space and part in another. Distances between them are arbitrary. Retrieval quality degrades in a way that looks random rather than systematic — some queries fine, some inexplicably poor.

Nothing errors, because there's nothing structurally wrong. The vectors are all the right shape.
more: Store the embedding model name, its version and a preprocessing version alongside every vector, and assert on startup that the query path uses the same combination. It's a few lines, and it converts a class of silent multi-week degradation into a loud failure at deploy time — which is exactly the trade you want.
diagram2:
Causes:
  library upgrade changes normalisation
  provider updates an unversioned model
  preprocessing changed for new docs only

Result:
  part of the index in space A
  part in space B
  distances between them are meaningless

Symptom: some queries fine, some inexplicably bad.
No error — the vectors are the right shape.

Store model + version + preprocessing per vector.
Assert on startup. Fail loudly at deploy.

means: The runnable system that scores model outputs against a dataset. Without one, every change is judged by whoever tried three prompts and liked the result.
example: A harness that runs 300 cases through the current and candidate configuration and prints a scored diff turns a two-day argument into a four-minute answer.
diagram:
dataset + config → run → score → report
  ↓
per-case scores, aggregate, diff vs baseline

Must be: runnable in CI, reproducible,
         fast enough that people actually run it
how:
A harness is the code that runs your dataset through a configuration, scores the outputs and reports the result. It's the difference between "this feels better" and a number.

Three properties determine whether it gets used. It has to be runnable with one command, or people won't. It has to be fast enough to sit inside the development loop — minutes, not hours — which usually means parallelising the calls. And it has to produce a comparison against a baseline, because an absolute score answers nothing on its own.

The output that matters most is per-case, not aggregate. "84% versus 81%" tells you the direction. The list of cases that regressed tells you what broke, and that's what you act on.

Build it before you start optimising anything, not after.
more: Wire it into CI on any change to prompts, models or retrieval configuration, and post the delta on the pull request. Once the score is visible next to the diff, arguments about whether a change helps stop being arguments. That single integration does more for quality discipline than any amount of process.
diagram2:
one command → dataset × config → scores → report

Must be:
  ├ one command, or nobody runs it
  ├ minutes not hours (parallelise the calls)
  └ compared to a baseline, always

Report per case, not just an aggregate:
  84% vs 81%           → direction
  6 cases regressed    → what to actually fix ✓

Post the delta on the PR.
The argument ends there.

means: The mechanism that turns user signal into a usable label. Thumbs are cheap and low-signal; corrections are expensive and high-signal.
example: Thumbs-down tells you something was wrong. An edited answer tells you what right looks like — which is the only one of the two you can train on.
diagram:
implicit: copied, retried, abandoned, escalated
explicit: thumbs, edits, corrections

Thumbs-down: "wrong" (weak)
Edited output: "here is correct" (strong) ✓
how:
Feedback comes in two grades and they're worth very different amounts.

Implicit signals are free and abundant: did the user copy the answer, retry the question, abandon the session, escalate to support. They're noisy — a user might retry because they thought of a better question — but they cover all traffic.

Explicit signals are scarcer and stronger: a thumbs rating, a correction, an edit. Among these, corrections are worth far more than ratings, because a rating tells you an answer was wrong while a correction tells you what right would have been.

The design lesson is to make correcting easy. If the interface only offers thumbs, you collect the weak signal. If it lets users edit the output and saves the edit, you collect training data as a byproduct of normal use.
more: Beware selection bias in explicit feedback. People rate when they're annoyed or delighted, rarely when things are merely fine, so your explicit dataset over-represents extremes. Use it to find failure modes, and use implicit signals or a sampled review for anything you intend to treat as a rate.
diagram2:
IMPLICIT — free, noisy, covers everything
  copied · retried · abandoned · escalated

EXPLICIT — scarce, strong, biased to extremes
  thumbs < correction < edited output

Make correcting easy:
  thumbs only      → weak signal
  editable output  → training data from normal use ✓

Explicit feedback over-represents extremes.
Use it to FIND failures.
Use implicit or sampled review to MEASURE rates.

means: The path from source document to indexed, retrievable chunk. Each stage fails differently and needs its own observability and retry semantics.
example: A pipeline that silently drops PDFs it can't parse leaves gaps nobody notices until a user asks about a missing document. Per-stage counters make the gap visible.
diagram:
fetch → parse → clean → chunk → enrich
      → embed → upsert → verify
  ↓
count in vs count out at EVERY stage
Failures go to a DLQ, never to /dev/null
how:
Between a source document and a retrievable chunk sit half a dozen stages — fetch, parse, clean, chunk, enrich, embed, upsert — and each fails in its own way.

The characteristic failure of these pipelines is silence. A PDF the parser can't read produces zero chunks. An embedding call that times out produces nothing. In both cases the pipeline continues happily and the document simply isn't there, and nobody finds out until a user asks about it and gets nothing.

The defence is counting at every boundary. Documents fetched, documents parsed, chunks produced, chunks embedded, chunks upserted. When the numbers stop matching, you know which stage dropped things and roughly how many.

Failures go to a dead-letter queue with the reason attached, never to a swallowed exception.
more: Make the whole pipeline idempotent and resumable, keyed on a stable document identifier plus a content hash. You will need to reprocess — after a parser fix, a chunking change, an embedding upgrade — and reprocessing should update in place rather than creating duplicates. Designing that in from the start costs little; retrofitting it after a duplicated corpus costs a lot.
diagram2:
fetch → parse → clean → chunk → enrich → embed → upsert

Count in and out at EVERY boundary:
  fetched  1,000
  parsed     994   ← 6 unparseable, where are they?
  chunked  8,210
  embedded 8,210
  upserted 8,210

Failures → DLQ with the reason attached.
Never a swallowed exception.

Idempotent on (doc id + content hash),
because you WILL reprocess.

means: Running a maintained corpus of known bypass techniques against every model or prompt change, because a model update can silently reopen a closed hole.
example: A prompt refactor that improved answer quality also re-enabled two previously blocked bypasses. The automated suite caught it before release.
diagram:
corpus of known techniques (roleplay, encoding,
  hypothetical framing, instruction override, ...)
  ↓ run on every prompt/model change
  ↓ bypass rate tracked over time

New model version = rerun everything
how:
Jailbreak techniques are public, catalogued and continuously evolving: roleplay framing, hypothetical scenarios, encoding the request, instruction override, incremental escalation across turns.

Maintaining a corpus of them and running it automatically on every model or prompt change is straightforward and catches a specific problem that manual review does not.

That problem is silent reopening. A prompt refactor that improves answer quality can re-enable a bypass that was closed months ago, because nothing about the refactor looked security-relevant. A provider model update can do the same with no change on your side at all.

Tracking bypass rate over time turns this into a number you watch rather than something you rediscover.
more: Keep the corpus updated — techniques that work now didn't exist a year ago, and a static corpus slowly stops testing anything current. And test the whole system rather than the model alone: a bypass that gets the model to produce something disallowed is far less serious if the output classifier catches it, and knowing which layer held is what tells you where to invest.
diagram2:
Corpus of known techniques:
  roleplay · hypothetical framing · encoding
  instruction override · multi-turn escalation

Run on EVERY prompt or model change.

Catches the silent reopening:
  a quality-focused prompt refactor
  re-enables a bypass closed months ago ✗
  a provider update does it with no change from you
