Track bypass rate over time.
Test the SYSTEM, not the model —
which layer held tells you where to invest.

means: Allocating a total time budget across retrieval, reranking, generation and post-processing, so nobody optimises a stage that wasn't the problem.
example: A 3-second budget: 200ms retrieval, 150ms rerank, 400ms TTFT, rest streaming. Written down, it made it obvious that reranking was not worth optimising.
diagram:
total 3.0s
  ├ retrieval    200ms
  ├ rerank       150ms
  ├ TTFT         400ms
  └ streaming    remainder

Measure each stage separately or you will
optimise the wrong one
how:
Without a budget, latency work goes wherever someone's attention landed rather than where the time actually is.

A budget allocates a total target across stages. For a RAG endpoint targeting three seconds: query processing, retrieval, reranking, prefill up to first token, then streaming for the remainder.

Writing it down does two useful things immediately. It reveals which stages are worth optimising — a reranker taking 150ms of a 3,000ms budget is not your problem no matter how inefficient it looks. And it forces a decision about the target, which otherwise stays vague and unfalsifiable.

Measure each stage separately in your traces, not just the total. A total tells you there's a problem; the breakdown tells you where.
more: Budget time to first token separately from total, because they're perceived completely differently. A user tolerates a long streamed answer and does not tolerate silence. It's often correct to accept a slower total in exchange for a faster start — retrieving fewer chunks, for instance, cuts prefill and improves the felt experience even if generation then runs longer.
diagram2:
Total budget 3.0s
  ├ query processing   100ms
  ├ retrieval          200ms
  ├ reranking          150ms
  ├ prefill → TTFT     400ms  ← budget separately
  └ streaming          remainder

Reranking at 150/3000 is not your problem,
however inefficient it looks.

Measure each stage in traces.
Total says there's a problem.
The breakdown says where.

means: The operational practice around LLM applications: versioning prompts and models, evaluating changes, monitoring quality and cost, and rolling back safely.
example: A team shipping prompt edits straight to production with no eval, no version history and no cost dashboard has an LLM demo. Adding those three makes it a product.
diagram:
version (prompt + model + retrieval config)
  ↓ evaluate offline against a golden set
  ↓ canary on live traffic
  ↓ monitor quality, latency, cost
  ↓ roll back as one unit

Prompt changes are deploys. Treat them like deploys.
how:
Traditional software is deterministic: the same input produces the same output, and a test either passes or fails. LLM systems break both assumptions. Output varies, quality is a distribution rather than a boolean, and the model underneath can change without you deploying anything.

LLMOps is the practice that adapts normal engineering discipline to that reality.

Concretely it means four things. Version everything that affects output — prompt, model, retrieval configuration, tool definitions — as one unit, because changing any of them changes behaviour. Evaluate changes against a fixed dataset rather than by trying a few examples. Monitor quality continuously, not just latency and errors. And be able to roll back the whole bundle.

None of it is exotic. It's the same discipline you already apply to code, extended to artifacts that don't look like code.
more: The mental shift that unlocks the rest is treating a prompt change as a deployment. Teams routinely let prompts be edited in a database by whoever noticed a problem, with no version history, no evaluation and no rollback — while the code path around it goes through review and CI. The prompt has more effect on output than most of that code.
diagram2:
One versioned bundle:
  prompt v14 + model claude-x-2026-03
            + retrieval config + tools

  ↓ eval against the golden set
  ↓ canary on a slice of traffic
  ↓ monitor quality, latency, cost
  ↓ roll back as ONE unit

Editing a prompt in prod with no version history
is a deploy with no CI, no review, no rollback.

means: Training small adapter matrices instead of all weights. Roughly 0.1% of the parameters, a fraction of the memory, and swappable at serve time.
example: Full fine-tuning a 13B model needs multiple high-memory GPUs. LoRA fits on one, produces a ~50MB adapter, and lets you host many task adapters over one base.
diagram:
full fine-tune: all ~13B weights, huge memory
LoRA: freeze base, train low-rank adapters
      ~0.1% of params, ~50MB artifact ✓
      swap adapters per tenant/task at serve time
how:
Fine-tuning normally updates every weight in the model. For a 13-billion-parameter model that means holding the weights, their gradients and optimiser state in memory at once — multiple high-memory GPUs for a modest task.

LoRA is based on an observation: the *change* fine-tuning makes tends to be low-rank, meaning it can be well approximated by a much smaller structure. So freeze the original weights entirely and train small matrices alongside them, whose product represents the update.

You end up training around 0.1% as many parameters. It fits on one GPU, trains in hours, and produces an artifact measured in tens of megabytes rather than tens of gigabytes.

The operational consequence is the interesting part: because the base is untouched, adapters can be swapped at serve time. One base model in memory, many task-specific behaviours.
more: That swapping property enables designs that would otherwise be impossible — a per-tenant or per-task adapter, selected per request, served from one loaded base model. Compare that with hosting a separate full fine-tune per tenant, which is prohibitive at almost any scale.
diagram2:
Full fine-tune: update all ~13B weights
  weights + gradients + optimiser state
  → multiple high-memory GPUs

LoRA: freeze the base, train small matrices
  → ~0.1% of parameters
  → one GPU, hours, ~50MB artifact ✓

Because the base is untouched:
  one base model in memory
  + adapter swapped per request
  → per-tenant behaviour, one deployment

means: Providers retire models on their schedule, not yours. Migration needs a rehearsed process, because the deadline is not negotiable.
example: A deprecation notice gave three months. Teams with pinned versions, an eval harness and a gateway migrated in a day; teams without spent the full quarter on it.
diagram:
deprecation notice → dated deadline
  ↓ eval current vs replacement on your set
  ↓ fix prompt regressions
  ↓ shadow, then canary, then cut over

A gateway + eval harness turns this
from a quarter into an afternoon
how:
Providers retire models on their schedule. You get notice, typically a few months, and then the model stops working whether or not you're ready.

The gap between teams is enormous and comes down entirely to what was in place beforehand.

A team with pinned versions, an evaluation set and a gateway runs the evaluation against the replacement, sees which cases regress, fixes those prompts, shadows briefly and cuts over — days, not weeks.

A team without those has no way to know whether the replacement is worse, no way to find which prompts break, and model identifiers scattered across several services. That team spends the entire notice period on it, and often ships a quality regression anyway because nobody could measure the difference.

The deadline is identical. The preparation isn't.
more: Treat it as routine dependency maintenance and do it early rather than at the deadline. Migrating with weeks of margin means a problem is an inconvenience; migrating in the final week means a problem is an incident. Same work, entirely different risk profile.
diagram2:
Deprecation notice → a fixed, non-negotiable date

Prepared:
  eval current vs replacement on your set
  fix the prompts that regress
  shadow briefly → canary → cut over
  → days

Unprepared:
  no way to measure the difference
  no way to find which prompts break
  model ids scattered across services
  → the whole notice period, and often
    a shipped regression nobody could detect

Migrate early. Same work, different risk.

means: A single internal service in front of every model provider, handling auth, routing, retries, fallback, caching, rate limits and cost accounting.
example: Without one, six services each hold provider keys, implement their own retries, and nobody can total the spend. A gateway makes all of that one implementation.
diagram:
services → gateway → provider A / B / self-hosted
             ├ auth + key management
             ├ routing + fallback
             ├ retries + rate limit handling
             ├ caching (exact + semantic)
             └ token accounting + cost attribution
how:
Once more than one service calls a model, the same concerns appear in each of them: authentication, retries, timeouts, fallback, rate limiting, caching, cost tracking. Implemented separately, they're implemented differently and inconsistently.

A gateway is one internal service every call goes through. Provider credentials live in one place. Retry and fallback logic is written once. Caching is shared across services rather than per-process. And every request is accounted for, so total spend is a query rather than an estimate.

The cost accounting alone often justifies it. Without a gateway you have a monthly invoice and no idea which feature caused it; with one you have cost per feature, per tenant, per model.

It also makes provider migration tractable — changing model or provider becomes a gateway configuration change rather than a coordinated deploy across six services.
more: Because everything routes through it, it's a single point of failure and needs treating as production infrastructure: health checks, its own capacity headroom, and a way to bypass it in an emergency. Keep it thin — routing, policy, accounting — and resist letting business logic accumulate in it, or every team ends up blocked on the gateway team.
diagram2:
services → gateway → provider A / B / self-hosted
             ├ credentials in one place
             ├ retries + fallback, written once
             ├ shared cache (not per-process)
             ├ rate limiting per tenant
             └ token accounting per feature

Without it: one invoice, no attribution.
With it:    cost per feature, per tenant.

It IS a SPOF — treat it as production infra.
Keep it thin. Business logic in it blocks everyone.

means: A catalogue of model versions with their training data, metrics, and deployment status. It's what makes 'which model produced this output?' answerable.
example: A support ticket about a bad answer from six weeks ago is untraceable unless you know exactly which model version, prompt version and index snapshot served it.
diagram:
registry entry:
  model id + version, base model, training data ref,
  eval scores, approver, deployed where, when

Every inference logs the version it used
how:
When someone reports a bad output from six weeks ago, the first question is what actually produced it. Without a registry that question has no answer.

A registry is a catalogue of every model version you've used or trained, with the metadata that makes it identifiable: base model, training data reference, evaluation scores, who approved it, where it's deployed, and when.

The half that makes it work is the other side — every inference logs which registry entry served it. A catalogue nobody references from production tells you what exists, not what happened.

With both halves you can answer the questions that matter during an incident: what changed, when, what did it score before it shipped, and what does rolling back mean in practice.
more: This matters more with self-hosted or fine-tuned models, where you own the artifact and its lineage. For third-party APIs a registry can be much lighter — the model version string plus your evaluation results for it is often enough. Don't build a training-grade registry for a system that only calls an API.
diagram2:
Registry entry:
  id + version · base model · training data ref
  eval scores · approver · deployed where · when

Production side:
  every inference logs the version it used

Together they answer:
  "what produced this bad output on 3 March?"
  "what did it score before we shipped it?"
  "what does rollback actually mean here?"

A catalogue nothing references is documentation.

means: Requesting a specific dated model version rather than a floating alias, so the provider updating the model doesn't silently change your product.
example: An app on a floating alias woke up to a new model with different formatting behaviour and a 9-point accuracy drop. Nothing in their repo had changed.
diagram:
floating alias → provider updates → your behaviour changes ✗
pinned version  → you control when you move ✓

Process: pin → new version released →
         eval both → migrate deliberately
how:
Providers offer two ways to name a model: a floating alias that always points at the current version, and a dated identifier that never changes.

The alias is convenient and it hands control of your product's behaviour to someone else's release schedule. When the provider ships an update, your output changes — formatting shifts, edge-case handling differs, accuracy moves in either direction — with no deploy on your side and nothing in your changelog to explain it.

Pinning to a dated version means the model is a dependency you upgrade deliberately, the same as any library.

The cost is that you must actually do the upgrades, because pinned versions eventually get deprecated. That's a real obligation, and it's still far better than being surprised.
more: Pinning is what makes evaluation meaningful. If the model can change underneath you, a score from last month describes a system that no longer exists, and you can't attribute a quality change to your own work. Pin first, then build the evaluation harness — in that order, or the harness measures noise.
diagram2:
Floating alias:
  provider ships an update
  → your output changes
  → no deploy, no changelog entry, no warning ✗

Pinned dated version:
  → you upgrade when you choose ✓
  → obligation: versions get deprecated,
    so you must actually do it

Pin BEFORE building evals.
Otherwise the eval measures the provider's
release schedule, not your changes.

means: Sending synthetic requests to a freshly started model server so weights are loaded and kernels compiled before real traffic arrives.
example: The first request after a self-hosted deploy took 14 seconds. A warmup step in the readiness probe meant the pod only accepted traffic once it was actually fast.
diagram:
pod starts → load weights → compile kernels
  ↓ warmup requests
  ↓ THEN mark ready ✓

Readiness that ignores warmup routes users
into the slow path
how:
A freshly started model server is not ready to serve well. Weights load from disk, CUDA kernels compile on first use, and memory allocators settle into their steady-state pattern.

The consequence is that the first request after a deploy can take many times longer than the steady-state latency. On a self-hosted deployment that can be ten seconds against a normal few hundred milliseconds.

The failure is in how readiness is usually wired. A readiness probe that only checks the process is listening marks the pod healthy immediately, the load balancer sends real traffic, and the first users get the slow path.

Warmup means sending synthetic requests representative of real ones — including realistic sequence lengths — and only reporting ready once they complete at normal speed.
more: This interacts badly with autoscaling. Scaling out under load adds instances that are slow exactly when the system is already stressed, so the new capacity initially makes things worse. Scale earlier than seems necessary, and keep warm headroom rather than provisioning at the moment of need.
diagram2:
pod starts
  ↓ load weights · compile kernels · settle memory
  ↓ warmup requests at realistic sequence lengths
  ↓ THEN report ready ✓

Readiness that only checks "is it listening":
  → traffic arrives immediately
  → first users get a 10s request

Interacts badly with autoscaling:
  new instances are slow exactly when
  the system is already stressed
  → scale early, keep warm headroom

means: Failing over to another provider or model when the primary errors, rate limits or times out. Provider outages are real and not rare.
example: A provider degradation took the primary path down for 40 minutes. Automatic fallback to a secondary meant elevated latency instead of a full feature outage.
diagram:
primary → 5xx / 429 / timeout
  ↓ retry with backoff
  ↓ still failing → secondary provider
  ↓ still failing → degraded mode / queue

Prompts must be portable enough to survive the switch
how:
Model providers have outages, degradations and capacity limits like any other service. If a single provider failing takes your feature down entirely, you've accepted their availability as your ceiling.

Fallback means detecting failure — errors, rate limits, timeouts — and routing to an alternative: another provider, a different model from the same provider, or a self-hosted deployment.

The requirement it imposes is prompt portability. A prompt heavily tuned to one model's quirks may perform noticeably worse elsewhere, so the fallback path needs its own evaluation rather than an assumption that it works.

Which means the fallback should be exercised regularly, not only during an incident. An untested fallback discovered to be broken during an outage is worse than none, because you planned around it.
more: Define what degraded looks like below the fallback. If both providers are unavailable, options include serving from cache, queueing the request for later, or returning a clear, honest error. Deciding this in advance is much better than discovering during an incident that the failure mode is an unhandled exception and a blank screen.
diagram2:
primary → 5xx / 429 / timeout
  ↓ retry with backoff
  ↓ still failing → secondary provider
  ↓ still failing → degraded mode

Degraded mode, decided IN ADVANCE:
  serve from cache · queue for later
  · honest error message

Requirements:
  prompts portable enough to survive the switch
  fallback path has its OWN eval
  exercised routinely, not only in incidents

An untested fallback is worse than none.

means: Images, audio and PDFs consume tokens on very different scales from text, and fail in different ways. Budget and validate them separately.
example: A single high-resolution image can cost as much as several pages of text. Downscaling to the minimum resolution that preserves legibility cut image spend substantially.
diagram:
image tokens ∝ resolution (tile count)
  ↓ downscale to the minimum legible size
  ↓ validate format, size and page count at the edge
  ↓ budget separately from text

A 20-page scanned PDF is not "one request"
how:
Images, audio and PDFs consume tokens on a completely different scale from text, and the relationship isn't obvious from file size.

Images are typically divided into tiles, and token cost scales with resolution. A single high-resolution photograph can cost as much as several pages of text. A twenty-page scanned PDF is not one request — it's twenty images, and it should be budgeted as such.

The most effective optimisation is downscaling to the smallest resolution at which the content is still legible. Sending a 4000-pixel-wide photograph of a receipt when 1200 pixels reads perfectly is paying several times over for nothing.

Validate at the edge too: format, dimensions, file size and page count, before anything reaches a model. A user uploading a 300-page PDF should get a clear rejection, not a large bill.
more: Failure modes differ from text as well. A corrupt image, an unsupported codec or a password-protected PDF fails in ways a text pipeline never encounters, and each needs a specific, comprehensible error. "Something went wrong" on a file upload is a support ticket; "this PDF is password-protected" is a user fixing it themselves.
diagram2:
Image tokens ∝ resolution (tile count),
not file size.

  4000px photo of a receipt  → expensive
  1200px, still legible      → a fraction ✓

A 20-page scanned PDF is 20 images,
not one request. Budget it that way.

Validate at the edge:
  format · dimensions · size · page count
  → reject a 300-page upload clearly,
    don't process it into a large bill

Give specific errors:
  "this PDF is password-protected" ✓

means: Offline evaluation scores a fixed dataset before shipping. Online measures real user outcomes after. Offline gates the deploy; online tells you the truth.
example: Offline accuracy rose 4 points and online thumbs-up fell. The golden set didn't contain the messy real queries users actually send — a sampling problem, not a model one.
diagram:
Offline: fixed set, fast, deterministic, pre-deploy
Online:  real traffic, real outcomes, post-deploy
         (thumbs, task completion, escalation rate)

Offline up + online down = your dataset is wrong
how:
Offline evaluation runs a fixed dataset before you ship. It's fast, repeatable, and cheap enough to run on every change — which is exactly what makes it a deployment gate.

Online evaluation measures what happens with real users afterwards: did they accept the answer, retry, escalate to support, complete the task. Slower, noisier, and the only thing that measures the outcome you actually care about.

They disagree more often than you'd expect, and the disagreement is informative rather than annoying.

Offline improving while online worsens almost always means your dataset doesn't represent real traffic — you've optimised for the cases you collected, which are usually the tidy ones. Offline flat while online improves usually means your scoring is missing something users notice, like tone or brevity.
more: The fix for a diverging dataset is to resample from production regularly rather than treating the golden set as permanent. Real usage shifts as the product grows, and a dataset built at launch describes a user population that has since changed. Refresh a portion of it on a schedule, keeping the historical cases as regression tests.
diagram2:
OFFLINE  fixed set · fast · gates the deploy
ONLINE   real users · slow · the actual outcome

When they disagree:
  offline ↑  online ↓
    → dataset doesn't match real traffic
    → resample from production

  offline flat  online ↑
    → your scoring misses what users value
    → fix the rubric

Refresh part of the set on a schedule.
Keep old cases as regressions.

means: Handling structurally invalid output deterministically — repair, re-ask with the validation error, then fail loudly — rather than letting a parse error surface as a 500.
example: Rather than crashing on malformed JSON, the pipeline attempts a repair, then re-asks once including the exact validation error, then fails with a clear message.
diagram:
parse → invalid?
  1. deterministic repair (trim fences, fix quotes)
  2. re-ask once, including the validator's error
  3. still invalid → fail loudly, log the raw output

Log every repair — a rising repair rate is a regression
how:
Even with constrained decoding, output sometimes fails validation — a value of the wrong type, a missing required field, a truncated response because the token limit was hit mid-object.

Without a defined path, this surfaces as an unhandled exception and a 500 for the user.

A repair ladder handles it deterministically. First, cheap mechanical fixes: strip markdown code fences, trim trailing commas, close an unterminated string. Second, re-ask once with the specific validation error included, since the model corrects readily when told exactly what was wrong. Third, if it still fails, fail loudly with the raw output logged.

Three defined steps, then a clean failure — not an exception propagating from a JSON parser three layers up.
more: Log every repair, and treat the repair rate as a quality metric. It should be low and stable; a sudden rise means something changed — a model update, a prompt edit, an input distribution shift. Because repairs succeed, this degradation is completely invisible unless you're counting them.
diagram2:
parse → invalid?
  1. mechanical repair
     strip ``` fences · trailing commas
     close unterminated strings
  2. re-ask ONCE, including the exact
     validation error
  3. still invalid → fail loudly, log raw output

Three steps, then a clean failure.
Not a parser exception three layers up.

Track the REPAIR RATE as a metric:
  it rises → model update, prompt edit,
             or input distribution shift
  invisible otherwise, because repairs succeed.

means: Detecting and removing personal data before it reaches a model, a log, or a training set. Once it's in a provider's logs, it's out of your control.
example: A support transcript with card details and phone numbers was being sent verbatim to a provider and stored in traces. Redaction at the boundary made it compliant.
diagram:
input → detect (regex + NER) → redact/tokenise
  ↓ model sees placeholders
  ↓ rehydrate in the response if needed

Redact in: prompts, traces, eval sets, training data
Test the detector — recall matters more than precision
how:
Anything you send to a provider may be logged on their side, retained under their policy, and is outside your control. Anything you store in your own traces is subject to your retention and access rules — and traces are usually the least governed data you have.

A redaction pipeline detects personal data and removes or replaces it before either happens.

Detection combines approaches: regular expressions for structured formats like card numbers, email addresses and national IDs; named entity recognition for names, addresses and organisations. Neither alone is sufficient — regex misses anything unstructured, NER misses formats it wasn't trained on.

Where the original value is needed in the response, tokenise rather than delete: replace with a placeholder, and substitute the real value back after generation.
more: Tune detection for recall over precision. Over-redacting degrades an answer; under-redacting is a compliance incident. And redact consistently across every path — prompts, trace logs, evaluation datasets, fine-tuning data. A carefully redacted prompt path is undone by an evaluation set built from raw production requests.
diagram2:
input → detect (regex + NER) → redact or tokenise
  ↓ the model sees placeholders
  ↓ substitute real values back after generation

Regex alone: misses unstructured PII
NER alone:   misses unusual formats
  → use both

Tune for RECALL:
  over-redact → a worse answer
  under-redact → a compliance incident

Redact on EVERY path:
  prompts · traces · eval sets · fine-tuning data

means: Reducing prompt tokens without losing the information that matters — trimming few-shot examples, summarising history, dropping low-value retrieved chunks.
example: Cutting from 12 retrieved chunks to 5 reranked ones removed 60% of input tokens and improved accuracy, because the model stopped drowning in near-misses.
diagram:
12 chunks → 5 reranked chunks
  tokens -60%, accuracy UP ✓

Also: trim few-shots once the format is learned,
      summarise old turns, drop redundant boilerplate
Measure quality after every cut
how:
Input tokens are paid on every request and dominate cost in most production systems, because the fixed preamble is far larger than anything the user types.

Compression is removing tokens that aren't earning their place. The candidates: few-shot examples the model no longer needs once the format is established, retrieved chunks beyond the genuinely relevant ones, verbose instructions that could be stated once, boilerplate repeated across sections, and conversation history that could be summarised.

The counterintuitive part is that this often improves quality rather than trading against it. Fewer, better-chosen chunks means less near-miss material for the model to get distracted by, and less content in the weak middle region of the context.

Cutting from forty retrieved chunks to five reranked ones is the canonical example: significantly cheaper and measurably more accurate.
more: Verify with your evaluation set after each cut rather than assuming. Compression is one of the few optimisations that can genuinely improve both cost and quality, and it can also quietly remove the one example that was carrying a difficult case. Cut, measure, keep or revert — one change at a time.
diagram2:
Candidates for removal:
  few-shot examples the model no longer needs
  retrieved chunks beyond the relevant ones
  verbose instructions · repeated boilerplate
  raw conversation history

40 chunks → 5 reranked
  tokens −60% · accuracy UP ✓
  (fewer near-misses to get distracted by,
   less content in the weak middle)

One cut at a time, eval after each.
It can also remove the example carrying a hard case.

means: A central store where prompts live with metadata, so they can be updated without a code deploy and reused across services consistently.
example: Three services each carrying their own copy of the classification prompt drift apart within a month. One registry entry, fetched and cached, keeps them identical.
diagram:
service A ┐
service B ├→ registry: "classify_intent" v7
service C ┘

Cache locally with a TTL — the registry
must not become a hard runtime dependency
how:
Once several services use the same prompt — a classifier, a summariser, an extraction template — copies drift. Someone improves one and the others keep the old version, and now the same task behaves differently depending on which service handled it.

A registry stores prompts centrally so all consumers read one definition, and so prompts can be updated without redeploying every service.

That second property is the main reason to adopt one, and it's also the risk. A registry the application calls on every request is a new hard dependency on the request path — if it's slow or down, so are you.

The standard mitigation is to fetch and cache locally with a TTL, and to ship a bundled fallback copy so a cold start with an unreachable registry still works.
more: Being able to change prompts without deploying is genuinely useful and quietly removes them from your review process. Keep the same controls you'd apply to code: an approval step, an evaluation run before publish, and version history. Otherwise you've built a way to change production behaviour with no review, which is exactly what it looks like at 6pm on a Friday.
diagram2:
service A ┐
service B ├→ registry: "classify_intent" v7
service C ┘

Solves: drift between copies,
        updating without a deploy

Risk: a hard dependency on the request path
Mitigation:
  fetch + cache with TTL
  bundle a fallback copy in the image
  never block a cold start on the registry

Keep approval + eval before publish.

means: Treating prompts as versioned artifacts with history, diffs and rollback, rather than strings edited in a database or hardcoded in a handler.
example: Quality dropped last Tuesday. Without prompt version history nobody can say what changed. With it, the diff is one line someone edited to fix a different bug.
diagram:
prompt v14 → v15 (one line changed)
  ↓ eval delta recorded
  ↓ deployed 12 Mar, rolled back 13 Mar

In git, or in a registry with the same guarantees
how:
A prompt determines output as directly as code does, and is usually treated with far less care — edited live, stored as a string in a config table, changed by whoever was debugging.

The consequence appears the first time quality drops. "It got worse sometime last week" is unanswerable without a history of what the prompt was and when it changed.

Versioning means every prompt change is recorded with a diff, a timestamp, an author, and ideally the evaluation delta it produced. You can see what changed, compare, and revert.

The simplest implementation that works is keeping prompts in the repository as files, so they inherit git history, review and rollback for free. Reach for a database-backed registry only when you specifically need to change prompts without deploying.
more: Version the prompt together with the model and retrieval settings, not separately. A prompt tuned for one model version can perform noticeably worse on another, so "prompt v14" alone is not a reproducible description of a system. What you want to be able to restore is the whole configuration, in one step.
diagram2:
"Quality dropped sometime last week"

No history:
  → nobody can say what changed ✗

With history:
  v14 → v15, 12 Mar, author, one line changed
  eval delta: -6 points on extraction
  → revert in one step ✓

Simplest thing that works:
  prompts as files in the repo
  → git gives you diff, review, blame, revert

Version prompt + model + retrieval as ONE unit.

means: Respecting the provider's per-minute token and request budgets, because ignoring them turns a load spike into a wall of 429s.
example: A batch job consumed the whole organisation's token budget and the interactive product started failing. Separate keys plus a client-side limiter fixed it.
diagram:
read Retry-After / rate limit headers
  ↓ client-side limiter BEFORE calling
  ↓ separate budgets: interactive vs batch
  ↓ queue and defer batch work

Never let background work starve the user-facing path
how:
Providers cap requests and tokens per minute per account. Cross the line and you get 429s, and if you retry naively you extend the throttling.

The first thing to get right is respecting the response. Rate limit headers tell you your remaining budget and when it resets; a Retry-After header tells you exactly how long to wait. Honouring those is more effective than any backoff you'd invent.

The second is limiting on your side before calling, so you shape traffic rather than discovering the limit by hitting it.

The third is the one that causes real incidents: separating workloads. Batch jobs and interactive requests share one account budget by default, so a backfill can consume the entire quota and take down the user-facing product while doing nothing wrong.
more: Use separate API keys or explicit budget allocations for interactive versus background work, and give background jobs a hard ceiling well below the total. Background work is by definition able to wait; users are not. Making that explicit in configuration is what stops a well-intentioned bulk job from becoming an outage.
diagram2:
Respect the response:
  rate limit headers → remaining budget, reset time
  Retry-After        → exactly how long to wait

Limit on YOUR side before calling.

The one that causes incidents:
  batch backfill + interactive traffic
  share one account quota
  → the backfill eats it → users get 429s ✗

Separate keys or explicit allocations.
Background work can wait. Users cannot.

means: Watching quality signals continuously, not only at deploy. Model behaviour, user input and retrieved data all shift underneath a system nobody changed.
example: A weekly automated eval run on a sampled slice of live traffic caught a 6-point drop three days after an upstream index change that no deploy accompanied.
diagram:
continuous signals:
  sampled auto-eval, groundedness scores,
  abstention rate, thumbs, escalation rate,
  retry rate, schema repair rate, latency, cost

Alert on trend, not on a single bad answer
how:
Standard monitoring tells you the system is up and responding. For an AI feature that's necessary and nowhere near sufficient — it can be fast, error-free and producing worse answers every week.

Quality monitoring watches signals that track output quality continuously rather than at deploy time.

The useful ones are mostly free. Abstention rate, refusal rate, retry rate, schema repair rate, thumbs-down rate, escalation to human support, and a groundedness score on a sample. Add an automated evaluation run on a slice of live traffic for a directly comparable number.

The reason this matters more than for conventional services is that AI systems degrade without deploys. A provider update, a corpus change or a shift in user behaviour moves quality with nothing changing on your side, and nothing in conventional monitoring would notice.
more: Alert on trends rather than individual outputs. One bad answer is noise; a groundedness score declining over ten days is a signal. Set the alerting window in days for slow-moving quality metrics, and keep the fast alerts for the operational signals — latency, errors, cost rate — where a spike genuinely is an incident.
diagram2:
Up, fast, no errors — and getting worse weekly.
Conventional monitoring shows all green.

Signals, mostly free:
  abstention rate · refusal rate · retry rate
  schema repair rate · thumbs-down · escalations
  + groundedness on a sample
  + scheduled eval on a live-traffic slice

Alert on TRENDS, in days:
  one bad answer                → noise
  groundedness down over 10 days → signal

Keep fast alerts for latency, errors, cost rate.

means: Deliberately attacking your own AI system to find failures before users or adversaries do — jailbreaks, injections, data extraction, harmful outputs.
example: A structured red team session found three prompts that made an internal assistant reveal another tenant's document titles. All three were retrieval filter bugs.
diagram:
attack surfaces:
  direct jailbreak, indirect injection via content,
  data extraction, tool misuse, cross-tenant leakage,
  cost exhaustion

Findings become permanent regression cases
how:
Red teaming is attacking your own system deliberately, before someone else does it accidentally or maliciously.

It differs from normal testing in intent. Testing checks the system does what it should. Red teaming checks it can't be made to do what it shouldn't, which requires actively trying rather than verifying.

The surfaces worth attacking on an AI system: direct jailbreaks in user input, indirect injection through fetched content, extraction of the system prompt or of data from other tenants, tool misuse to reach things the agent shouldn't, and cost exhaustion through requests engineered to be expensive.

The tenant isolation one deserves particular attention in a multi-tenant RAG system, because a successful attack there is a data breach rather than an embarrassment.
more: Every finding becomes a permanent regression case, which is what turns red teaming from an event into a capability. Run it on any significant change — new tools, a new model version, a prompt restructure — since each can reopen something previously closed. A one-off exercise before launch has a short shelf life.
diagram2:
Testing:    does it do what it should?
Red team:   can it be MADE to do what it shouldn't?

Surfaces:
  ├ direct jailbreak in user input
  ├ indirect injection via fetched content
  ├ system prompt extraction
  ├ cross-tenant data extraction  ← a breach
  ├ tool misuse beyond intended scope
  └ cost exhaustion by expensive requests

Every finding → a permanent regression case.
Re-run on new tools, new model, restructured prompt.

means: How often the system declines. Both directions are failures — over-refusal makes a product unusable, under-refusal makes it unsafe.
example: A support assistant refused 14% of legitimate billing questions because the safety prompt was too broad. The fix was narrowing the policy, not removing it.
diagram:
over-refusal:  blocks legitimate work,
               users route around the product
under-refusal: policy violations reach users

Track both. Sample refusals weekly and read them.
how:
Refusals are the flip side of abstention: cases where the system declines on policy grounds rather than for lack of information.

Both directions are failures, and teams typically only measure one.

Under-refusal is the one everyone watches, because a policy violation reaching a user is visible and embarrassing.

Over-refusal is invisible on a safety dashboard and often more damaging to the product. A support assistant that refuses a normal billing question because the policy prompt was written too broadly doesn't generate an incident report — it generates users who stop trusting the tool and route around it. That erosion is quiet and hard to reverse.

The fix for over-refusal is almost always narrowing the policy rather than removing it, which requires knowing which requests were refused and why.
more: Log every refusal with the triggering request and the reason, and read a sample weekly. Patterns emerge quickly: a keyword that's innocuous in your domain, a topic scoped too broadly, a phrasing that trips a classifier. Each is a small fix, and each recovers legitimate use you were silently losing.
diagram2:
UNDER-refusal → violations reach users
  visible · embarrassing · everyone measures it

OVER-refusal → legitimate work blocked
  invisible on a safety dashboard
  users quietly stop trusting the tool ✗

Support assistant refusing 14% of normal
billing questions files no incident report.

Log every refusal + request + reason.
Read a sample weekly.
The fix is narrowing the policy, not removing it.

means: A set of cases that previously broke and must never break again. It grows from real incidents rather than being written up front.
example: Every production bug becomes a test case. Six months in, the suite is 180 cases and it catches the reintroduction of an old failure before anyone sees it.
diagram:
production bug found
  ↓ minimal reproducing case added to the suite
  ↓ fixed
  ↓ suite runs on every prompt/model change

The suite is a record of everything you learned the hard way
how:
A golden set measures general quality. A regression suite is narrower and, in day-to-day work, more valuable: it's the set of things that have already broken once.

It grows from incidents rather than being designed. Every production bug — a malformed output, a wrong classification, a hallucinated field, a jailbreak that worked — gets reduced to a minimal reproducing case and added.

Six months in it's a couple of hundred cases, and it encodes everything the team learned the hard way. New engineers get that knowledge automatically, because the suite fails when they reintroduce an old mistake.

Its value is specifically that it catches reintroduction. Fixing a bug in a prompt is easy; keeping it fixed through fifty subsequent prompt edits is what the suite does.
more: Keep every case tied to the incident it came from — a link, a date, one line of context. Two years on, someone will find a case that seems to be asserting something arbitrary and will be tempted to delete it. The link is what stops them, and the case that looks arbitrary is usually the one guarding something subtle.
diagram2:
production bug
  ↓ minimal reproducing case
  ↓ added to the suite, with a link to the incident
  ↓ fixed
  ↓ runs on every prompt or model change forever

Fixing a bug: easy.
Keeping it fixed through 50 later edits: the suite.

Keep the incident link on every case.
The one that looks arbitrary in two years
is usually guarding something subtle.

means: On failure, changing something before retrying — rephrasing the query, widening retrieval, raising temperature — rather than sending the identical request again.
example: Retrieval returned nothing for a query with an internal acronym. Retrying identically would fail identically; expanding the acronym found the document.
diagram:
attempt 1 fails
  ↓ don't repeat verbatim
  ↓ expand acronyms, widen k, drop filters,
    try a different model
  ↓ attempt 2

Identical retry = identical failure, twice the cost
how:
Retrying an identical request against a deterministic failure produces an identical failure, at twice the cost.

Retrying without change makes sense for transient problems — a timeout, a rate limit, a 503. It makes no sense when the request itself was the problem.

Reformulation changes something before the second attempt. If retrieval returned nothing, expand acronyms, drop restrictive filters, widen the number of results, or rewrite the query. If output failed validation, include the specific error. If the model refused something legitimate, rephrase to clarify intent.

The distinction to encode in your retry logic is between transient failures, where the same request will eventually work, and deterministic ones, where it never will.
more: Cap reformulation attempts as tightly as ordinary retries, and log what was changed each time. Otherwise a request that fails for a good reason — the information genuinely isn't in your corpus — burns budget cycling through rewrites, when the correct outcome was to abstain after the first attempt.
diagram2:
Transient (timeout, 429, 503):
  → retry the SAME request with backoff ✓

Deterministic (empty retrieval, validation fail):
  → identical retry = identical failure,
    twice the cost ✗
  → change something:
      expand acronyms · drop filters
      widen k · rewrite the query
      include the validation error

Cap attempts. Log what changed.
Otherwise "not in the corpus" burns budget
cycling through rewrites instead of abstaining.

means: Defining explicit criteria before judging, so scores mean the same thing across runs and reviewers.
example: 'Is this answer good?' produces noise. 'Is every claim supported by the context? Is the format valid? Is anything material omitted?' produces three scores you can act on.
diagram:
Instead of one vague score:
  groundedness  0/1  ← every claim supported?
  completeness  0/1  ← anything material missing?
  format        0/1  ← schema valid?
  tone          0/1

Now a regression tells you WHICH dimension broke
how:
"Is this answer good?" is not a measurement, because good is doing several jobs at once. An answer can be accurate but badly formatted, or well-written but unsupported by the sources, and one number can't distinguish them.

A rubric names the dimensions in advance and scores each separately. Groundedness: is every claim supported by the provided context? Completeness: is anything material missing? Format: does it validate against the schema? Tone: does it match the product voice?

The immediate benefit is that a regression becomes diagnostic. A drop in one dimension tells you where to look. A drop in a single blended score tells you only that something happened.

The secondary benefit is that writing the rubric forces the team to agree what quality means, which is frequently the first time that conversation happens explicitly.
more: Keep each criterion binary or on a very short scale. "Groundedness 0 or 1" is answerable consistently; "groundedness out of 10" is not, and reviewers will silently use different scales. If a dimension genuinely needs nuance, split it into two binary questions instead of widening the scale.
diagram2:
Instead of one blended score:

  groundedness  0/1  every claim supported?
  completeness  0/1  anything material missing?
  format        0/1  schema valid?
  tone          0/1  matches product voice?

Regression in one dimension → you know where to look
Regression in a blended score → you know nothing

Keep criteria binary.
"Out of 10" means different things to each reviewer.
Need nuance? Two binary questions, not a wider scale.

means: A separate model or ruleset screening inputs and outputs, independent of the main model's instructions. Prompt instructions alone are not a control.
example: An output classifier caught a response containing personal data that the system prompt had explicitly forbidden. The instruction failed; the independent check didn't.
diagram:
input  → classifier → block / flag / allow
model
output → classifier → block / redact / allow

Independent of the model's own compliance.
Measure its false positive rate too.
how:
A safety classifier is a separate model or ruleset that inspects input before it reaches the main model, or output before it reaches the user.

The reason it must be separate is the same reason guardrails exist at all. Instructions inside a prompt are requests the model weighs against everything else in its context, including anything an attacker put there. A rule that can be argued with is not a control.

A classifier runs as code. It doesn't matter what the main model was persuaded to produce — the check happens afterwards, independently, and its verdict isn't negotiable.

Input classifiers catch prompt injection attempts, out-of-scope requests and disallowed topics. Output classifiers catch leaked personal data, policy violations and content that shouldn't ship regardless of what prompted it.
more: Measure the classifier's own error rates in both directions. A filter blocking every violation while also blocking a third of legitimate requests has broken the product, and the safety dashboard will look excellent because it only counts catches. False positive rate deserves the same attention as recall, and usually gets none.
diagram2:
input  → [ classifier ] → model → [ classifier ] → user
           ↑ runs as CODE, not as an instruction

The model can be talked out of its prompt.
It cannot be talked out of code that runs after it.

Input:  injection · out of scope · disallowed topics
Output: leaked PII · policy · unshippable content

Measure BOTH directions:
  violations caught (recall)
  legitimate requests blocked (false positives)
    ↑ the safety dashboard never shows this one

means: Temperature 0 and a fixed seed reduce variance but do not guarantee identical output across provider updates, batch composition or hardware.
example: An eval that assumed exact-match reproducibility went red on an infrastructure change with no model change. Scoring on semantic equivalence was the correct fix.
diagram:
temp 0 + seed → mostly reproducible
NOT guaranteed across: provider updates,
  batch composition, GPU/kernel differences

Evals should tolerate benign variance,
not assume byte-identical output
how:
Temperature 0 and a fixed seed reduce variation substantially. They do not guarantee identical output, and building on that assumption creates confusing failures.

Several things break exact reproducibility even with sampling fixed. Providers update models behind version identifiers. Floating-point arithmetic on GPUs is not associative, so results depend on the order operations complete. And in a batched server, output can vary with what else was in the batch.

The practical consequence is for evaluation. An exact-match test that passes for months can fail after an infrastructure change with no model change, and the investigation is unpleasant because nothing in your system changed.

Score on semantic equivalence or against a rubric rather than string equality, except where the output genuinely is a fixed structure.
more: Determinism is a debugging aid, not a correctness property. It makes reproducing an issue easier and it doesn't make the answer right — temperature 0 gives you the model's most likely output consistently, including consistently wrong. Don't let reproducibility stand in for accuracy in how you talk about the system.
diagram2:
temp 0 + fixed seed → mostly reproducible

NOT guaranteed across:
  provider model updates
  GPU floating-point ordering (non-associative)
  batch composition in a batched server

Consequence for evals:
  exact-match tests fail after an infra change
  with no model change — painful to investigate

Score on semantic equivalence or a rubric.
Determinism helps debugging. It is not accuracy.

means: Sampling several independent answers and taking the majority. It raises accuracy on reasoning tasks at a multiple of the cost.
example: Five samples with majority voting lifted accuracy on a multi-step task from 71% to 84%, for five times the tokens. Worth it for high-stakes, wasteful for classification.
diagram:
sample 5 answers independently
  ↓ majority vote / agreement check
accuracy 71% → 84%, cost ×5

Reserve for high-stakes, low-volume decisions.
Disagreement is itself a useful uncertainty signal.
how:
Sampling above temperature 0 means the same prompt can produce different answers. Self-consistency turns that into a signal instead of a nuisance.

Generate several independent answers to the same question, then take the majority. On multi-step reasoning this improves accuracy meaningfully, because there are many ways to reason incorrectly and comparatively few ways to reason correctly — errors scatter while correct answers converge.

The cost is linear in the number of samples. Five samples is five times the tokens and, unless parallelised, five times the latency.

That makes it a poor default and a good tool for specific situations: high-stakes decisions, low volume, and cases where being wrong is much more expensive than the extra tokens.
more: The disagreement itself is valuable independently of the vote. If five samples produce five different answers, the model is uncertain in a way no confidence score reported it — and that's a strong signal to abstain or escalate rather than to pick the plurality. Use spread as an uncertainty measure, not just as a way to choose.
diagram2:
Sample 5 answers independently → majority vote
  accuracy 71% → 84%
  cost and latency ×5

Works because errors scatter and
correct answers converge.

Not a default. Reserve for:
  high stakes · low volume ·
  wrong is much costlier than extra tokens

The DISAGREEMENT is its own signal:
  5 samples, 5 different answers
  → abstain or escalate, don't take the plurality

means: Classifying an incoming request by intent and dispatching it to the right model, prompt or tool — often with a tiny classifier rather than a large model.
example: A cheap embedding classifier routes 70% of traffic to a small model and only escalates genuinely complex requests. Cost fell sharply with no measurable quality loss.
diagram:
query → intent classifier (embedding / small model)
  ├ FAQ         → cached answer
  ├ simple      → small model
  ├ document Q  → RAG pipeline
  └ complex     → large model

The router itself must be fast and cheap
how:
If every request goes to your most capable model, you pay premium rates for work a much cheaper one handles perfectly. Routing classifies the request first and sends it where it belongs.

The classifier has to be cheap, or it consumes the saving. A large model deciding which model to use is self-defeating. What works is a small embedding model comparing the query against example intents, a lightweight trained classifier, or in simple cases a heuristic on length and request type.

Typical routing tiers: an exact or semantic cache hit costs nothing; simple classification and extraction go to a small model; standard requests to a mid tier; genuinely complex analysis to the largest.

An escalation path improves it further — try the cheap model, and promote to a larger one when confidence is low or validation fails.
more: The risk is quality regression concentrated in whatever gets routed cheaply, invisible in your aggregate metrics because most traffic is unaffected. Evaluate per route, not overall, and check specifically that the small-model path meets the bar on the cases actually sent to it.
diagram2:
query → cheap classifier (embedding / heuristic)
  ├ cache hit      → 0 cost
  ├ simple         → small model     1x
  ├ standard       → mid model       5x
  └ complex        → large model    20x

Escalation:
  small model → low confidence → retry on large ✓

The classifier must be cheap.
A large model choosing the model defeats the point.

Evaluate PER ROUTE. Aggregate metrics hide
a regression confined to the cheap path.

means: Running a candidate model on mirrored production traffic without serving its output, then comparing against the live one.
example: Two weeks of shadowed traffic showed the candidate matched on 94% of outputs and was better on the disagreements — evidence no offline eval could have produced.
diagram:
live traffic → current model → user ✓
             └→ candidate → discarded, logged
                     ↓ compare + sample the diffs

Watch: double the cost, and any tool
with side effects must be stubbed
how:
Offline evaluation runs a fixed dataset. Real traffic is messier — inputs you didn't anticipate, distributions your set doesn't represent, edge cases nobody wrote down.

Shadow deployment mirrors live requests to a candidate model while the current one continues serving users. The candidate's output is logged and discarded, never shown.

You get evidence from real traffic at zero user risk, and you can compare outputs directly on identical inputs — which offline evaluation can't give you, because it can't contain the requests you didn't know to include.

The essential precaution is side effects. If the candidate path can call tools that send, write or charge, mirroring the traffic mirrors the actions. Everything with an external effect must be stubbed before any traffic is shadowed.
more: Focus the review on disagreements rather than the aggregate. If the candidate matches the current model on 94% of requests, those tell you nothing. The 6% where they differ is the entire signal, and reading a sample of those is usually a faster and more convincing decision than any summary statistic.
diagram2:
live request → current model → user ✓
            └→ candidate    → logged, discarded

Real traffic, zero user risk,
direct comparison on identical inputs.

MUST stub first:
  anything that sends, writes, pays or deletes
  → mirroring traffic mirrors ACTIONS ✗

Cost: roughly double inference spend while running.

Review the DISAGREEMENTS.
94% agreement tells you nothing.
The 6% is the whole signal.

means: A hard cap that stops AI spend when a per-tenant or global budget is exceeded, so a runaway loop can't produce a five-figure surprise.
example: A bugged agent retried in a loop overnight. A per-tenant hourly ceiling capped the damage at a defined amount instead of an unbounded bill.
diagram:
track spend per tenant / feature / hour
  ↓ soft limit  → alert, degrade to a cheaper model
  ↓ hard limit  → reject with a clear error

Agents especially: cap steps, tokens AND wall time
how:
A bug in a normal service produces errors. A bug in an AI system can produce a bill.

The dangerous shape is a loop — an agent retrying a failing tool, a job reprocessing the same documents, a retry path with no cap. Each individual call is legitimate and small. Overnight, unattended, they accumulate into a number nobody budgeted for.

A spend breaker tracks cost per tenant, per feature and globally over a window, and enforces limits. A soft limit alerts and degrades to a cheaper model. A hard limit rejects requests outright with a clear error.

It's the same reasoning as a circuit breaker for a failing dependency — stop automatically, because by the time a human notices, the damage is done.
more: Agents need tighter caps than request-response features, because a single run can make many calls. Bound steps, tokens and wall-clock time per run in addition to the spend limit, so a loop terminates on whichever bound trips first. And alert on the rate of spend, not just the total — a sharp increase is actionable hours before the absolute number crosses any threshold.
diagram2:
Track spend per tenant / feature / hour

  soft limit → alert + degrade to a cheaper model
  hard limit → reject with a clear error

Agents need extra bounds per run:
  max steps · max tokens · max wall time
  → terminate on whichever trips first

Alert on the RATE, not the total.
A sharp rise is actionable hours before
the absolute number crosses anything.

means: Using a model to create training or evaluation examples when real labelled data is scarce. Fast, and it inherits the generator's blind spots.
example: Synthetic edge cases filled gaps in a sparse eval set. They also over-represented the phrasings the generator likes, so real samples had to be mixed in.
diagram:
real data (scarce) + synthetic (abundant)
  ↓
covers edge cases you have no examples of ✓
inherits the generator's biases and phrasing ✗

Always validate a sample against reality
how:
When real labelled examples are scarce — a new feature, a rare edge case, a document type you've seen twice — a model can generate plausible ones.

It's genuinely useful for coverage. You can produce a hundred variations of an edge case you've encountered once, and give your evaluation set representation it otherwise couldn't have.

The limitation is structural: generated data reflects the generator. It uses the phrasings that model tends to produce, contains the errors it tends to make, and misses the failure modes it doesn't know about. Train or evaluate purely on synthetic data and you're measuring against a simulation of reality shaped by the same technology you're testing.

Real data is messier in ways that matter — truncated inputs, mixed languages, formatting nobody would invent.
more: Use it to augment rather than replace, and keep enough real examples that they anchor the distribution. A useful check: score the same system on the synthetic portion and the real portion separately. A large gap means the synthetic set is easier than reality, and your headline number is optimistic.
diagram2:
Good for:
  edge-case coverage · rare document types
  bootstrapping a new feature with no history

Inherits from the generator:
  its phrasings · its blind spots · its errors

Augment, don't replace.

Diagnostic:
  score synthetic and real portions separately
  large gap → synthetic is easier than reality
           → your headline number is optimistic

means: Splitting a complex request into smaller model calls that can each be validated, rather than one prompt asked to do everything at once.
example: One prompt doing extraction, validation and summarisation scored 68%. Three chained calls, each individually checkable, scored 89% and were debuggable.
diagram:
one mega-prompt → 68%, unfixable when wrong
  ↓ decompose
extract → validate → summarise → 89% ✓
  each step independently testable

Cost: more calls, more latency, more orchestration
how:
A single prompt asked to extract, validate, summarise and format has four ways to fail and gives you one output to inspect. When it's wrong, you can't tell which part broke.

Decomposition splits it into separate calls with defined interfaces between them. Extract, then validate the extraction, then summarise the validated data.

Two things improve. Accuracy, because each call has a narrower job and the intermediate results can be checked before proceeding. And debuggability, because a failure is localised to a specific step with visible inputs and outputs.

The cost is more calls, more latency and orchestration to write. It's worth it when a single prompt has plateaued below the quality you need, and unnecessary when it's already meeting the bar.
more: Decomposition also lets you route each step independently — a small model for extraction, a large one for the reasoning step that actually needs it. That often recovers the extra cost of multiple calls and then some, while keeping the accuracy improvement.
diagram2:
One mega-prompt:
  extract + validate + summarise + format
  → 68% · one output · unfixable when wrong

Decomposed:
  extract → validate → summarise
  → 89% · each step checkable ✓

Cost: more calls, more latency, orchestration

Worth it when a single prompt has plateaued.
Unnecessary when it already meets the bar.

Route each step separately:
  small model to extract, large to reason
  → often recovers the extra cost

means: Recording input, output and cached tokens per request, tagged by feature, tenant and model, so cost can be attributed rather than guessed.
example: A single monthly provider invoice tells you nothing. Per-feature accounting showed one rarely used export feature was 40% of total spend.
diagram:
per request: in / out / cached tokens,
              model, feature, tenant, trace id
  ↓
cost per feature, per tenant, per user
  ↓
answers "is this feature worth its cost?"
how:
A monthly provider invoice is one number and tells you nothing you can act on. Token accounting is recording usage per request with enough context to attribute it.

What to record: input tokens, output tokens, cached tokens, the model, and tags for feature, tenant, user and trace ID.

With those you can answer the questions that drive decisions. Which feature costs the most. Which tenants are unprofitable. Whether prompt caching is actually working. Whether last week's prompt change moved the bill.

The pattern that shows up almost every time this gets instrumented is a surprise: some feature nobody thought about accounting for a large share of spend. Usually a background job, a retry path, or an internal tool nobody counted.
more: Instrument this on day one rather than when cost becomes a concern, because retrofitting attribution means you have no history to compare against. The natural place is the model gateway, where every call already passes through, so it's one implementation rather than one per service.
diagram2:
Per request, record:
  in / out / cached tokens
  model + version
  tags: feature · tenant · user · trace id

Now answerable:
  which feature costs most?
  which tenants are unprofitable?
  is prompt caching actually working?
  did last week's prompt change move the bill?

Almost every first instrumentation finds a surprise —
usually a background job or a retry path.

Do it at the gateway. One implementation.

means: Running model-invoked tools with the minimum permissions and strict resource limits, because the model's chosen arguments are untrusted input.
example: A code-execution tool without a sandbox is remote code execution with extra steps. Network denied, filesystem scoped, CPU and wall-clock capped, no credentials in scope.
diagram:
tool call args = UNTRUSTED user input
  ↓ validate against a schema
  ↓ execute with: no network (or allowlist),
    scoped fs, cpu/memory/time caps,
    no ambient credentials
  ↓ cap output size before it re-enters context
how:
A tool call's arguments are chosen by the model, and the model's context can be influenced by anyone whose text reaches it — a user, a fetched web page, a document. Those arguments are untrusted input in the strictest sense.

A code execution tool without a sandbox is remote code execution with a language model as the attacker's interface. But the principle applies to every tool: a database query tool without scoping is arbitrary data access, and a file tool without a path restriction is arbitrary file access.

Sandboxing means executing with the minimum required capability. No network, or an explicit allowlist. Filesystem scoped to a temporary directory. CPU, memory and wall-clock limits. No ambient credentials in the environment.

And cap the output size before it re-enters the context, or a tool returning a large response becomes both a cost problem and an injection vector.
more: Run tools with the permissions of the end user rather than the service. A tool that can read any record will eventually be talked into reading the wrong one, and no prompt instruction prevents that reliably. Enforcing authorisation at the tool boundary is what makes the failure a denied request instead of a data leak.
diagram2:
Tool arguments are chosen by the MODEL,
whose context can be influenced by anyone.
  → treat them exactly like anonymous form input

Execute with minimum capability:
  ├ no network, or an explicit allowlist
  ├ filesystem scoped to a temp directory
  ├ CPU / memory / wall-clock caps
  ├ no ambient credentials in the environment
  └ cap output size before it re-enters context

Run as the END USER, not as the service.
Then a bad call is a denied request, not a leak.

means: The features or preprocessing at training time differing from serving time. The model is fed something it never learned on, and quality drops for no visible reason.
example: Training normalised whitespace and lowercased; the serving path didn't. Accuracy was 8 points lower in production than in every offline test.
diagram:
training:  clean → normalise → embed
serving:   raw → embed          ← skew ✗

Fix: one shared preprocessing module,
     used by both paths, tested against both
how:
The model sees whatever your code feeds it. If the preprocessing at training time differs at all from the preprocessing at serving time, the model receives inputs subtly unlike anything it learned on.

The differences are usually small and boring — whitespace normalised in one path and not the other, a different truncation length, fields concatenated in a different order, lowercasing applied inconsistently. None of them look like bugs.

The symptom is a persistent gap between offline and production accuracy that resists explanation. Offline everything is clean, because the same script prepared training and evaluation data. In production a different code path builds the input.

It's one of the most common causes of "it worked in testing" in machine learning systems, and one of the easiest to prevent.
more: The structural fix is one shared preprocessing module, imported by both the training pipeline and the serving path, with tests asserting they produce identical output for the same input. Any design where the two paths are implemented separately will drift eventually, regardless of how carefully the first version was written.
diagram2:
training:  raw → normalise whitespace → lowercase → embed
serving:   raw → embed
                 ↑ skew ✗

Symptom:
  offline 91%, production 83%
  no explanation, resists debugging

Fix — structurally, not by discipline:
  one preprocessing module
  imported by BOTH paths
  + a test asserting identical output

Separate implementations always drift.

means: Rebuilding an index into a new namespace and switching reads only after verification, instead of mutating the live one.
example: Re-embedding 40M chunks in place left the index half old and half new for six hours, and retrieval quality was unpredictable throughout.
diagram:
build index_v2 alongside index_v1 (live)
  ↓ verify: doc count, spot checks, recall@k
  ↓ swap the read alias → v2
  ↓ keep v1 for instant rollback, then drop
how:
Some changes require rebuilding the whole index: a new embedding model, a different chunking strategy, a change to what metadata is stored.

The instinct is to update in place, document by document, since the pipeline already supports upserts. That produces a long window where the index is half old and half new — internally inconsistent, with unpredictable retrieval quality, for however many hours or days the reprocessing takes.

Blue-green avoids this. Build a completely separate index, populate and verify it while the live one keeps serving unchanged, and switch reads only when you're satisfied. If something's wrong, you switch back instantly, because the old index is still there.

The verification step matters as much as the swap. Document counts, spot checks on known queries, and recall measured against your evaluation set — before any user traffic reaches it.
more: Keep the old index for a defined period after the swap rather than deleting immediately. Retrieval regressions surface over days, not minutes — someone notices on Thursday that a particular kind of question stopped working. Instant rollback during that window is worth the storage cost, which is trivial by comparison.
diagram2:
✗ in-place: half old, half new, for hours
   internally inconsistent, quality unpredictable

✓ blue-green:
   build index_v2 alongside v1 (v1 still serving)
   verify: doc counts · spot checks · recall@k
   swap the read alias
   keep v1 for a defined window

Rollback = swap the alias back. Instant.

Regressions surface over days, not minutes.
Don't delete v1 on Monday.

means: Serving many requests through the GPU together. Continuous batching adds and removes sequences mid-flight instead of waiting for the slowest to finish.
example: Static batching makes a 20-token response wait for a 2,000-token one in the same batch. Continuous batching (vLLM, TGI) raises throughput several-fold.
diagram:
Static: batch starts together, ends together
  short requests wait for the longest ✗
Continuous: slots freed and refilled per step ✓

Throughput up, per-request latency roughly flat
how:
A GPU processing one request at a time is enormously underused, because decode leaves it waiting on memory most of the time. Batching runs several requests together so that idle time gets filled.

Naive (static) batching gathers a group, runs them together, and waits for all of them to finish before starting the next group. The flaw is obvious once you see it: a 20-token reply in a batch with a 2,000-token reply sits finished but stuck, holding its slot, until the long one completes.

Continuous batching fixes this by working at the level of individual generation steps. When a sequence finishes, its slot is freed immediately and a waiting request takes it. Nothing waits for anything unrelated.

This is not a small optimisation — it's often several times the throughput on identical hardware.
more: This is the main reason to use a purpose-built server like vLLM or TGI rather than writing your own loop around the model. Continuous batching, paged KV cache management and optimised kernels are difficult to implement well, and the gap between a hand-rolled server and a real one is large enough to change your hardware bill.
diagram2:
STATIC batching
  [short  ]▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓ idle, still holding a slot
  [long   ]█████████████████████
           └ everyone waits for the slowest

CONTINUOUS batching
  [short  ]  → done → slot freed → [new request]
  [long   ]█████████████████████
           └ slots refilled every step ✓

means: The maximum tokens a model can attend to in one request — prompt plus output together. Beyond it, content is truncated or the call errors.
example: An 8k context model given a 10k-token document sees only part of it. Your summary silently omits the beginning, and nothing warns you.
diagram:
context = system + history + retrieved + output

10,000-token doc, 8,000-token window
[2,000 dropped][8,000 visible]
Reserve room for the response too
how:
The context window is the total amount of text the model can consider at once. Everything shares that one budget: your system prompt, the conversation so far, any documents you retrieved, and the answer it's about to write.

The critical part people get wrong is that output comes out of the same budget. If the window is 128,000 tokens and your prompt is 127,000, there is almost no room left to reply.

The other thing to internalise: the model has no memory between calls. A chat that feels continuous is just your application re-sending the whole conversation every single time. That's why long conversations get slower and more expensive — you're resending more text on every turn.
more: Over the window and you get one of two behaviours, and which one depends on the provider: a hard error, or silent truncation. Silent truncation is far more dangerous, because your summary of a long document quietly omits the beginning and nothing anywhere tells you. Always count tokens before sending, and always reserve headroom for the response.
diagram2:
One request's budget:

[ system 2k ][ history 40k ][ retrieved 60k ][ reply 4k ]
                                              ↑ reserve this

Forget the reserve → answer truncated mid-sentence
Exceed the window  → error, or silent drop (worse)

means: Input and output tokens are priced differently, and output is usually several times more expensive. Cost modelling is an engineering task, not a finance one.
example: A 12k-token system prompt on 200k daily requests dominates the bill even though users only send 40 tokens. Prompt caching and trimming were the highest-leverage fix.
diagram:
cost = in_tokens×rate_in + out_tokens×rate_out
  output typically 3-5x input rate

Levers: cache the prefix, trim the prompt,
route to smaller models, cap max_tokens
how:
Two things surprise people about LLM pricing. Input and output are billed at different rates, with output usually several times more expensive per token. And the input cost is dominated by whatever you send every single time, not by what the user types.

That second point is the one that matters. If your system prompt, tool definitions and retrieved context total 12,000 tokens and the user sends 40, then 99.7% of your input cost has nothing to do with the user at all.

So the levers are not where intuition suggests. Shortening user-facing responses helps a little. Trimming the fixed preamble, caching the stable prefix, and retrieving five chunks instead of forty helps enormously.

Model choice is a lever too, but usually the last one to reach for rather than the first.
more: Get per-request cost logged with tags — feature, tenant, model — from the very first day. A single monthly invoice tells you nothing actionable. Tagged data routinely reveals that one rarely used feature accounts for a large share of spend, and that is a five-minute product decision rather than a month of optimisation work.
diagram2:
cost = input × rate_in + output × rate_out
                              ↑ often 3-5x rate_in

A typical request:
  system + tools + context  12,000 tokens
  user message                  40 tokens
  response                     300 tokens
                    ↑ 99.7% of input is fixed

Levers, in order of impact:
  cache the prefix · retrieve less · trim the preamble
  cap max_tokens · then consider a smaller model

means: A fixed set of inputs with known-good outputs, run on every prompt or model change. Without it you're shipping vibes.
example: A prompt tweak that looks better on three examples drops accuracy from 91% to 84% on the 200-case golden set. You only know because you measured.
diagram:
golden set (200 cases, human-labelled)
  ↓ run on every prompt/model change
  ↓ score: exact match, rubric, LLM-judge
  ↓ regression? → block the deploy

"It felt better" is not a result
how:
A golden set is a fixed collection of inputs paired with known-good outputs, plus a way to score how close an answer is.

Its purpose is to convert opinion into measurement. Without one, "does this prompt change help?" is settled by whoever tried three examples and liked the result. With one, it's a number, and you can compare two options honestly.

Building it well matters more than building it large. It should be drawn from real traffic rather than invented, and it must include the hard cases — the ambiguous inputs, the malformed documents, the questions with no answer in your corpus. A set of easy cases scores high and tells you nothing.

A hundred well-chosen cases beat a thousand convenient ones.
more: Scoring depends on the task. Extraction and classification can be exact-match. Open-ended answers need a rubric, a model-based judge, or human review of a sample. Whichever you use, the set should be versioned and frozen — if it changes at the same time as the prompt, you can no longer tell which caused the score to move.
diagram2:
100-200 cases, from real traffic:
  ├ typical requests        (the bulk)
  ├ known edge cases        (from incidents)
  ├ adversarial inputs      (injection, nonsense)
  └ unanswerable questions  (should abstain)

run on EVERY prompt or model change
  ↓
score moves → you know why
score moves and the set also changed → you don't

means: Quality degrading over time with no change on your side, because the upstream model, your data or user behaviour changed.
example: Accuracy was 91% at launch. Six weeks later, no deploys, it's 78% — the provider updated the model and your prompt no longer fits it.
diagram:
Week 1: 91%
Week 4: 83%
Week 6: 78%   ← you changed nothing

Pin model versions. Run evals on a schedule,
not just on deploy.
how:
Drift is your quality falling over time while your code stays exactly the same.
