  ├ invoice     → invoice extractor
  ├ contract    → clause extractor
  ├ receipt     → receipt extractor
  └ unknown / low confidence → human queue ✓
                               ↑ the part usually missing

Without the unknown branch:
  a delivery note gets invoice-extracted
  → confident, structured, wrong
  → and the bug looks like an extraction bug

means: Hand-labelled documents used to measure field-level accuracy. Without it, 'the OCR is good' is an opinion.
example: A 200-document labelled set showed total amount at 97% and vendor address at 71%. Effort went where the number was actually bad.
diagram:
200 docs, every field hand-labelled
  ↓ measure per field, not overall
  invoice_number  99%
  total_amount    97%
  vendor_address  71%  ← fix this one
how:
"The OCR is good" is an opinion until you have documents where a human has recorded the correct value for every field, and you can measure against them.

The measurement that matters is per field, not overall. An aggregate accuracy of 94% is nearly useless information — it averages the fields that work with the ones that don't, and hides which is which.

Broken out, the picture is usually lopsided and immediately actionable: invoice number at 99%, total at 97%, supplier address at 71%. Now you know exactly where the remaining effort goes, and that most of the pipeline is fine.

Building the set is genuine manual work — a couple of hundred documents, every field labelled by hand — and it's the work that makes every subsequent decision measurable rather than argued.
more: Sample it to match reality, not convenience. If a fifth of production input is phone photographs, a fifth of the ground truth set should be too. A set built from clean digital PDFs will report excellent accuracy and predict nothing about the documents your users actually send.
diagram2:
200 documents, every field labelled by hand

Aggregate: 94%   ← tells you nothing

Per field:
  invoice_number   99%  ✓
  total_amount     97%  ✓
  line_items       89%
  supplier_address 71%  ← all the effort goes here

Sample to match production:
  20% phone photos in reality
  → 20% phone photos in the set

means: Routing low-confidence extractions to people, and feeding their corrections back as training data.
example: 15% of documents route to review. Corrections become labelled examples, and the review rate falls over time as the model improves on real failures.
diagram:
extraction
  ├ high confidence → auto-approve (85%)
  └ low confidence  → review queue (15%)
                        ↓ corrections
                     training data → fewer reviews
how:
No extraction pipeline reaches 100%, so the question isn't whether humans are involved but how efficiently.

A review queue routes low-confidence or validation-failing extractions to people, while everything else passes automatically. That single split is what makes the economics work — if 85% auto-processes, human effort applies to the remaining 15% rather than to everything.

The design detail that determines throughput is what the reviewer sees. Presenting a form of extracted values requires them to read the whole document to verify. Presenting the values with each one highlighted on the page image lets them confirm at a glance.

The difference is roughly an order of magnitude in review time, which is usually the difference between the queue keeping up and the queue growing.
more: Corrections are training data, and capturing them closes the loop: today's review population becomes tomorrow's improvement, and the review rate declines over time. Track that rate as a headline metric — if it isn't falling, the loop isn't actually connected, and you've built a permanent manual process wearing an automation label.
diagram2:
extraction
  ├ high confidence + validations pass → auto (85%)
  └ low confidence or failed validation → queue (15%)

Reviewer interface decides throughput:
  form of values only
    → must read the whole document  ~60s/doc
  values + highlighted source regions
    → confirm at a glance             ~6s/doc

corrections → labelled data → fewer reviews

If the review rate isn't falling,
the feedback loop isn't connected.

means: Turning recognised text into structured fields. Template rules are exact and brittle; models generalise and hallucinate.
example: Template rules handled 6 known invoice vendors perfectly and failed on the 7th. An LLM handled all of them at 94% and occasionally invented a field.
diagram:
Template/regex: exact, brittle, per-vendor
Layout model:   generalises, needs training data
LLM on OCR text: flexible, can hallucinate
   ↓
Hybrid: LLM extract + validate against
        the OCR tokens actually present
how:
OCR gives you text. What you actually need is structured fields — invoice number, date, total — and getting from one to the other is its own problem.

Three approaches, with different failure characteristics.

Template rules match known layouts by position or regex. Exact and fast for a vendor you've configured, completely broken for a vendor you haven't. They scale linearly with the number of vendors, which stops working somewhere around a few dozen.

Layout models learn the visual relationship between labels and values, so they generalise to unseen layouts. They need training data.

An LLM over the OCR text handles arbitrary formats with no per-vendor work, and will occasionally invent a value that was never on the page.

That last failure mode is the one that determines the design.
more: The hybrid that works in practice: extract with a model, then verify every returned value actually appears among the OCR tokens, and check arithmetic where it exists — line items should sum to the total. That single validation step catches most fabrication, and turns "confidently wrong" into "flagged for review", which is a completely different operational problem.
diagram2:
Template rules   exact · brittle · per-vendor
Layout model     generalises · needs training data
LLM on OCR text  flexible · can invent values ✗

Hybrid that works:

  LLM extracts {"total": "4,500"}
    ↓ verify: does "4,500" exist in OCR tokens?
    ↓ verify: do line items sum to 4,500?
    ↓ fail either → route to review ✓

Turns silent fabrication into a flagged case.

means: Detecting the structure — columns, tables, headers, reading order — before extracting text. Skipping it scrambles multi-column documents.
example: A two-column contract read without layout analysis interleaves the columns line by line, producing text that is grammatically nonsense.
diagram:
raw OCR (no layout):
  "Term 1 ... Term 8 ... shall not ... liability"
   ↑ columns interleaved ✗

with layout: regions detected → correct reading order ✓
how:
Before recognising any characters, the system has to work out the geometry of the page: where the text blocks are, which are columns, what's a table, what's a header, and crucially what order a human would read them in.

Skip it and OCR reads strictly left to right across the full page width. On a two-column contract that interleaves the columns line by line, producing text that is grammatically incoherent — the words are all correct and the meaning is destroyed.

This failure is nastier than a recognition error because nothing looks wrong at the character level. Confidence scores are high. The text is real. It's just in an order that means nothing, and every downstream step inherits the damage.

Layout analysis segments the page into regions first, then recognises each region separately and reassembles in reading order.
more: It also supplies the structure downstream steps depend on. Knowing a region is a table means you can extract rows and columns rather than a stream of numbers. Knowing a line is a heading means you can chunk on it for retrieval. Layout is where a document stops being a picture of text and becomes a document.
diagram2:
Two-column page, no layout analysis:

  "Term 1. The parties  Term 8. Liability
   agree that...        shall not exceed..."
  read left-to-right across BOTH columns
  → "Term 1. The parties Term 8. Liability"
  → grammatically meaningless ✗

High confidence. Real words. Useless order.

With layout analysis:
  detect regions → recognise each → reassemble ✓
  and you learn what's a table, a heading, a footer

means: Per-character or per-word certainty from the engine. It's the routing signal for what needs human review.
example: Fields below 80% confidence go to a review queue; above 95% auto-approve. That single rule cut manual review volume by 70%.
diagram:
word "₹4,500" conf 0.42  → review queue
word "Invoice" conf 0.99  → accept

Route by confidence, don't treat all output equally
how:
OCR engines don't return text — they return text plus, for each word or character, a number expressing how certain the engine was.

Most pipelines discard that number, which throws away the most operationally useful signal in the whole system. Confidence is what lets you treat a clean typed invoice differently from a crumpled fax, automatically, without a human looking at either.

The pattern is threshold routing. Above a high threshold, accept automatically. Below a low one, send to human review. In between, apply validation rules — does the total match the line items, is the date plausible, does the invoice number match the expected format.

That single mechanism is usually what makes a document pipeline economically viable, because it concentrates human attention on the small fraction that needs it.
more: Set thresholds per field rather than per document, because their stakes differ. A misread supplier name is an inconvenience; a misread payment amount is a financial error. And calibrate against your own ground truth set — engine confidence values are not comparable across engines or even across versions, so an inherited threshold means nothing.
diagram2:
Per field, not per document:

  invoice_number  0.97  → auto-accept
  supplier_name   0.88  → accept, low stakes
  total_amount    0.71  → REVIEW, high stakes
  due_date        0.94  → validate format, accept

Typical outcome:
  85% auto-processed
  15% reviewed by a human
  → the economics of the whole pipeline

Calibrate thresholds on YOUR ground truth.

means: Processing pages independently to keep tail latency sane, then reassembling. The main scaling lever in document pipelines.
example: A 400-page PDF processed serially takes 9 minutes and blocks the queue. Fanned out across 20 workers, it finishes in 30 seconds.
diagram:
400-page PDF
  ↓ split into page jobs
  ↓ 20 workers in parallel
  ↓ reassemble by page number
9 min → 30 sec

Track partial failure per page, not per document
how:
Document processing is slow per page, and page count varies enormously — one invoice, or a four-hundred-page filing.

Processing serially means a single large document occupies a worker for minutes. Everything queued behind it waits, including hundreds of one-page documents that would each take under a second. That's head-of-line blocking, and it shows up as wildly unpredictable latency for users whose documents are small.

Because pages are independent for recognition, the fix is straightforward: split into per-page jobs, fan them out across workers, and reassemble by page number.

The step people miss is tracking failure per page rather than per document. One page that won't parse should not discard the other three hundred and ninety-nine that processed fine.
more: Some operations genuinely can't be parallelised — tables continuing across pages, or documents whose classification depends on the whole. Handle those in a reassembly pass after per-page work completes, rather than forcing the whole document through a serial path for the sake of the few operations that need it.
diagram2:
SERIAL
  [400-page filing ████████████ 9 min]
  [1pg][1pg][1pg]  ← all waiting behind it ✗

PARALLEL
  split into 400 page jobs
  → 20 workers → reassemble by page number
  → 30 seconds ✓

Track failure PER PAGE:
  page 187 fails → 399 pages still succeed
  → partial result + one page flagged

Cross-page work (tables, classification)
happens in a reassembly pass.

means: Recovering rows and columns from a visual grid. Merged cells, spanning headers and borderless tables are where it breaks.
example: A borderless table with a merged header cell shifted every value one column left. Nothing errored; the numbers were just quietly wrong.
diagram:
Hard cases:
  ├ borderless tables
  ├ merged / spanning cells
  ├ multi-line cells
  └ tables split across pages

Always validate: column count, totals row
how:
A table is a visual convention. Humans read alignment and spacing as structure; a computer sees a scatter of text at coordinates and has to infer the grid.

Bordered tables are relatively easy — detect the lines, and the cells are defined. Everything else is inference from alignment, and that's where it breaks.

The dangerous failure is not an error. A merged header cell spanning two columns, or a borderless table where one column is slightly ragged, can shift every value one column to the left. Nothing throws. The output is a well-formed table of numbers in the wrong fields, and it looks entirely plausible downstream.

That's why table extraction needs validation rather than trust: column counts, totals that should reconcile, values that should match their expected type.
more: Tables spanning pages are their own problem: the header appears once, and rows on later pages arrive with no column context. Handling that requires stitching continuation rows to the original header, which the extractor won't do for you. It's worth testing explicitly, because multi-page tables are common in exactly the documents that matter — financial statements and long invoices.
diagram2:
Where it breaks:
  ├ no borders — structure inferred from alignment
  ├ merged / spanning header cells
  ├ multi-line cells (is that a new row?)
  └ tables continuing across pages

The dangerous case:
  a merged header shifts every value one column left
  → no error, plausible-looking numbers, all wrong ✗

Always validate:
  expected column count · totals reconcile
  types per column · page-continuation stitching

means: Future, Queueable, Batch and Scheduled — different tools with different limits. Async transactions get roughly double the synchronous governor limits.
example: A callout in a trigger must be async. Queueable is generally preferred over @future: it takes objects, chains, and returns a trackable job ID.
diagram:
@future     simple, primitives only, no chaining
Queueable   objects, chainable, job ID ✓ default
Batch       50M+ records, chunked, stateful
Scheduled   cron

Async ≈ 2x the sync limits

means: Writing every trigger and method to handle collections rather than single records. Non-negotiable, because triggers fire in batches of up to 200.
example: A trigger querying inside a for-loop works for one record in testing and dies on a 200-record import. Query once outside, then map.

means: Sharing controls which records; FLS controls which fields. Apex doesn't enforce FLS automatically — you check it, or you leak field values.
example: A user without access to Salary__c sees it in a custom Lightning component because the Apex controller never checked. `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` or `stripInaccessible` fixes it.
diagram:
Sharing → which RECORDS
FLS/CRUD → which FIELDS + operations

SELECT ... WITH USER_MODE
Security.stripInaccessible(...)
Schema.sObjectType.X.isAccessible()

means: Hard per-transaction caps Salesforce enforces on a multi-tenant platform. Exceeding one throws an uncatchable exception and rolls back.
example: 100 SOQL queries and 150 DML statements per synchronous transaction. A query inside a loop over 200 records hits the limit and fails the whole operation.
diagram:
Per synchronous transaction:
  SOQL queries      100
  DML statements    150
  records retrieved 50,000
  CPU time          10s

Exceeded → LimitException, full rollback

means: External calls from Salesforce must respect callout limits, timeouts and the rule that a callout cannot follow uncommitted DML in the same transaction.
example: A trigger performing DML then a callout throws 'uncommitted work pending'. Publishing an event or enqueuing a Queueable separates them cleanly.
diagram:
DML then callout in one txn → exception ✗

trigger → Queueable / Platform Event
        → callout in a fresh transaction ✓

Limits: 100 callouts, 120s total per txn

means: You can't modify setup objects (User, Group) and standard objects in the same transaction. Very common in test setup.
example: A test creating a User and an Account together throws MixedDMLOperation. `System.runAs()` separates the two contexts.
diagram:
insert user;      ← setup object
insert account;   ← standard object
  → MixedDMLOperation ✗

System.runAs(someUser) { insert account; } ✓

means: Salesforce doesn't guarantee execution order between multiple triggers on the same object. One trigger delegating to a handler class is the standard pattern.
example: Three triggers on Account fire in an undefined order. Debugging why a field is overwritten becomes impossible until they're consolidated.
diagram:
AccountTrigger (the only one)
   ↓ delegates
AccountTriggerHandler
   ├ beforeInsert()
   ├ afterUpdate()
   └ ...
Explicit, testable, ordered

means: Salesforce's pub/sub event bus for decoupling internal logic and integrating with external systems, with its own delivery limits.
example: Instead of a trigger calling an external API synchronously, it publishes an event; a subscriber handles delivery. The transaction stops depending on an external system.
diagram:
publish event → event bus
  ├ Apex trigger subscriber
  ├ Flow subscriber
  └ external CometD/Pub-Sub API subscriber

Decoupled, replayable within the retention window

means: Apex runs in system context by default and ignores record sharing rules unless the class declares `with sharing`.
example: A controller declared `without sharing` returns records the running user should never see. It's a data-exposure bug that no test catches by default.
diagram:
with sharing    → enforce sharing rules ✓
without sharing → system context, sees everything
inherited sharing → inherit from the caller ✓

Default for controllers: with sharing

means: SOQL queries one object and its relationships with known filters. SOSL searches text across multiple objects at once.
example: 'Find all records mentioning Acme across Accounts, Contacts and Cases' is SOSL. 'All open opportunities for account X' is SOQL.
diagram:
SOQL: SELECT ... FROM Account WHERE ...
  one object + relationships, precise filters

SOSL: FIND 'Acme' IN ALL FIELDS
      RETURNING Account, Contact, Case
  full-text across many objects

means: Salesforce requires 75% Apex coverage to deploy to production. Coverage is a deployment gate, not evidence that anything is tested.
example: A test executing code with zero assertions passes and counts toward coverage. It gates the deploy and catches nothing.
diagram:
75% org-wide coverage to deploy
  ↓
Coverage ≠ correctness
Assert behaviour, test bulk (200 records),
test negative paths and limits

means: Trigger.new, Trigger.old, Trigger.newMap and the isInsert/isUpdate flags. Trigger.old doesn't exist on insert and Trigger.new doesn't on delete.
example: Reading Trigger.old in an insert context throws a null reference. Guard every branch with the correct context flags.
diagram:
insert: Trigger.new ✓  Trigger.old ✗ null
update: both ✓
delete: Trigger.old ✓  Trigger.new ✗ null

Always guard with isInsert / isUpdate / isDelete
